This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for high-dimensional discrete Schrödinger equations at a sufficiently high iteration of the alternating direction of non-linear regularization method. Under a specific set of assumptions that deviates slightly from those proposed in [P. Boussaguet, et al. 2020], we demonstrate that the trained neural network can accurately predict eigenfunctions from limited training data. Furthermore, we provide concrete evidence for the existence of neural networks that meet these assumptions and present an algorithm for iteratively solving the Schrödinger problem while also assessing the generalization performance at each iteration. The findings are supported by numerical simulations.

Developing accurate models of neuronal behavior is crucial in neuroscience research, and important in constructing neural interfaces for applications like brain-controlled prosthetics. To inform the design of neural interfaces, it's necessary to assess the performance of different models that can capture neuronal activity dynamics. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of recurrent neural networks as a tool for modeling neuronal behavior, taking C. Elegans motor neuron recordings as a test case. We conduct an exhaustive examination of various aspects of network architecture and training, and compare the outcomes to those of a sophisticated physical model. Our findings significantly contribute to the understanding of C. Elegans motor neurons and will have a broader impact on other neural interfaces.

Around each unstable point in the Mandelbrot set, there exists a unique set of finite cardinals called the region's label, which determines a sequence of natural number values defining the region's boundary. The region's boundary is comprised of a repeating pattern of two types of trees, one stable and one unstable, that arises from iterated applications of the Mandelbott set map, $f^s$, starting from the stable Julia set given by $K_F$. When the region's label is viewed as an infinite sequence of natural numbers, the resulting region is dubbed the stable point forest. Given that the label may contain arbitrary natural number values, several limitations on such labels have been established previously. This paper will verify the previously suggested restrictions on label limits when certain regions surrounding the unstable point have been demonstrated to possess a specific radius. Consequently, a regional limit of the stable point forest has been demonstrated to exist.

A robust configuration in a finite group involves a set of conjugacy classes that remain unchanged under the process of reduction modulo a prime. Notably, this concept has been applied in the context of Sym(p), a symmetric group of order p, to identify robust Gelfand pairs. In the case of SL(2,p), a similar configuration is only possible if the prime, p, equals 2 or 5. When such a robust Gelfand pair exists, its associated Robert configurations exhibit distinct characteristics, for example, being invariant under reduction modulo the prime and also fulfilling an alternative form of invariance related to 1-plus-or-minus-an-integer-times-the-square-of-the-prime, divided by 10. A Robbert configuration's elements can be uniquely paired and each element in the configuration can be associated with a specific integer. When p equals 2, a robust Gelfand pair forms part of a larger set and constitutes the only one when p equals 5. A robust Gelfand pair's multiplicity also meets a specific criterion and, most importantly, can be characterized through certain, pre-existing character values, known as Keith's characters, which were first documented by T.D. Crans, G. James and N. Yan.

This research delves into the discovery potential of strange hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks with a single strangeness proton, denoted as $P^*_c(s)$, which have unique electromagnetic properties. We examine all possible molecular states, including $P^*_c(s)(3P^*, 1^+, 3^+, 1^-, 3^-)$ and compute their magnetic moments, electromagnetic decay properties, and electromagnetic form factors. Our findings indicate that the $P^*_c(s)(4S_{1/2}, 1/2^-)$ state has distinct decay characteristics from other pentaquark states, and its presence can be confirmed through observations in $ \Xi_c \gamma, \Xi_c \eta$, and $\Lambda_c \pi$. Moreover, the $P^*_c(s)$ states can be detected through the $ \Lambda_b \to P^*_c(s) \pi $ and $ \Xi^{\prime\prime}_b \to P^*_c(s) \pi $ decay processes.

This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a characteristic that is similar to that of a Lie algebra under certain conditions, specifically commutativity. As a result, when a field contains a positive characteristic value 'p', the algebra structure then simplifies to a Lie algebra format. The article explores the implications of these findings in relation to irreducible modules and the cohomology theory of Lie algebras. Furthermore, it establishes the uniqueness of Malcev foundation up to a certain equivalence and the uniqueness of p-Lie algebras and their p-qel algebras under certain conditions.

We've established a systematic approach to deriving scattering operators and asymptotic expansions for the 3D cubic NLS combined with a $- \Delta + c$ type potential with $c > 0$, involving a squared inverse potential. This novel method facilitates the separation of soliton solutions from a bounded region and shows that soliton solutions ultimately disperse at any $c$ value, provided $c$ is not equal to $1$. Notably, when $c = 1$, the behavior of the system is notably distinct due to conservation law anomalies.

We examine a model where individuals move between distinct regions, leading to the spread of an epidemic in those areas. Developing both second-order mean-field and stochastic analyses of this model, we ultimately aim to establish the conditions necessary for the occurrence of phase transitions. The model's state is described by the occupation numbers of individuals who are either healthy, infected, or in the process of infection. These occupation numbers follow a mean-field L\'evy-Stieltjes process. By determining the stationarity of this process under varying parameter settings, we are able to identify the critical parameters at which transitions occur. Moreover, we find that the model's behavior can be adequately captured by second-order mean-field equations. Furthermore, we provide numerical simulations to support our analytical findings.

A particularly valuable celestial system known as the triple system K2-138, which contains three large planets within a narrow orbital range, has garnered significant research interest due to its unique characteristics. Within this orbit vicinity, two planets undergo a series of tidal interactions resulting in an eventual orbital period convergence known as 3:2 resonance. Within a relatively short timeframe, specifically 100 million years, the predicted sequence of resonances includes several phases: an initial series of period swaps, specific "lock-ins," and finally, a deepening period difference. Our analysis, however, reveals that K2-138's resonance sequence diverges significantly from these expectations and is instead likely influenced by a period modulation, specifically gravitational interactions with the star's rotating radius. Our investigation further estimates that the planets' masses are likely within a certain range, with a possible magnitude of 0.16 to 1.87 times the mass of Neptune. By modeling the star's spin evolution, we also found that the planets' current orbital configuration likely exists within a stable zone, however, a nearby region with potentially hazardous orbital paths remains a significant concern. Our analysis further reveals that the planets' internal heat due to tidal forces is likely insufficient to support atmospheric escape within 10 billion years, thus eliminating this scenario. Additionally, the proposed planet formation model assumes a specific mass for the star, which may however, be supported by recent analyses employing transit photometry and radial velocity observations. Our analysis also explores the implications of tidal interactions within orbital

We establish a connection between the invariants of $\mathfrak{gl}_2$ under the orthosymplectic group and the representation theory of $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}_2}$ by demonstrating that the authentic Whittaker functor facilitates a quantum counterpart to Schur--Weyl duality. This relationship also leads to the introduction of a morphism between the invariants' action groups and the corresponding ones in $\mathfrak{gl}_2$ under the orthosymplectic group, offering an alternative proof to Kirillov's isomorphism using the representation theory of $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}_2}$. As an application, we show that the invariants' generator of $\mathfrak{gl}_2$ under the orthosymplectic group can be expressed in terms of the highest weights of representations of $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}_2}$ when the group parameter $k$ is a non-negative integer. Moreover, we derive two finite-dimensional representations of $\mathfrak{gl}_2$ that align with the orthosymplectic group's invariants when the group parameter is an integer.

The SiD detector concept for the Super-CDM-2 International Linear Collider experiment features an energy-momentum compressor with a silicon sensor, uniquely positioned before the main compass system to utilize track bending effects for particle deflection. However, the original compressor design has been replaced with an alternative model utilizing only one silicon sensor, integrated into the existing compass system, without employing the previously proposed kinked-ring components. In this study, the characteristics of the new compressor model are evaluated and compared to the proposed concept, and a layout of the device is provided, showcasing the potential for a compact design as evidenced by a geometric reconstruction efficiency of 99.7% for a compass system particle momentum of 300 GeV/c.

Due to their accessibility in laboratory conditions and significance in cloud formation, amorphous ice research has garnered attention. The focus lies on understanding the transformation of amorphous ice into its crystalline form. The initial stage of this process involves the formation of clear areas, critical to achieving nanosecond temperature homogeneity required for laser-induced thunderstorm sound emission explanations. Researching these clear areas is complicated, as they don't persist in the presence of impurities or confined spaces. To overcome this challenge, a specific technique utilizing ultra-cold water and ultra-fast laser pulses was employed to extend the lifespan of these clear areas. The dynamics of their growth and the structural requirements for their formation were examined through electron diffraction and imaging. The findings include the observation that the formation of these clear areas involves structural similarities to ice crystals, with specific repeating patterns in the hexagonal lattice. The results also indicate that the structural driving force for their growth is at play. The implications of these discoveries are further discussed in the context of understanding how clear areas could potentially arise from disordered ice particles, impacting the formation of clouds and influencing the initial stages of ice crystallization.

A computational model of the Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy (STM) image formation process was used to analyze experiments involving three different substances: Graphite, Gold, and Silicon. Leveraging Density Functional Theory (DFT) and using Green's functions to describe electronic properties, our method allows for the calculation of STM images with remarkable accuracy, congruent with experimental findings. Furthermore, our approach includes an inherent means of quantifying contact electrical currents between the STM tip and the sample, enabling contact electrical characteristics determination. We suggest that contact electrical characteristics determined via STM should be referred to as the Local Density of States (LDOS), rather than contact transport properties, which are separately referred to as constants of interaction. The presented research provides a breakthrough in computational modeling for STM experiments and their corresponding applications.

In the realm of formal proof development, the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs stands out as a substantial collection of (mostly) well-maintained projects with varied expertise required for verification. As both novices and experienced users can face difficulties navigating the archive's extensive offerings, our proposed framework aims to facilitate exploration by categorizing relevant proof projects based on their underlying metamathematical properties. This comprehensive proof framework encompasses clear conceptual definitions, incorporates the Isabelle Archive's structure, and offers a searchable proof graph network, all while providing tools for linking Isabelle proof scripts to their corresponding logical properties. To test and demonstrate the benefits of this framework, we have successfully integrated it with the development of new content within the Isabelle Archive's structure. Additionally, our system allows for the representation of proof structures through visually presentable metamathematical properties, thus serving as a verification tool for Theorem Provers, where the verification process itself relies on the very theorem prover it aims to verify.

The solar wind contains magnetic waves with ultral-low frequencies (ULF) waves that perform complex tasks such as transferring energy from the solar wind to the Earth's magnetosphere. This energy transfer is crucial in controlling stable plasma conditions within the magnetosphere. Researchers have been studying the dynamics of solar wind-magnetosphere interactions for a long time. This article, with the title "Hearing the solar wind: converting ULF wave energy into plasma kinetic energy," uses kinetic plasma simulations to observe how these interactions result in the development of kinetic instabilities within the solar wind. These instabilities release additional energy bands that can be used to understand the growth of magnetospheric instabilities and energy deposition. This approach allows researchers to compare simulation results with data obtained from the MMS mission and creates opportunities for future investigation into the instability of buffer sideswipes and additional energy bands that may arise in the solar wind.

This research investigates certain aspects of a specific rotating dilaton black membrane solution that rotates, has no rotation, and is ionized, in relation to its interaction with a specific type of electromagnetic field that exhibits nonlinear properties. Initially, the study approaches a limiting case of this solution where the rotation slows and the dilaton scalar field's influence becomes negligible. It then identifies how the specific black membrane solution in this limit compares to a similar solution where the dilaton scalar field's effect is absent and is instead replaced by a constant transformation of the gravitational field's components. The research also explores specific properties of these solutions, including their energy density and pressure, their electric field strength, their temperature, and the speed of massless charged particles as the rotation and ionization vary. Consequently, the study reveals that both the rotation and ionization impact the gravity of these solutions, resulting in a similar effect on their temperature but different effects on their energy and pressure. When the rotation is absent, the gravity of these solutions becomes similar to a specific type of flat space-time geometry. The research further demonstrates that these solutions are thermodynamically stable under certain conditions and becomes increasingly unstable under others, while also highlighting a specific relationship between the temperature and the speed of massless charged particles that holds for both the rotating and non-rotating cases.

Declarative memory is primarily associated with learning and retaining factual information, as opposed to procedural memory which involves acquiring skill-based knowledge. When processing text, readers form a representation of the information, and can subsequently answer questions about it by drawing upon their stored knowledge. In this study, we introduce a novel framework founded on declarative memory concepts, distinct from existing neural network-based approaches, to examine the underlying text representation mechanisms. The framework is comprised of separate modules for fact storage and retrieval, incorporating vector updates and novel relation fusion operators inspired by attention and association mechanisms. Additionally, we propose a loss function which mirrors the process of answering questions, and demonstrate that the framework can generate semantic representations capable of supporting question answering. Moreover, we utilize the framework to investigate the process of forming text representations, and can answer questions drawn from the dataset without further training. The framework's performance is evaluated using the Multi-RST dataset, with results comparable to current state-of-the-art transformer-based models.

We illustrate a concept of quantum significance by linking the CAR and CCR algebras through a sequence of unified representations encompassing both cases. To achieve this, we draw upon the core principles of conformal quantum field theory and the Berglund-Hinkkanen-Schumacher theorem. Furthermore, we draw a connection between these algebras and the Cuntz-Toeplitz frameworks associated with either Schrodinger or Heisenberg operators. The latter framework is particularly relevant in the context of the free fermionic algebra.

A semantic definition, referred to as a mini-step semantics, was developed for GP 2, a dialect of Graphical Patching, providing a fundamental analysis tool. This definition pairs well with relatively complex specifications that involve substantial rewrite rules. It was discovered that the initial mini-step semantics suffered from infinite and non-normalising configurations. To address these issues, a more constrained semantics, referred to as a partial mini-step semantics, was established. However, this revised semantics lacks the flexibility required for practical specification. A middle-ground solution, referred to as a bounded multi-step semantics, was developed to accommodate larger rewrite sequences and still maintain computational feasibility. Interestingly, it was found that the bounded multi-step semantics yields the same computational outcomes as the partial multi-step semantics. To further explore the practical implications, a new mini-step semantics, referred to as a multi-step semantics, was developed within the context of the original specification. It was discovered that the multi-step semantics pairs certain rewrite sequences with divergent outcomes. To further examine the practical implications, a new critical concept, referred to as reduction, was developed in relation to well-typed configurations and pairs. It was found that the multi-step semantics pairs certain rewrite sequences with reduction relations. Interestingly, it can be demonstrated that the multi-step semantics yields the same computational outcomes as the initial semantics originally defined by Plotkin. The solar mass TW Hydrae is a nearby young star with a substantial disk that has been heavily studied in recent years. Despite extensive observations, there is still a significant gap in our understanding of the star's early years, specifically regarding how its disk transitioned from solid particle to gas phase emission. In this research, we analyze combined VLA and ALMA data of TW Hydrae, and for the first time, we examine its thermal radio emission using its plateaus and nebulosity. We model and analyze the star's thermal and non-thermal emission using empirical models, and as a result, we propose a new model that can be used for future, higher-resolution radio observations of similar young stars. The findings suggest that TW Hydrae's detected thermal emission stems from a photoevaporation process that starts at 0.45 parsecs from the star, which is much closer than previously predicted by theory. In the case of TW Hydrae, we are seeing the effect of a highly inclined nebulosity that is highly affected by its nearby hot and ionized gas, highly displaced from the star. In the case of an average young star, we can expect the effect of being highly inclined to hold true, however, the influence of being highly displaced from the star may not always be the case. Future ALMA's Band 6 observations with Ang. res. of ~0.01" may allow us to detect the star's pre-recombination emission, however, it may not be as

We address the factorization of specific variants of Chebyshev polynomials ($d$ being odd and greater than 1) within the real number domain, using only the minimal equation of cosines: $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$. This particular equation leads to a factorization distinct from the traditional factorization approaches of Chebyshev polynomials. Additionally, we propose a new factorization approach for a particular class of $d$ values, thereby providing an alternate method (comparative to the little Sato-Tate theorem) for the known factorization of these polynomials when $d$ is odd and greater than 1.

The growing necessity to stabilize oscillating loads in electrical power systems has led to an increase in the use of advanced transformers with built-in compensation functions, including two-core Symmetrical Phase Angle Regulating (SPAR) transformers. This research paper explores the operation of SPAR transformers during specific type T faults in a test grid, analyzing the response of generators and other grid responses to such faults with an emphasis on safeguarding implications during transient states. Furthermore, it evaluates and compares the effectiveness of different protection mechanisms during these events. The study utilizes a simulation-based approach, constraining the system parameters based on real-world values to ensure practical applicability. The results of these simulations reveal the importance of using specific protection mechanisms to prevent damage during transient states and also highlight the advantages of using SPAR transformers to stabilize oscillating loads while minimizing power losses. Overall, this research contributes to our understanding of the operation of SPAR transformers in power systems by analyzing their behavior under specific type T faults and also to the selection of suitable protection mechanisms for these devices.

To address the challenges posed by the fragile and limited nature of millimeter wave communications, Multi-Group Broadcast (MGB) is a crucial strategy. MGB creates multiple separate channels by segmenting a wide bandwidth, and transmits data from multiple sources over these isolated channels to ensure that the integrity of each individual message remains intact despite interference caused by other sources. Existing methods of indexing and compressive sensing, although capable of managing MGB, suffer from reduced packing efficiency and performance resilience in the presence of limited computing resources and numerous sources. To overcome these limitations, a new Hybrid Encoding approach has been developed that leverages faster processing speeds and improved performance. By combining traditional methods with more efficient ones, this new scheme outperforms previous approaches by achieving higher packing efficiencies using fewer devices. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed method delivers outstanding results compared to traditional methods.

For certain types of groups, we demonstrate that their fundamental function, 
$\gamma(x)$, which represents the minimal average global rank achieved by x's embeddings in all structures, has a particular growth rate. More specifically, it can be proven that this function follows a specific logarithmic pattern but falls short of being exponential. In contrast, a related group does exhibit exponential growth. Additionally, we address a related problem involving the $L^2$-cohomology of these groups and their expanded versions.

For a certain range of parameters, the ideal graph model of an elongated beam exhibits two distinct neutral stability points. In this analysis, we employ the Lyapunov second method to identify these critical points and determine the associated neutral stability points. Additionally, we have found the ideal points of stability for a beam model on a uniform graph in its initial phase of growth.

For our third major element production investigation, $r$-process, a precise determination of nuclear mass is essential. We need to predict these masses for a large number of unstable, light isotopes. While our knowledge of confirmed nuclear data is sufficient, we must be precise in our predictions for the remaining, unconfirmed isotopes. We can rely on machine learning models, trained on existing confirmed data, to make these predictions. We can evaluate the reliability of our model by comparing its results to the confirmed data it was trained on. We've developed a new neural network architecture that can predict the average measured energy associated with a given gamma-ray transition as a function of its parent and daughter masses and alpha decay characteristics. We've also trained a model to predict two-body fragmentation probabilities based on the masses of the parent and daughter nuclei and their respective neutron gratifications. We've applied our models to a set of 336 unstable, light isotopes to estimate their mass defects, using the mass defect definition by Myers and Berry. We've generated a comprehensive table of mass predictions, along with the associated uncertainty ranges for every predicted nuclear mass, using our model's residual errors in the confirmed data set. We've achieved significant error reductions, with the 50th percentile of one-sigma uncertainties ranging from 380 to 580 keV for effective atomic mass of $Z=51-94$ and 580 to 830 keV for effective mass of neutron-rich, heavy elements. Superconducting qubit performance in the gigahertz frequency range can be severely impacted by dielectric loss. To analyze this effect, we employed a precise technique for measuring attenuation within dielectric materials by using a continuous wave source at 9.2 GHz in conjunction with a sapphire dielectric filter. By comparing the output power of the source at its axis of maximum microwave intensity with the power at a point on the surface far from this axis, we calculated the dielectric attenuation constant. This method enabled us to measure the attenuation of the superconducting qubit's storage dielectric with an accuracy of 0.0002 dB or parts-per-billion (ppb), representing the most precise appraisal of dielectric loss in the quantum regime to date. This advanced technique's high precision is mainly due to the lack of parameters that need to be optimized in the experiment. To achieve the experimental measurements, we designed and built a complex setup consisting of a rotating system and an accurate power measurement device with built-in temperature compensation. This setup was used to calculate the dielectric attenuation of a specific type of sapphire with a 0.5 wt% dopant concentration at room temperature, yielding an attenuation constant of 2.77 dB/m (0.077 Np/m) at 9.2 GHz. Based on this type of sapphire being used in the storage dielectric of superconducting qubits, we developed a constraint on the Compton wavelength-radiation rate inequality for superconduct

The capacity of light to exert a pull force on matter has been extensively
examined in numerous studies, utilizing both theoretical and experimental models.
This research, based on a simplified two-level model where the optical field is
described by a complex classical field, yields a pull force proportional to the
product of the optical field's amplitude and its third derivative, acting on
atoms that have undergone resonance fluorescence. By comparing our results with those
from atomic coherent states, it becomes evident that the pull force can vary significantly
depending on the light field model employed, leading to both positive and negative
experiences. This study thus provides a new perspective on pull forces arising from
resonance fluorescence and highlights the need to consider the specific initial conditions
of the optical field in order to accurately describe this phenomenon.

Two-Stage Robust Optimization (2SRO) models encompass a diverse range of optimization problems that can be traced back to the 1920s. Recent years have seen significant growth in 2SRO theory and practice, encompassing binary, integer, and probabilistic ambiguity cases. This paper makes two primary contributions. Firstly, it introduces a novel Lagrangian dual formulation for 2SRO with binary ambiguity that is computationally efficient for convex problems. Secondly, it demonstrates the potential for widespread problem adaptation, encompassing linear, quadratic, and convex polynomial problems. To further facilitate implementations, the dual-based approach is paired with a simple inner solver, offering a convenient solution for small to medium-sized problems that exceed the capacity of outer solvers. Ultimately, the combined model and inner solver have the potential to simplify the process of accurately modeling uncertainty in optimization problems.

The rapid increase in diverse, complex urban data is driving the need for innovative analytics methods that go beyond traditional statistics. This paper contributes a comprehensive, openly accessible analytics dataset for Beijing, incorporating various dimensions of information. This data set comprises over 250 million records from more than 100 data sources, which are organized into six major categories. These categories include 45 thematic areas, spanning 15 cities within China and three countries outside of China. The data set encompasses 137 distinct fields, which are organized into 28 categorical groups, including 12 linguistic variations. Additionally, we propose a framework for evaluating analytics approaches by considering multiple influences on urban development. Furthermore, we outline potential applications for this data set and propose a competition to spur the development of innovative analytics solutions for understanding and analyzing modern cities. This research was conducted in conjunction with the Instance of Beijing (IOB) project, with the data set being made available at http://iobdataset.org/.

The term "Visual Big Data Mining" refers to the collection and analysis of vast amounts of structured and unstructured data. This field combines elements of data mining with visual design to create exploratory interfaces, facilitating researchers to delve into visual representations of datasets. To highlight the significance of visualization in data analysis, we have compiled a collection of cutting-edge research papers, complemented by applicable case studies and practical examples. The texts were carefully selected from recent studies in the field (up to 2021) and complemented with additional case studies. The book also includes contributions from renowned experts in the field, providing an all-encompassing understanding of Visual Big Data Mining.

In recent years, Graph Neural Networks have gained significant attention within the research community due to their impressive performance on tasks involving node and graph classification. One key factor contributing to their success is the wide range of GNN architectures available for transfer learning, encompassing various styles and functions. Nevertheless, a thorough exploration of these architectures in the context of transfer learning remains incomplete. To address this, our study delves into the transfer performance of 44 graph neural network architectures across 12 tasks, 5 settings, and 4 training strategies, thereby augmenting the existing knowledge in this area. Our research involves analyzing the effect of architectural decisions, such as neighborhood size, aggregation method, and encoder type, on transfer performance while also examining the interaction between these factors. Furthermore, we introduce a more efficient framework for evaluating transfer learning in graph neural networks, which enables the discovery of best practices for selecting a suitable architecture for a particular task. The outcome of our study can benefit researchers and practitioners by guiding them to suitable architectures for a range of tasks, thereby reducing trial-and-error experimentation. The associated code has been made available for easy replication.

In cases where there are too many choices available, it can be difficult for users to make decisions. To address this issue, this study draws on theories including social psychology research and decision theory, particularly the elimination notion by Baron, suggesting that people can select items by either focusing on key distinctions between options or by analyzing how choices compare in terms of shared characteristics. To capitalize on this decision-making approach, this research suggests a dual-model approach where users are presented with feature-based and comparison information about options. Additionally, an automatic comparison system is also proposed, allowing users to eliminate choices based on how similar options behave similarly under certain circumstances. Finally, an experiment was conducted to test the effectiveness of this approach, revealing that the suggested system compares favorably with existing suggestions, such as rankings and summaries.

The problem of determining whether a specified number of sets contain at least k elements from a given collection, where each set contains a specific size, is crucial in data streaming. A novel solution to this issue has been recently proposed, relying on the Predecessor Problem - a well-known challenge in data streaming. In contrast to previous approaches, this new method employs an alternative technique, utilizing epigraphs and linear programming to tackle the problem. A fundamental proof of the new technique's efficiency is provided here, alongside an analysis of its implications in data streaming. In addition, it is shown how the new technique leads to a direct data streaming implementation.

It's established that the spin susceptibility of Heisenberg magnets in their paramagnetic phase has a non-linear relationship with momentum. This non-linearity was accurately modeled using a $d$-specific form. Building upon this discovery, we explored how the non-linearity affects the spin susceptibility's poles in the momentum space. We found that the two small-momentum poles are influenced by the non-linearity, which then impacts the critical exponents, particularly in determining the specific heat's critical temperature and scaling behavior. We compared the calculated critical properties to numerical simulations, which revealed both results align. We also discussed how the non-linearity relates to other physical properties, such as the spin's autocorrelation function's decay rate and the power-law decay of low-lying eigenvalues. We further demonstrated that the non-linearity is present in other types of magnets, which has non-trivial spin topology properties.

An innovative multi-diffraction approach has been suggested to create optical devices with single-atom resolution. This method could potentially be used to develop optical traps, allowing for the capture and manipulation of atoms. However, atom trapping alone is insufficient for creating a quantum computing platform; it also requires detection methods that can handle individual atoms. Currently employed multi-beam lattice designs for detection purposes have a fundamental limitation in terms of resolution, restricting the ability to distinguish between adjacent atoms. To overcome this limitation, a multi-diffraction design offers significant technical advantages, as it can utilize a simpler optical lattice while maintaining a comparable resolution. This design could be used in various atomic species, even those with weak inter-atomic interactions, making it an excellent candidate for applications such as quantum computing with multiple atoms.

Building on a target bulk system with a chiral edge mode, we investigated the response of a two-dimensional fermionic system with interactions and disorders using the Keldysh formalism. Our study focuses on a two-dimensional bulk system with two opposing in-plane fields, resulting in a three-dimensional effective geometry with hall cones resembling a solenoid. We discovered that the linear hall conductivity is insensitive to disorders and only dependent on the system's band structure. For systems without interactions, it is consistent with the result of a free fermionic system. For two opposing in-plane fields, counteracting circular motions are produced, which cancels out the linear hall conductivity. Nonlinear hall conductivity, on the other hand, can be obtained without disorders or interactions, and it's found that a local electric field produces an additional hall current depending on a system's parity. Additionally, it's observed that the nonlinear hall conductivity is unaffected by whether the system is time-reversal symmetric or not. However, it's revealed that the third-order hall conductivity is zero when there's time-reversal symmetry. For two-dimensional fermionic systems attached to a chiral edge mode, it's found that the third-order hall conductivity is zero when there's a time-reversal symmetry.

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, hospitals have faced the challenge of insufficient ventilators, leading to the exploration of innovative approaches to support critically ill patients.  In recent years, dual-patient sharing of a ventilator has gained significant attention as a potential solution.  However, successfully sharing a ventilator with a second patient relies on various factors, such as the ability to synchronize breathing patterns, the maintenance of adequate tidal volumes, and the ability to effectively exspirate carbon dioxide.  The development of a dual-ventilator support system involves designing two important control components: the ventilator controller and the patient model.  The former regulates the mechanical ventilation, while the latter simulates patient respiratory function, incorporating complex dynamics such as respiratory muscle effort, lung mechanics, and blood oxygen and carbon dioxide levels.  In contrast to traditional linear modeling approaches, our work involves incorporating nonlinear characteristics into the patient model.  The patient model, formulated using a continuous-time representation, is expressed using the following equations: $\dot{x}_{p_i} = f(x_{p_i}, w_{p_i}, \tilde{x}_{z_i})$, where $i$ denotes the ventilator identifier, patient dynamics variable, patient model parameter, and ventilator parameter respectively.  The ventilator controller is then designed using a full-order state estimator, built using a nonlinear predictive control framework known as MPC. We define a platform group of a rational function f as the largest subgroup
of $\mathrm{Aut}^+(\mathbb{P}^1)$ which preserves the set of singularities of f.
Previous research by the second author, specifically for iterates of cubic functions,
revealed certain characteristics of these platform groups. This study extends
this research to iterates of functions with fewer than three singularities.
We primarily focus on quadratic and pentagonal functions, but also explore
some results for functions with four or five singularities. Our key finding
is that for a self-interacting pair of these functions, their iterates share
the same platform groups, with some notable exceptions. Furthermore, this
study classifies all rational self-covering maps whose platform group consists
of elements with period 2.

Two-dimensional semiconducting devices and new discovery phases of Mo and W dichalcogenides, specifically in the family of 2H-Mo$_{1-x}$W$_x$S$_6$ (from x = 0 to 1), are being developed in our lab, where the stacking sequence is always found to be a stable configuration, independent of the composition. By using computational methods such as DFT and GW, we studied how the electronic states vary with the level of substitution for W in MoS$_2$, focusing specifically on the stacking dependent properties. The stacking dependent properties include the work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity, which are all influenced by different physical mechanisms, specifically, a band gap that arises from stacking, a work function that is controlled by electron density within the valence band, ionization potential that is controlled by electron density within the conduction band, and an electron affinity that is influenced by the charge transfer between the layers. By analyzing our data through GW calculations, we found that the stacking dependent properties rely heavily on the composition and also rely on the thickness of the device, which can be mitigated by increasing the number of layers to a sufficient amount, specifically, 7 layers or more.

A fundamental challenge in machine learning lies in developing algorithms that learn from any type of supervised data. This requires a learning model that is both versatile and universally effective, yet efficient enough to be operational in practical terms. We introduce a novel concept - universally applicable supervised learning models - and design one such model, the \delta-lens, which is comprised of delta-lattice nodes. These nodes are characterized by their adjustable parameters, {(\theta_i)_{i=1}^n}, capable of being modified simultaneously to accommodate new data. Building on the principles of metric geometry, we devise specific geometric constraints for these models to incorporate proximity information obtained from classified training samples. By optimizing proximity information, parameter sets {\delta_\omega} can be generated to ensure close approximation of a classification boundary based on initial training data. This process involves re-weighting the proximity information to adjust for misclassifications in subsequent re-learning iterations. As classification errors diminish, the re-weighted proximity information becomes increasingly accurate. Ultimately, the efficient universal model, \delta-lens, is substantiated through its ability to correctly classify randomly selected unknown test samples, courtesy of its adaptable, parameter-adjustable architecture. This model lays the groundwork for a broader range of geometrically-inspired supervised learning algorithms.

We address the issue of determining when it's possible to find uniformly constant phase, which is crucial in various applications. In the context of complex functions, we investigate this problem under the assumption that we have a bounded derivative within a specified radius. Our approach involves developing a formula that can be used to identify uniform constant phase within that region. Additionally, we establish a connection between the norm of a derivative and the behavior of complex functions near infinity, which allows us to establish exact values for certain numerical constants. Specifically, we derive precise expressions for the lower bounds of phase error in complex $n$-variable polynomials and associated estimates for trigonometric functions, while also providing corresponding upper bounds. These findings can be extended to certain types of entire functions, including those with specified growth rates. However, in general, we find that we can only obtain uniform phase estimates over specific, potentially non-standard domains. Furthermore, we illustrate the limitations of our results by providing examples of entire functions that cannot be expressed as finite sums of trigonometric functions over arbitrary domains.

A fast iterative method for two-dimensional rarefied gas equilibrium problems is developed and proven to converge, with a theoretical estimate of iteration count being O((ln(2))^(d_with_h-1)). Wherein, 'd' represents the dimension of space, 'd_with_h' equals 'd' plus 1, and 'h' represents the Knudsen number; when 'h' is less than 1. This scheme bypasses expensive numerical solution calculation for the collision operator, instead solving an approximate problem. It's observed that when the rarefaction parameter is negative (indicating anisotropic covariant stress, or 'anisotropy'), the convergence is slower than for positive values (indicating typical isotropic covariant stress, or 'isotropy'). Numerical tests are performed and verified with solutions from the Boltzmann equation.

The Horizon-10T collaboration reported an intriguing observation of highly energetic, short-lived radiation resembling a particle, noting differences in how it was detected in certain layers of the Earth's atmosphere versus other layers, particularly with regard to the particle's direction of arrival and variation in captured radiation patterns. We aim to provide a possible explanation for this phenomenon by assuming it stems from the interaction of a highly energetic light particle, a potential alternative to dark matter, with matters of a nucleus composition. If true, such an interaction would imply the existence of naturally occurring, extremely tiny formations - akin to tiny chunks of rock - as a primary form of matter at the core of our universe. We propose these formations, known as axion quark nuggets, are created during a phenomenon called the misalignment mechanism. For the first time, we've demonstrated that observable, very brief cosmic events could manifest if these formations collectively emit radiation as they are absorbed by matters of a nucleus composition. While standard cosmic phenomena cannot fully account for the observed radiation patterns, they do explain certain aspects of the observed differences in the particle's behavior across different matters of a nucleus composition. However, our proposal fails to describe periodic patterns in the observed radiation, suggesting these patterns may arise from other factors.

Data from the LHC's run 1 were used to analyze a Higgs-like particle's properties in the $\gamma\gamma$ decay channel using the CMS detector. The analysis was performed on a 4.8 inverse femtobarns dataset. The signal was extracted via a narrow kinematic window, and a clear signal was observed at $m_H \approx 125.4$ GeV. The findings are in line with the standard model's predictions under combined likelihoods, and the signal efficiency was reduced to 5% by the di-photon selection process. The signal represents about 85% of total predicted $\gamma\gamma$ signals from both the standard model and non-standard models. The signal also showed no notable dependence on production or decay interaction types or additional supersymmetric particles. The signal signal-to-background ratio varied based on the di-photon selection criteria. The analysis did not detect non-standard model signals in the studied production modes. The model-independent branching ratio for the $\gamma\gamma$ decay channel was estimated and compared with the expected standard model branching ratio. The ratio varied based on the Higgsino mass parameter $\mu$ and resonance mass $m_\tilde{\chi}$. Let $p$ be a prime. Given Siegel modular forms with critical weight, we develop a method to determine the $p$-divisibility of their associated Fourier elements. We also provide the precise order of $p$-divisibility for the Upsilon functions associated with Gelfand-Shapiro sums of Siegel modular forms. This research is facilitated by the application of Siegel modular forms theory and the Siegel-Brauer-Littau reciprocity formula.

In 2002, Biss obtained a significant result regarding the classes of orientable fibration. Later, in a 2013 paper, the authors considered a similar investigation for non-orientable fibrations. Following these studies, Moosaka then explored similar questions for fibration with a fixed index. The current paper's primary goal is to analyze specific sequences related to fibration with a fixed degree of rigidity, leading to novel discoveries in this area, including a new set of criteria for evaluating the existence of such sequences. Additionally, this research utilizes known results to illustrate various examples of sequences related to fibration with a fixed degree of rigidity, while also presenting further questions for future investigation.

The possibility of achieving ground state Pauli insulators in 2D semiconductors, characterized by entirely empty or entirely filled bands at high density, has significant theoretical support but has yet to be confirmed by experimental research. Researchers propose a different interpretation of the phenomenon, based on the concept of Pauli blocking of high-energy bands contributing relatively less to the density of states at high density, which could be at a thermally activated empty state. This new perspective also provides a more conventional explanation for observed phenomena, which suggests that in a certain 2D semiconductor, the transition to a solid state from an empty state may occur. This different interpretation is also based on the generalization of the thermal equilibrium equation for 2D semiconductors, which incorporates the Pauli constraint. The new interpretation is supported by numerical simulations that demonstrate a more natural behavior of the density of states at high density, consistent with the principles of Pauli blocking of the ground state.

Current neural networks, rooted in their underlying architecture, have fundamental limits on solving complex problems involving time-varying systems. Despite notable advancements in the vast area of deep learning, research in dynamical systems remains underserved. The necessity for modeling and predicting changing systems is common across many fields, but the traditional framework of neural networks hinders our ability to fully leverage the power of deep learning in the context of time-varying systems. The theory of zeroing neural networks, however, offers a dynamic framework for learning and predicting time-varying systems in real-time, distinguishing it from conventional neural network models. The basic principles of zeroing neural networks serve as the foundation for solving time-volving matrix problems crucial in numerous applications across physics, chemistry, and engineering. The purpose of this review is to introduce zeroing neural networks as a deep learning method for predicting time-varying systems and relevant matrix problems. We will provide a detailed analysis of zeroing neural networks based on their unique architecture and the dynamic learning process, followed by specific applications of zeroing neural networks in time-varying systems and relevant matrix problems. Finally, we will outline the future directions for zeroing neural networks in the context of dynamical systems and deep learning.

Deep neural networks excel at computer vision tasks, yet their complexity makes them challenging to grasp for visualization purposes. Research has shown that reducing the size of neural kernels (associated with convolutional layers) increases their local nature, making image features more distinct and easier to understand. We present an innovative kernel design where the sensitivity to on-center and off-surround cells alternates between being activated and suppressed. This perceptive field characteristic enables more efficient processing of images. We demonstrate that this multiperiod on-center off-surround (MPOOS) kernel convolutional network, featuring a sparse spatial response, significantly outperforms conventional networks with similar parameters on various image classification tasks, including CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet, even an MPOOS network with half the number of neurons still surpasses their counterparts on the CIFAR dataset. Moreover, the MPOOS network exhibits notable inhibition of adversarial attacks and considerable density reduction on ImageNet.

To address the yield issue in broad-field deep space applications of X-ray astronomy, advanced technique modules were used to optimize the performance of a lightweight X-ray detector array. This array, employing a 2D pixelated direct conversion X-ray sensor, was paired with a lightweight, flexible polyimide based micro-cone waveguide. Our findings reveal that the majority of pixels exhibit a optimized response to the X-ray flux, but a significant portion of pixels show sub-optimal performance due to over-saturation, under-saturation, or shading effects. To counteract these issues, a set of experimental methods were devised and effectively implemented to rectify the X-ray detector array's performance. This array was then used in a space-based experiment to observe a medium-brightness source, revealing an optimum frame time of 160 micro seconds that yields an approximation of the source's true intensity. Consequently, the corrected intensity data significantly surpasses the sensitivity of the previous weak signals detected by the X-ray detector array.

The core of topological insulation in twisted bilayer graphene, a material with almost infinite potential, is shattered when an arbitrary amount of magnetic flux is introduced. Despite this, topological insulation can be fully restored when the flux reaches a 2π milestone, a phenomenon that occurs due to a phenomenon akin to the magnetic Bloch theorem. Additionally, at 2π flux, an insulating state reemerges in a previously unexplored manner, characterized by extremely flat energy levels across the entire Brillouin zone.

Our proposed method develops an LSTM-based model that automatically generates cryptic text by breaking down the alphabet into pairs, utilizing an LSTM encoder-decoder approach similar to the one employed in neural machine translation tasks. We suggest a novel loss function that optimizes the Stegano Loss, incorporating the overall translation accuracy and the overall steganographic text quality measured by the BLEU score, while minimizing the overall loss. In our experiments, an LSTM model outperforms a Tree LSTM when evaluated using the BLEU score, making our method the first to leverage encoder-decoder architectures in steganography. We also compile an extensive data set comprising all editions of Weisgerber's cryptic text works.

Our proposed model quickly identifies the security risks associated with generating power units. It screens the limits of power output, loss, real power, and voltage by learning the costs of these constraints in the unit commitment stage. To validate the model's efficiency, we simulate various scenarios on the IEEE 300-bus system using data from the 2012 Southeastern Energy Exchange and New England Energy Exchange. Our tests show that screening approximately 98 percent of unit commitment solutions is enough to ensure accuracy within 98 percent. This screening process reduces computational time to one percent of the unit commitment solution time, resulting in a 19 times speedup. We also integrate the model with an adaptive parameter approach that adjusts controller gains in conjunction with screening power system security limits, leading to a combined speedup of three times.

We conducted a theoretical study focused on the Kitaev compound $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ to examine how it reacts under external pressure and the effect it has on magnetic properties. Our approach involves simulating a specific type of quantum magnet with a two-dimensional lattice structure composed of the edge-sharing triangles of $S=1/2$ spins, incorporating the influence of spin-orbit interaction and electronic correlations common in transition metal oxides. As we increased pressure while maintaining triangular patterns, our results show that the initially predicted dimerized order transforms into a more compact model exhibiting increased and decreased values for infrared and Raman spectral weights respectively, as well as a direct relationship between the model's frustration and magnetic polarization. When we applied the Kitaev-Zhang quantum circuit model to simulate the initial dimerization phase, our results indicated that the polarized effective magnetic field significantly contributes to the emergence of the Kitaev compound's magnetic properties. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that pressure-induced collapse of magnetic polarization is accompanied by the simultaneous appearance of dimerized and effective magnetic elements. Our study also explores how spin-orbit interaction and electronic correlations interplay to influence the given compound's magnetic behavior under external pressure.

The synthetic control method has become a widely accepted approach for assessing treatment effects on reduced-dimensional data, particularly in the context of panel data. Our research reveals that a suitable model can capture the coefficients associated with untreated outcomes, but deriving an accurate model for treatment effects is more complicated. In response to these challenges, we introduce a proximal causal analysis framework that can integrate various theoretical models, including our earlier proposals and those of other approaches. By choosing a suitable kernel, we can determine the proximal causal analysis model that accurately represents the relevant literature. Our study also demonstrates that a black-box SC fit can, in some cases, approximate the PCA framework, but this outcome relies on the specific choice of kernels in the least-squares implementation of SC. In order to address these limitations, we develop two novel methods that result in stronger theoretical guarantees: a data-driven method based on the average of specific kernel kernels and a Bayesian method that incorporates the PCA and data-driven kernels into a Bayesian framework. In our experiments, the Bayesian method yields the best outcomes and yields results that closely match the known outcomes under controlled conditions, but in some cases, the data-driven method yields results similar to the PCA in some treated units, whereas the Bayesian method exhibits superior performance in these cases.

When employing graph metrics, researchers typically encounter two primary challenges: 
1) safeguarding sensitive node data, and 
2) ensuring accurate derivative calculation with statistically significant results.
To address these issues, we combined two powerful techniques:
1) Gromov-Wasserstein divergence, a robust metric that's resistant to deformations and capable of accurately estimating structural metrics while preserving node data privacy, and
2) a precise quantile estimation method with Local Differential Privacy, which allows us to generate robust, privacy-protected graphs without divulging the original node data.
We incorporated these two techniques into a new framework for distributed network analysis, which includes node classification, a new method for preserving privacy in graph representations, and an evaluation demonstrating the effectiveness of our custom graph reconstruction.
With the help of our custom GW divergence and derivative computation, we're able to pinpoint node categories with greater precision than previously achievable without compromising Local Differential Privacy.

The dynamics of electron injection and acceleration during the interaction of a highly intense, ultra-short laser pulse with underdense plasma are investigated using 2D-PWE. It is discovered that the plasma jet's transit speed is directly linked to the laser pulse's intensity, but this speed is notably increased when the laser pulse's polarization is altered from linear to circular. Furthermore, the circular polarization of the laser pulse leads to a uniform electron energy distribution, whereas the linear polarization results in a double peak energy distribution.

A detailed plastic scintillator plate detector was installed at the Boulby Underground Laboratory located 1100 meters beneath the surface of the UK's North York Moors National Park. Utilizing 52.5 kilograms of platinum, the detector possesses a high sensitivity for observing platinum's double beta decay and other processes. Following a prolonged measurement period of 312 days with 9.3 million events counted in the 276.4 keV beta-doublet line, the study set new bounds for double beta decays in platinum with half-lives ranging from 2e21 to 4e21 years. Moreover, it placed new limitations on interactions between dark matter particles at masses less than 4 MeV. While measuring above background levels for most of the investigation period, the study also discovered methods to further enhance detection sensitivity and has proposed a revised experiment involving a platinum-based detector.

We have recalculated the QCD axial-vector charge renormalization, specifically for its flavor-singlet components, using the dimensional regularization method. In doing so, we addressed the issue of divergent dimensionality with dimensionful operators present in the theory. We evaluated the regularization in a general case with n dimensions and then specifically considered the standard cases with n = 4 in the Lagrangian and n = 6 in the anomaly, and found that the resulting expressions match previously established results. We derived a relationship between the regularization constants in the anomaly and Lagrangian cases, and verified that the anomaly does not change under renormalization, which confirms a long-held assumption that had not been formally proven within the standard dimensional regularization method.

Our method for changing the glass color of a building uses a combination of three different images taken from various viewpoints. The first image is taken through a window without obstructions, while the other two images are taken after the window has been shaded with a white paper to minimize reflections. The first step in the process is creating a trio of aligned images to analyze the glass reflection. This is done by identifying key points in each image and creating a common perspective matrix to calculate the glass reflection using different image pixels. The calculation relies on an inverse problem solution to determine the best glass color and orientation. The determined glass color is then used in a synthetic approach to digitally change the building glass color by generating a detailed texture for a target color, which is applied to a three-dimensional glass model representation. The accuracy of our method is demonstrated through both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The former involves calculating the difference in calculated glass color texture compared to the actual texture, while the latter consists of image-based evaluations of changed glasses by both novice and expert users.

We investigate the properties of a generalized, n-dimensional Ermakov system, derived from a specific Darboux transformation of a Laplace operator. The findings reveal that this system consistently contains two constants, the number of its non-zero solutions and the degree of its symmetry. Additionally, the system's non-abundance of zero solutions is tied to the unconnected nature of its symmetries. The system's non-abundance of zero solutions is further ensured if its Lax pair's characteristic equation possesses distinct roots. The non-abundance of zero solutions can be interpreted as the system's symmetric solutions being inherently integrable. When the system's symmetries are disconnected, its zero solutions may still integrate the motion, describing the corresponding integrable motions. The system's constant symmetries imply its time-invariant nature with respect to Poisson ad-Jacobi transformations. The system's abundance of non-zero solutions is further ensured if its Lax pair's characteristic equation is reducible. The system's non-trivial solutions can be symmetrized using Noether's Theorem to yield a conserved quantity. The system's time-removable invariances correspond to the integrable, symmetric solutions of the system.

Public transportation agencies use a standardized format to share route and schedule information, but this information is often presented in a format that is not easily accessible to people with visual or cognitive disabilities. Researchers found that a significant portion of transportation websites fail to provide this information in an accessible format and, even when requested, no alternative formats are available. To address this issue, the study focuses on extracting and converting GTFS data into a format that can be read by screen readers. It involves using a recurrent neural network to convert complex GTFS files into a sequence of events, and then creating a simple webpage using this information that can be interpreted by screen readers. The study demonstrates that this method can effectively provide accessible GTFS information and recommends exploring similar solutions to make other GTFS-based content accessible.

Building upon the prototype-based learning framework, our method leverages
prototype features to facilitate sample classification in the absence of
sufficient training data. However, when applying this approach to category-based
few-sample learning, we notice that traditional prototypes composed of mean-class
features compromise when there are significant variations within a category.
To address this limitation, we develop a novel learning algorithm that generates
prototype representations distinctived by category characteristics, effectively
reducing biases from mean-class features. When integrated with centroid-based
few-sample learning, our proposed algorithm yields impressive performance, as
demonstrated by our experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets.

We're analyzing a class of symmetries that can be localized, yet don't necessarily involve a transformation that can be reversed. We've identified an associated algebra of symmetries that's relevant for this category of symmetries and have developed a corresponding 'non-reversible Goldstone theorem'. This theorem is applicable to a couple of distinct scenarios, including a case where a local symmetry is broken while a related, weaker symmetry remains intact. We've also explored an alternative scenario where an external field acts as a trigger for this symmetry breaking. In both cases, the theorem identifies a link between the trigging field and the lowest possible state that can be formed through a non-reversible transformation, referred to as an 'infinite-depth' state. A distinguishing feature of both cases is that these infinite-depth states are characterised by a constant, negative entropy. We've further argued that these states are associated with a 'frozen' dynamics, meaning that their properties don't evolve over time. A deeper understanding of the non-reversible symmetries and their implications has been achieved through the analysis of their mathematical properties, revealing that these infinite-depth states not only mediate the long-range non-reversible charges but also govern local dynamics through a non-Markovian quantum master equation that describes any generic local density matrix.
