The host galaxies of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are key indicators of how mass is assembled in galaxies throughout time. Galaxies at specific stages are associated with active nuclei, from the earliest formation to the present day. To gain valuable insights into galaxy evolution, it's crucial to construct detailed host galaxy models that can be used in conjunction with other analytical tools. Our research leverages machine learning to create three host galaxy models (bulge+disk, elliptical, and irregular) for a significant sample of AGN, (approximately 1141) with redshifts less than 1, taken from the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam's wide survey. Two cutting-edge machine learning algorithms, Random Forest and K-Means, are used in conjunction with galaxy isophote shape parameters to automate the classification process. Our findings reveal that (1) approximately 52% of galaxies are classified as belonging to the irregular category, consistent with the established understanding that nuclear activity is frequently found in poorly defined galaxy structures; (2) a quarter of the sample is classified as bulge+disk, (17%) as elliptical, and (11%) as uncertain; (3) a more significant proportion of galaxies with distorted shapes are identified as AGN, while those with more regular structures are less commonly detected with any specific AGN features, other than nuclear activity itself; (4) the morphology of galaxies with redshifts less than 1 is influenced by their mass; (5

This research examines the characteristics of quantum atomic correlations in an external field with a specific focus on optical coherent states. We delve into aspects such as correlation function magnitudes, Houston distributions, and higher-order correlation properties. The spatial and temporal patterns of these correlations are determined through an in-depth analysis of the field-ionized atom, considering two types of short-range potentials. One potential model features a potential that increases as the square of the distance, mimicking a harmonic oscillator, whereas the other model features a linearly increasing potential. The study shows that a harmonic potential yields more pronounced correlations than a linear potential. Additionally, when compared to Gaussian distributions, optical coherent state distributions exhibit distinct advantages in terms of higher order correlation properties. This, in turn, leads to the observation of more intense spatial patterns and longer temporal durations. It is interesting to note that a coherent state distribution can be approximated as a Gaussian distribution with sufficient spatial and temporal distance from the correlation peak.

This research extends the current understanding of deep learning with complex numbers by relaxing the constraint that its complex outputs must match their conjugate counterparts. With this relaxation, we can exploit the full potential of complex number arithmetic in deep learning models. Our investigation features three key contributions. Firstly, we develop a novel set equalization technique for complex-valued deep networks that have not undergone conjugate symmetry. Secondly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this new set equalization approach through comprehensive experiments with complex-weight networks, which outperform their conjugate-symmetric counterparts in terms of performance. Thirdly, we further understand the optimal characteristics of complex number functions by lowering constraints on their output domains. Our experiments with complex-valued convolutional neural networks for image classification tasks show that allowing complex outputs to take on arbitrary values can lead to better performance.

The non-linear QCD evolution Hierarchy is the origin of the non-linear saturation regime that can be observed in various processes at high energies. Several key phenomena such as the energy dependence of the saturation momentum, the momentum dependence of the gluon distribution (gluon geometrical scaling), and moment correlations (moments correlations) arise from this regime, making them fundamental properties of high-energy gluon distributions in proton and nuclear targets. This text outlines the theoretical foundation of the QCD energy evolution, elaborates on these phenomena, and predicts that such patterns will be observed in future experiments with electron-proton and ion collisions at various facilities, such as the FCC, RHIC-II, and EIC.

Through in-depth chemical analysis, our team has evaluated the composition of nine distant, low-metal content stars residing near the center of the galaxy. These stars were discovered using an optical detector and are estimated to have been formed around 10-13 billion years ago. Our findings indicate significant variability in the amounts of heavy elements present in these stars. Further examination of the ratios of heavy to light elements in these stars suggests a broad range, from one-twentieth to one-twentieth-fifth of the elemental abundance in our sun. We have investigated multiple theoretical mechanisms that might cause such disparities in the amounts of heavy elements. These include a process called 'rocky planet filtering,' which suggests that small planets formed early in a galaxy's development draw massive amounts of heavy elements towards them, effectively eliminating them from the remaining material. Another mechanism through 'effective surface area,' which implies that chemical elements are dispersed more efficiently into space from smaller, low mass stars. Our analysis indicates that both of these processes contribute to the variation in the amounts of heavy elements observed in these stars, but cannot fully explain the full range of our data. These results provide valuable insight into the chemical make-up of very early galaxies and offer crucial information regarding the variation of heavy elements in the universe during its formative years.

A data-driven approach known as pseudo-value estimation, developed for forecasting financial literacy based on demographic information, relies on machine learning algorithms to create accurate predictions. This algorithm, first introduced for binary forecasts, has been enhanced to accommodate multiple classes, allowing it to model varying probabilities of multiple future outcomes. When used in pseudo-value estimation, this algorithmic improvement enables the creation of dynamic treatment effect predictions that cater to changing future treatment scenarios. To validate the efficacy of this algorithm, a cloud-based tool has been developed to compare its performance with that of traditional machine learning models, specifically for forecasting financial literacy. This tool allows users to input their data and adjust parameters such as feature scaling and the random seed for the algorithm, enabling reproducible research and results. Unlike conventional pseudo-value estimation, which requires a single future probability estimate, this algorithm can generate multiple predictions for different treatment scenarios, making it accessible through a user-friendly interface. This algorithm has several key benefits, including the ability to forecast up to three future probabilities, the ability to run independently of the original treatment probability, and the ability to use multiple future scenarios in addition to the original next period probability.

We introduce SQUID, a novel, distributed quantum underling for distributed universal computing. The name SQUID is derived from the 19th century phrase for an unimportant person and the common material used in superconducting quantum processors. The paper outlines how our approach allows for the construction of a fully functional, all-quantum, all-distributed universal computing system, including a quantum-based Amdahl's model, thus paving the way for the development of quantum back-ends that can seamlessly integrate with classical front-ends. Furthermore, our approach enables the utilization of quantum processors with imperfect two-qubit gates. Additionally, we describe a corresponding programming framework that enables the development of distributed quantum programs. The name SQUID is also derived from the name of the European squid species and the 19th century English phrase for a minor official.

Researchers, Chen and Chen, recently explored distorted nearly slant submanifolds in nearly complex manifolds. This paper extends their findings to the realm of nearly complex contact manifolds. A new class of distorted product pointwise slant submanifolds is introduced, with more than one dimension in each factor. These submanifolds exhibit slant behavior that varies across components, while maintaining pointwise slant characteristics. A geometric framework is developed to clarify the relationship between submanifolds and their respective factors. Additionally, examples have been constructed to demonstrate the main class of submanifolds in both 6 and 10 dimensional spaces.

The principle of portable and inert detectors of keV light nuclear reactions can be applied to analyzing processes not caused by collisions, utilizing the device's sensitivity to the motion of atomic particles instead. We explore this possibility by simulating how radiative color centers move within a crystal lattice, then look at consequences for low energy nuclear reaction detection and discuss potential inactive reactions, focusing on effects from electric and magnetic fields, with an emphasis on detecting and analyzing reactions that occur at low energies. We suggest conducting experiments using techniques that don't damage samples, like studying the movement of atomic particles in time and the movement of atomic groups within a crystal lattice, to gain more insight into these reactions. These methods have already been implemented in experiments studying (3He, 4He) xenon and (3H, 1H) silicon reactions, with the goal of identifying and analyzing low energy inactive reactions that do not respond to magnetic fields, like those involving symmetrical nuclei and atomic particles.

To analyze colloidal particle movement in a gradient of activity, we studied the dynamic interaction between the particles and the surrounding active medium using a model based on a mesoscale model for active fluids. Our research discovered that particles of distinct sizes behave differently in this scenario, with smaller particles ascending more closely toward the medium's highest level of activity. This is due to a decrease in their movement speed within the medium, which is influenced by a measure called the hydrodynamic interaction coupling parameter. For particles of a broader range of sizes, we found that their movement within the medium is largely driven by random fluctuations, preventing them from migrating toward the medium's most active level of activity. This unique and size-dependent behavior offers new possibilities for the controlled manipulation of colloidal particles.

This study delves into the numerical computation of the spectral density of certain magnetic operators in fractional quantum Hall phenomena across multiple sublattices. The research finds a notable effect known as magnetorotons, characterized by the synchronization of spectral weight transfers among different sublattices, leading to a collective resonance effect. The work also uncovers a general principle governing total spectral density in a gapped system, which could be used as a model for a'magnetic dark matter' phenomenon. The research utilizes a SU(N) lattice model with both nearest-neighbor and next-to-nearest-neighbor interactions on a two-dimensional square lattice and includes a study of the model's phase diagram. The findings show that the proposed principle is an inherent property of systems exhibiting exceptional magnetoroton effects.

Many outbreaks on networks share similarities with physical systems, particularly those exhibiting self-organized criticality. However, unlike physical systems where one can rely on a comprehensive understanding, identifying effective strategies for outbreaks on networks lacks a clear framework. This study introduces a simple, yet effective method rooted in geometry to address clustering in outbreaks on networks. By transforming the outbreak into a continuous process and focusing on its characteristic functions, the proposed approach develops an initial clustering technique and, further, refines it through the application of well-established clustering algorithms. To demonstrate its potential, the developed clustering method is applied to a renowned model of outbreaks: the Fern\'{e}ndez-Ba\~{a}rez model, showcasing its ability to capture essential system features and yield superior results compared to existing techniques. Additionally, the proposed approach has broader implications, linking clustering problems to physical system self-similarity and offering insights into system criticality.

The X'es (also known as Gibbs rings or ring artifacts) that appear in CMB map backgrounds are caused by binary data reductions that have a period of less than half the format of the map in a spherical domain. These ring artifacts occur at points close to the map's origin due to the lack of data in this area, where spherical harmonic coefficients up to a certain order are all set to zero. Since the WMAP team discovered X'es, which were a problem for analyzing spherical data but not the data itself, this issue has been extensively researched. This article solves the problem of X'es near the map's origin by using Gibbs ring artifacts and provides with simple algorithms to counteract them. These algorithms can be used in spherical harmonic map analysis without any limitations to the order of the map's expansion. This work is a breakthrough in the field of spherical harmonic map analysis.

Our research involves a complex goal-conditioned reinforcement learning scenario where an agent is directed to achieve goals in novel environments by receiving natural language instructions. However, when language is used to instruct agents, critical details in instruction meaning may be masked by ambiguity, causing agents to misinterpret commands and hinder their ability to achieve desired goals. To address this challenge, we have developed three essential abilities that an intelligent agent should possess: (a) the capacity to ask informative questions regarding task objectives, (b) the ability to ask questions selectively, and (c) the ability to adjust its behavior based on the responses to these inquiries. Through this investigation, we have created a controlled experimental setting, referred to as GoalNavi, to evaluate our hypotheses and examine goals, thereby providing a framework to evaluate an agent's comprehension of ambiguous instructional language. Furthermore, we have proposed a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework that is capable of automatically identifying relevant information for achieving task objectives. Our research results demonstrate an agent that autonomously inquires and then uses information to achieve goals it is directed to accomplish.

Quantum channel tomography holds significant importance but remains challenging due to the need for a near-optimal number of measurements and associated statistical reliability. We've developed an approach using the shadow of a quantum channel, consisting of its positive, trace-perturbative maps. Specifically, this method applies to channels with a trace-distance contraction ratio of less than one and supports estimation of any channel operator, calculation of its matrix elements in certain channel types, and simulation of its shadow procedure. This framework also enables straightforward modeling and serving as a baseline for quantum channel estimation. We've demonstrated that the shadow of a quantum channel can be efficiently estimated from a minimal number of classical distributions, which are obtained from the channel's action on specific input states. This results in nearly optimal, O(n) measurements being required to achieve bias. Moreover, d-dimensional quantum channels can be identified with a polylogarithmic number of measurements. Shadow-estimated models of quantum channels have also shown remarkable practical utility in driving state and process estimation to nearly optimal bounds. Notably, when applied to interacting many-body quantum systems, our approach yields a polynomial understanding of dynamics, which can be extended to adjacent scales of time and system sizes while maintaining a polylogarithmic understanding of the estimation error. This breakthrough is based on an estimation of the channel's shadow that enables sequential modeling of the system's dynamics at increasingly finer time and spatial resolutions.

This research focuses on establishing inequalities related to the Cheeger constant for two-dimensional shapes with a positively curved boundary. We specifically look at areas enclosed by two strictly convex lines. In an earlier study, F. Chiti, G. Griffiths, and N. Strugatchov demonstrated some such inequalities, and this work goes further to confirm that these inequalities are optimal. A different set of inequalities, which are related to a different shape optimisation problem, have also been established in this research, and we provide examples to show that they cannot be improved upon. Additionally, we make connections between our findings and previous results by P. Borel and S. Ganguly, as well as M. Papanikou and N. Tomisaki. Our methods of analysis include employing key concepts from barrier technique, convexity, and optimisation.

Following significant disruption to daily life and businesses from the COVID-19 pandemic,
a range of technologies emerged to help minimize its impact. These include
temperature-scanning capsules, social distancing sensors, and display units designed
to educate the public. A novel application of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has
emerged as well, particularly in areas where streets are heavily populated. By
equipping UAVs with infection-preventing devices, or displaying public health messages
related to the pandemic, they have become an essential tool for maintaining social
distancing. In this paper, we present a simulation-based framework for optimizing the
pathways followed by UAVs in urban environments, with the goal of minimizing the
travel time required for the completion of a time-sensitive schedule. A series of
case studies have been conducted to examine the effectiveness of the proposed
algorithm in diverse scenarios.

In multilayer graphene, particularly in a bilayer model, we uncovered a unique non-relativistic theory that exhibits Dirac properties due to Coulomb interactions. This led to the identification of both relativistic and non-relativistic Fermi liquids and non-liquids, all within the same parameter range. Utilizing the renormalization group approach, our continuous RG flow equations accurately captured these distinct phases, replicating previously obtained two-dimensional results and predicting the existence of three distinct universality classes: a relativistic ferromagnet, a non-relativistic Fermi liquid, and a non-ferromagnetic non-liquid. The observed phase diagrams revealed multiple-body instability within bilayer graphene.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions. For Sc2TbN@C80, the conformation directly relates to the presence of an antiferromagnetic structure, as seen on a Nb(111) surface. This study examines how temperature influences the conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 on a newly developed hexagonal BN/Ni(111) surface using non-contact atomic force microscopy. The investigation reveals that at low temperatures, the molecule exhibits an AFM structure but transitions to a FM structure as the temperature increases to 100 K. As the temperature rises to a point where thermal diffusion significantly impacts the molecule's state, the FM structure persists until a new AFM structure emerges at higher temperatures. The thermal scaling of the phase transition between these structures shows a distinct deviation from the Schottky double logarithmic plots, indicating a thermal activation energy of approximately 39.5 MeV that contradicts the expected and observed behaviors. The matter is further discussed with consideration of the influence of thermal diffusion near the Curie point.

The following security considerations must be kept in mind when implementing
information-theoretic security in IoT networks: sufficiently robust bit error
rates, energy efficiency on par with energy-constrained devices, and compatibility
with existing systems using symmetric key encryption. The trade-off between
security and energy consumption in such networks was analyzed, incorporating
computational complexity to mitigate information-theoretic limitations. An IoT
device security model was introduced to assess the balance between bit error rate
and energy consumption, with both variables adjustable. Next, a novel secure
cryptography framework, involving secure data encoding and decoding processes via
a noise-correcting channel, was proposed to optimize ITRS-compatible bit error
rates and energy consumption. The framework's efficiency was demonstrated through
substitution of various error-correcting codes, with the results showing that the
new protocol outperforms previous approaches using Hartley, Shannon, and SEA
arithmetic operations in terms of both security and energy efficiency. The
framework's also allowed for the simultaneous implementation of both security and
energy constraints, simultaneously satisfying the requirements of the ITRS and
previous lightweight devices.

Accurate measurements in quantum physics often rely on the implementation of precise experimental designs that balance conflicting limitations, such as constraints on measurement precision and accuracy. The standard approach to quantifying uncertainty in these experiments is the Bayesian statistical analysis, widely used in many scientific studies. Our work proposes a novel Bayesian method to determine the optimal sequence of measurements for a particular type of quantum experiment: Ramsey sequence measurements. This method considers multiple factors that limit accurate frequency measurements, including systematic error sources and minimum measurement intervals. It's capable of automatically adjusting to changes in these constraints and can even account for uncertain values. The approach has been validated with three distinct scenarios: when one or multiple error sources are present or the frequency drift is quantifiable. The results confirm the effectiveness of this framework in leading the experiment towards a precise frequency measurement, a crucial outcome in many quantum physics applications.

A theoretically sound and multi-scale framework for measuring network centrality is needed that avoids the limitations of current approaches. A novel centrality metric, the Gromov centrality, has been proposed, which is based on the concept of network triangles and the triangle inequality surplus. This surplus quantifies the deviation of shortest paths from geodesic paths, offering a theoretical basis for the centrality metric. A geometric interpretation of the Gromov centrality reveals its connection to the network's underlying geometry. Analysis of synthetic and real-world datasets has demonstrated the capabilities of the Gromov centrality to guide discovery of network patterns and identify key nodes, even in large and complex networks.

The Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravity is presented as an alternative to conventional gravity theories. Featuring a simplified single-force model where the gravitational force directly affects inertial frames, this theory reduces to Newton's all-at-a-distance law in scenarios without rotation or other inertial frame distortions. In situations involving toroidal gravitational fields, the theory's predictions diverge significantly from classical outcomes, raising fundamental questions about the structure of compact objects like black holes and neutron stars, as well as the nature of gravitational waves, and the characteristics of gravitational waves produced during supernova events.

We define a particular operation on matrix pencil families, allowing the construction of lower dimensional examples from higher dimensional ones, while maintaining a strict equivalence standard. Each step in the construction process involves either row or column operations. Utilizing this method, new examples of 3x3 matrix pencils with five parameters are generated and we demonstrate that some of these examples cannot be transformed into other parameterized forms through row or column operations. Additionally, we exploit connections between matrix pencil families and free Lie algebras to create a set of invariant polynomials for the constructed 3x3 matrix pencils, yielding new combinatorial objects called nilpotent free Lie algebras.

A novel method is presented to compute the Green function of a twisted torus consisting of a flat manifold with a specified connection, for which no general formula was previously available. Our technique, based on the geometric T-duality of a flat torus, enables the construction of orthogonal twistor spaces for twisted tori, leading to a geometric method to establish T-duality on these manifolds. The proposed method is demonstrated through three case studies. Furthermore, it is shown that the connection on the twisted torus can be reconstructed from the Green function, provided that the T-duality transformation is comprehensively understood, offering a significant outcome beyond the immediate context of T-duality.

We show that any planar metric $(X,d)$ can be embedded into a treewidth-$4$ graph $G$ such that the distance between any two points $s$ and $t$ in $G$ in the embedded metric $d'$ is equal to $d(s, t)$, and $d'$ is consistent when $X$ is restricted to any subgraph $H$ of $X$. Furthermore, we prove that if $X$ contains no cycles, we can find a tree $T$ with treewidth-at-most-$3$ in $X$ such that the distance between any two points $s$ and $t$ in $T$ in the minimum-span tree metric $d'$ is equal to $d(s, t)$.

For a broad class of smooth, monotonic, discrete-time dynamical systems, we've proven the local convergence of almost all smooth, odd, continuous time re-scalings to their underlying generic, hyperbolic vector fields. This finding is significant in itself, and when combined with known results, allows us to infer that this class of systems shares various global characteristics with non-resonant, hyperbolic vector fields, as well as locally universally sensitive, non-local universality sensitive, and piecewise linear locally universally sensitive systems.

The potential of using quantum computers to simulate molecular systems, especially smaller systems that outperform classical counterparts, has been demonstrated. Among the various algorithms employed, the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) stands out for its versatility. Our research proposes a modified adaptive VQE approach called Quba-advVQE, featuring an updated measurement routine. Instead of traditional state-excitation measurements, we utilize a more efficient method that only samples the excited states of a single qubit. This innovation greatly reduces the number of required measurements. By incorporating an adaptive circuit technique called mid-circuit tomography, we can determine the complete quantum state. Our robust implementation called quba-advVQE provides a basis for further research into hybrid quantum-classical algorithms and allows for simulations of larger molecular systems.

Our Profound generative model builds upon an existing framework in
https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00862, incorporating a decoder based on a
regularized mean squared error, rather than minimizing the distance between
input and output, as is traditional in autoencoders. This change allows the
decoder to be interpreted as an inverse function, providing a clear theoretical
framework. We confirm that our model is an accurate implementation of an
existing theoretical concept within a particular network architecture in
https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.08292. Although previously considered impractical
due to its numerical instability, our model can be trained directly without
preprocessing inputs, as we have developed an algorithm that determines optimal
network weights by minimizing representation distortion. This makes our model
equivalent to an autoencoder, with the traditional view of an autoencoder being
a special case of our model. We verify the effectiveness of our model by
investigating the local exploration of a theoretical optimal function within a
particular network architecture in https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.08292.

A strongly amplified gravitational wave background from cosmological scales is predicted by some models of inflation to have a spectral energy density twice that emitted by primordial cosmic fluctuations. Although not directly observable due to its extremely low frequency, this extra radiation causes problems for a aligned model that is consistent with NANOGrav data, making it difficult to resolve the Hubble tension and comply with cosmological constraints. However, a realistically high-frequency damped amplitude could prevent this additional radiation from conflicting with current cosmological standards if the detection of low-frequency gravitational waves by Advanced LIGO-Virgo remains below a certain threshold or if the cosmic fluctuations are slightly less accurate than predicted.

Two comets, C/2015 ER61 and C/2017 K2, were investigated using ALMA's Atacama Compact Array. It's been discovered that CS is a key molecular species emanating from these comets, particularly HCS+, HCS, and CS+. Our findings with Nucleus-Center Distance show a significant increase in CS emission but a less pronounced trend for HCN. We've analyzed the emission patterns of CS and found them to align with the temperature of the nucleus, N2 frozen ice, and light curve light curves, suggesting a distributed source of CS. In the case of C/2015 ER61, we've found CS to show a polar opposition effect while exhibiting a double peak HCN light curve, indicating the presence of a polar CS source. Moreover, we've found the CS/HCN ratio to vary across the comets, indicating diverse CS/HCN proportions in their ices. Our observations imply ER61 has a high CO to HCN ratio, making it the second such comet with this characteristic since HCN monitoring began. Our observations of C/2017 K2 also reveal an increased CS emission as it approaches the Sun, as does HCN. In the case of C/2017 K2, we've found the CS emission to be concentrated around polar regions and to show a strong polar CS emission. Our observations show a decreased HCN emission compared to CS. We suggest a novel, uncomplicated strategy for producing speech without any
direction or guidance. Unlike top-notch generative models that necessitate considerable
resources, our approach is straightforward to implement and requires minimal computing
power. Additionally, we have made our process flexible by enabling two options for
guidance: using transcriptions from speech-to-text software or speech samples provided
by a text-to-speech system. We have tested our technique with two datasets and
obtained promising results, surpassing a basic generative model in both quality and
efficiency. Examples of the speech generated using our technique can be heard at:
https://smt.pl/en/projects/simple-speech-generation/.

In the context of an interaction-free Reissner-Nordström black hole in the thermodynamically stable state, we've determined the heat function and entropy from the Euclidean action, and also defined the Arrows of black hole within the canonical ensemble, while evaluating the same in the grand canonical ensemble as a Legendre transformation. Furthermore, by incorporating the Tsallis stability criteria of thermodynamic systems into the statistical distribution of holographic dark energy, we've derived the stability criteria for HGDE and observed that the microscopical distribution of HGDE is affected by the parameter $sk$ associated with Tsallis distribution.

Multi-objective optimization problems are ubiquitous in various fields, including economics, engineering, economics, and mathematics. They are characterized by a set of decision variables, some of which are restricted to specific integer values, and the objective functions depend on variable interactions often involving non-linear components. A novel algorithm presented here aims to tackle such complex optimization problems. It combines multi-start optimization with a modified branch and bound variant of the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm version II, originally designed for two-objective optimization problems. For efficient solutions, a surrogate model based on Gaussian Processes is integrated into each computational process. A comprehensive evaluation using 11 publicly available MO MINLP test problems reveals that our proposed approach significantly reduces computational time compared to NSGAII, at the cost of slight deviations from Pareto-optimality. Nonetheless, the proposed method excels its counterparts, including a customized hybridization of SCSC with Pareto-PSO, as demonstrated through various performance metrics. Additionally, the proposed approach offers several possibilities for further enhancement.

The concept of connectedness and completeness in topological groups is well-defined and corresponds to a specific factor through a certain map when considered within the realm of synthetic differential geometry. We prove that a specific factor is always surjective for connected and integral Lie groupoids, providing an alternative definition. Consequently, if a finitely generated arithmetic subgroup of a Lie group has a solution in the underlying Lie group, then its corresponding quotient through a certain map is also divisible. We explore several implications of this finding. Furthermore, we represent a specific form of integral complete manifold locally as a product of a finite-dimensional factor space. Additionally, we provide a direct synthetic proof of a certain result that was initially demonstrated by Moerdijk and Weizmann in the context of manifolds, asserting that a locally exponential Mal'tvesti-Lie groupoid is inherently locally exponential.

The exponential rise in biomedical data is leading to a number of positive outcomes, particularly in research fields where comprehensive datasets are essential for making accurate predictions," explains Dr. Naima Aziz, researcher at the University of Chicago's Biological and Chemical Engineering Program. "By promoting data standardization and adopting technologies like cyberinfrastructure, we can streamline data exchange and accelerate discovery. "As data volumes increase, identifying meaningful patterns becomes more difficult, prompting researchers to seek novel computational methods for analysis," states Dr. Aziz. "By providing platforms for data visualization and integration, we can simplify the process of data analysis and make it more accessible to a broader range of researchers." Dr. Aziz and her colleagues are developing technologies to support data exchange and integration, along with educational initiatives to promote collaboration and reduce barriers to data sharing. "By providing platforms for data visualization and integration, we can simplify the process of data analysis and make it more accessible to a broader range of researchers," they explain. "Our goal is to create platform-independent tools that can be easily adopted across various digital tools and tools of the trade for data analysis."

In the field of aspect-based sentiment analysis, most models rely on explicitly marked sentiment labels, yet this task is beneficial when incorporating implicitly labeled data. This implies that models should learn to extract implicit sentiment information from unlabeled text. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed using various types of unlabeled data. Despite the effectiveness of these methods, they often require additional processing to avoid overreliance on loosely related data. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a supervised pre-training approach that conserves the original text's meaning during encoding while simultaneously utilizing unlabeled data with the same pre-trained model. This innovative method achieves significant enhancements over existing approaches when incorporating various types of unlabeled data, ultimately surpassing the performance of fully supervised models when incorporated into the NBSA dataset, as measured by macro F1 score. To support the research community, the dataset consisting of implicitly sentiment information is made publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengfang2021/SICAP.

Researchers often aim to analyze the relationship between an exposure and an outcome through a mediator, leveraging survey studies for this purpose. For findings to be applicable to real-world interventions, the results usually rely on data from two groups: those with and without the outcome. We investigate whether it's possible to determine how an exposure influences an outcome by considering its effect on a mediator, which itself affects the outcome, all while accounting for confounding variables. We establish that this relationship can be consistently estimated when using case-control data by drawing participants at random from a population. We demonstrate that a conventional statistical method can be used to evaluate the relationship between multiple variables, which allows us to determine the effect of an exposure on an outcome by considering its effect on a mediator. We illustrate this method with an example related to a smoking ban on a particular platform.

This research delves into secure communication networks with multiple users that incorporate reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations and imperfections. To achieve these studies, a new and complex sturdy transmission design is developed, which combines block diagonalization with the introduction of artificial noise. In this design, the RIS phase shifts are adjusted to both optimize the transmission signal power and the correlation matrix of the effective channel at the user end, while also being optimized in relation to the eavesdropper's channel. A global maximum is sought through an iterative algorithm that involves solving two separate optimization problems, the first related to the RIS phase shifts and the second involving the transmit beamformers. Both of these optimization problems are convex in nature, allowing for their solution to be obtained through a variety of numerical methods. To reduce computational complexity, an alternative algorithm is developed, which simplifies the second optimization problem by assuming that the effective channel at the RIS end is constant, thereby reducing the complexity of the optimization problem. Consequently, the second optimization problem can be solved directly and this would lead to a simplified algorithm that relies on the Alternating Direction Method of Optimization.

In the study of decision-making skills, researchers have always sought to grasp how these skills operate and influence perception, preference, and decision-making processes. A crucial aspect of this research involves improving or adapting to past experiences. We introduce the concept of decision-making skills, focusing on how skills shape and alter perceptions through selection and categorization. We create a system using neural networks, which we teach to mimic a mechanism where a hypothetical future outcome depends on the past history of an individual. We collected a significant dataset comprising a sizeable group of people over a prolonged period, examining how people decide to classify existing objects as they gain new knowledge and how they choose to select objects from a pool. We trained our model using this dataset and found that it effectively simulates the behavior of a hypothetical future individual based on their past decisions and how they've evolved over time. We also discovered that our model generates value more efficiently than traditional methods, allowing it to better represent an individual's decision-making skills when working with limited data. By using an individual's past decisions to understand their decision-making skills, we found that these skills can be leveraged to improve an individual's ability to categorize objects and select relevant items. Additionally, we determined that our model effectively captures an individual's decision-making skills more accurately and at a faster rate than traditional methods.

The solar wind's behavior near the Sun's atmosphere remains a leading mystery in solar physics, despite extensive studies of the phenomenon.  To better understand this behavior, researchers are motivated to investigate recurring changes in the solar wind's characteristics, especially those related to the Sun's active regions.  A study of data from the Parker Solar Probe's first close approach to the Sun found evidence that active region observations, which were only possible because of the mission's close distance, are crucial for understanding the solar wind's behavior throughout the heliosphere.  During this encounter, the solar wind's velocity, composition, and other characteristics slowed or changed due to the solar wind's conditions on the Sun, which the team termed the solar breeze.  The solar breeze energy appears to be associated with the movement of magnetic fields and the change in the solar wind's conditions due to the presence of the Sun's active regions.  The team's observations also found that the solar breeze energy is linked to the solar wind's acceleration due to the release of energy from the Sun, which the team termed the solar wind acceleration rate.  The findings from the study, which the team titled 'Solar Breeze Energy Flows', are the first to show the transfer of the solar wind's energy from the Sun's active regions into the static energy of the Sun's atmosphere, which the team suggested could be one way the Sun's atmosphere remains stable. We examine noncommutative countable principal bundles with base a C*-algebra operated upon by a discrete, unimodular group. Under the condition that the bundle's monodromy action exhibits only finite-dimensional spectrum elements, we construct a noncommutative countable principal bundle with base A x G, where A represents the algebra, G is the group acting on A, and x is G's operation on A. Furthermore, this construction satisfies a key universal property in relation to the original monodromy action. In the course of our investigation, we establish the existence of noncommutative compact principal bundles, specifically for the base C*-algebras A x G where A is a unimodular C*-algebra operated upon by G. We also revise and extend a theorem concerning the construction of noncommutative countable principal extensions from G-algebras, broadening its scope to include actions with finite-dimensional spectrum elements. We also provide a relevant example related to a noncommutative rotator bundle with a three-dimensional classical fiber.

In the context of $q$-deformed optomechanical research, our study on a $q$-deformed laser cavity provides novel insights into optomechanical coupling, potentially leading to enhanced mechanical stiffness and novel effects. By examining a simple model with negative mass, we discovered the unusual phenomenon of superluminal light propagation within the cavity. The introduction of a negative mechanical stiffness $k_n<0$ allowed for the observation of dark-sound behavior. Our work in this area offers significant opportunities for exploring the intersection of optomechanics and quantum deformation.

Lattice calculations for a 2-dimensional lattice version of the Dual-Rotors Model, which contains a baryon-antibaryon pair as the ground state, have shown that P and C odd states with Welfare indices greater than 3 exhibit adverse R-parity behavior. Furthermore, key characteristics of these states, including their R-parity, baryon content, and orientation in rest frame, are similar to those assumed for the pions in the valence approximation of the Dual-Rotors Model.

A novel, highly adaptable, deep learning-based computational model has been introduced for solving partial differential equations. This model, capable of being applied to both hyperbolic and parabolic PDEs, uses an especially developed loss function that considers the average values within larger spatial domains. It does not require detailed spatial data but instead can effectively process coarse-scale numerical or real-world data. The model's exceptional performance lies in its ability to handle diverse PDE types with high accuracy using low-resolution feature representations. It demonstrates exceptional adaptability, applicable in both spatial and temporal dimensions, and can easily be modified for different boundary conditions. The model's exceptional performance is especially evident in its ability to solve the Burgers equation with high fidelity, reproducing the underlying inertial dynamics at a high level of accuracy.

The ALICE Collaboration is set to release its initial findings on the study of proton-lead collisions at the LHC's Run 3 by the end of 2022. The experiment is undergoing a significant upgrade for Run 3, with multiple enhancements in the detector system to prepare for an extended investigation of the LHC's entire duration. The next run will feature upgraded hardware, including the new Forward Calorimeter System, the improved Tracklet trigger system, and the upgraded internal gas jet detector. The electron spectrometer is also being renovated to broaden the energy collection. The electron spectrometer is being rebuilt for Run 3 to gather data on heavy flavor electrons from both proton-proton and proton-lead collisions. The experiment will feature a significant increase in the number of events analyzed through a new generation of software changes. The objective of the new design is to collect a more extensive number of data during proton-lead collisions and a more detailed understanding of the internal gas jet experiment.

We demonstrate the emergence of geometric Berry phases within a timelike worldtube, exemplified by a Timelike Worldtube Cavity (TWC), which simulates the effects of Hawking radiation and the Unruh effect using quantum field techniques.  These geometric phases that occur along the TWC are a result of the disentanglement between future and past light cones when the TWC is static, and new phases emerge when the TWC moves, causing re-entanglement between the two light cones.  We compute the time-dependent Berry phase generated by a particle moving within a TWC in flat space, which can be used to determine the local acceleration of the TWC.  Moreover, because acceleration in one section of the TWC causes radiation-induced phase transitions across the entire structure, it may be possible to observe the Unruh effect without detecting Hawking radiation.

Event discovery is crucial for detecting and tracking real-world happenings.
Understanding this concept is more complicated than other NLP tasks due to its
particular extraction requirements. Existing extraction datasets for events have
significant limitations, largely being confined to a single language or heavily
incomplete. To address this knowledge gap, we introduce the MEE, a groundbreaking
multilingual event discovery dataset that caters to English and five other languages
like Spanish, German, Chinese, Arabic, and Russian. Each record in MEE includes
three key components: a description, a list of associated sub-events, and a group
of relevant keywords. We visually display the dataset for better understanding,
along with the methodologies used to create it, involving the annotation of 21,663
notable events by multiple annotators. Moreover, MEE is complemented by a large,
English-only dataset called FullNews, which was obtained by merging the outputs of
multiple named entity recognition models. This integrated dataset contains 394k news
articles and 572k event records. We conduct comprehensive experiments using both
MEE and FullNews to evaluate six state-of-the-art models under different scenarios,
showcasing MEE's immense utility and its potential to drive future research in NLP.

This research investigates a fundamental issue in global vector bundle theory, specifically the question of whether a particular push-forward operation involving a Hermitian holomorphic connection has a positive characteristic form. We propose a standard condition, related to the Kobayashi hyperbolicity of the base space, to address this concern. Furthermore, we generate numerous instances of positive global forms on homogeneous domains by applying our framework to domains of Finsler type, thereby extending earlier findings related to pseudoconvex domains. We also re-examine some prior concepts and yield a deeper understanding of their relationships.

Comprehending the deviations from equilibrium in compact binary systems requires accounting for the movements of matter across the boundary between the star and accretion disk. Researchers used existing data from Cyg X-1 to examine the link between the movement of the star's boundary layers and X-ray observations spanning 0.1-30 keV during a specific type of intense bright period. Specifically, they focused on the effects of two processes - the star pulling on its disk versus the disk pushing back, and disk expansion due to the star's boundary layer. Through model fits, they discovered that the movement of the star's boundary layers occurs approximately every 0.1-0 to 10 seconds, resulted in the following findings: when the disk pulls away from the star, resulting ionization leads to a change in the type of X-ray emission, while also impacting the star's boundary layer to cause a specific type of X-ray movement patterns; as a result of the star's boundary layer expanding due to the additional mass, the star's boundary layer thickness increased, to roughly half the size of the entire accretion layer; finally, they proposed that certain patterns observed in the light from Cyg X-1 are a result of fluctuations in the amount of matter on the star's boundary layer.

A theoretical model involving an orthonormal, unitary field is proposed to explain anomalous magnetic drag and Gompertz growth patterns in biological systems. The model relies on an unconventional electrodynamics theory with a dual component originating from a single, non-Unitary charge operator. The dual component exhibits analogous properties to the Aharonov-Bohm phase, while the remaining part is comparable to the usual Maxwell field. Considering the non-Unitary aspect of the field, a term analogous to the Berestetsky drag is introduced with adjustments to non-Unitary part propagation, giving rise to an unusual, drag-like effect. Additionally, the potential of the proposed model is demonstrated through a biological application by analyzing the dynamics of a string voltage and its implications on particle motion.

The complexity of the parsing task is largely due to the richness in language syntax and semantics. To improve parsing efficiency, reduced dependency trees like shallow parsing are often employed. However, their main limitation is their inability to accurately analyze sentence semantics, requiring multiple reduced dependency trees to effectively analyze a single sentence. To address this issue, this research proposes a new framework called Collaborative Universal Analysis (CUA). The CUA framework consists of two primary modules: Syntax and Semantic Analysis. The Syntax module creates a detailed representation of the sentence structure using a universal dependency parsing framework, while the Semantic module leverages the universal syntax to identify the semantic components and builds a semantic dependency tree. As a novel approach, CUA is capable of achieving syntax and semantic analysis in tandem within the same model. Moreover, this framework enables a seamless transition between universal syntax and semantic analysis by sharing resources and regulating the complexity of the semantic tree. To achieve this, two new models called AttCUA and MultiCUA are developed. The AttCUA model integrates a attention mechanism to balance the complexity of the syntax and semantic trees, while the MultiCUA model employs multiple networks to analyze syntax and semantics separately. As a result, this framework can produce accurate universal dependency parsing and semantic dependency parsing results. Evaluations using the standard metrics UAS and LAS reveal that the CUA models outperform other models across multiple datasets. For example, the CUA models excel in sentence length and create more accurate semantic analysis results than previous models. The

The massive neutron stars or black holes that result from binary neutron star or neutron star-black hole mergers can drive powerful jets that are observable by the James Webb Space Telescope. To fully understand these jets, we need to simulate how they form after the merger, taking into account the presence of a disk that feeds the jet. We used the magnetohydrodynamic model to study how jets emerge from a disk that's fed by neutrino cooling and has a magnetar-like magnetic field, and found that the jet's power increases with the speed of the postmerger flow. Most of the simulations showed that the jet's power decreases over time due to the disruption of the magnetar field, but in simulations where the magnetic field is restored, the jet's power increases again. We found that the restored magnetic field is likely the result of the interaction between the disk and magnetic fields, indicating that the disk plays a crucial role in determining the jet's power. We also found that the jet's composition is primarily made up of protons, and that the jet's speed is approximately the speed of light, with a large majority of the merged matter ejected at speeds of hundreds of astronomical units per second, with the ejected matter forming the jet. The ejected matter also goes through a chemical transformation, specifically, and this transformation relies on the speed of the postmerger flow and the size of the region where the merged matter is trapped.

Our research employs data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program to determine the occurrence rate of tidal features in the residuals of 3848 essential single, major-axis-oriented galaxies and their minor-axis companions. These features were present in around 30% of our sample and we found their lengths to generally correspond to one fifth to one half of the parent galaxy's diameter. The fraction of early-type galaxies that exhibit tidal features varies significantly with radial distance, being more prevalent in those located at a distance further out. The observed features can be categorized into 77% stellar and 23% planetary nebula. Our analysis also explores the relationships between certain color parameters and the proportions of tidal features, as well as the effects of nuclear brightness. The results indicate that a higher fraction of blue tidal features exists when the parent galaxy exhibits blue or spiral characteristics, while red tidal features are more prevalent in late-type galaxies. Furthermore, tidal features are less prevalent in galaxies that have experienced significant disk compression. The implications of our findings are significant both in terms of their connection to galaxy evolution via mergers and also to the potential use of tidal features as indicators of galaxy history.

This paper presents a thorough examination of a previously proposed model for the azimuthally symmetric theory of gravitation (ASTG) based on a specific solution found in the equations of the theory. This solution, which features a quadratic expression in the density/pressure relationship, prompted concerns that it represented a case of an ill-posed problem. These concerns were incorrectly assumed in earlier work. The correct interpretation of this solution reveals a model capable of explaining certain phenomena that have been difficult to account for within the framework of general relativity. A step-by-step derivation of this solution is provided for ease of replication by others, followed by an analysis of how ASTG can account for specific ejection events, revealing striking parallels with the pattern of this effect.

A newly proposed model of fast radio bursts, known as the molecular condenser model, not only accounts for their observed properties, but also provides boundaries for their concurrent and delayed emissions. These bounds, based on the event's duration and brightness, have shown to restrict the variety of FRB 181108's optical flashes, suggesting that the Pulsarbot model may be insufficient in explaining this specific event. The study finds that the Pulsarbot model's overprediction of optical brightness is due to a combination of excessive magnetosphere density and a prolonged radiation period. In contrast, the Condenser model, with its shorter emission periods, is capable of producing optical signals that conform to the event's observed bounds. These constraints can also be applied to other FRB events that exhibit lasting mJy radio signals, and could serve as a remedy for the Pulsarbot model's overprediction of optical flashes. The study further indicates that the Condenser model's emissions, predicted to be highly localized with large scale heights, are subject to strong limits of $H\lesssim3\times10^{10}R$.

The cutting-edge research in high-power laser systems is pushing the boundaries of physics, science, and technology, but its progression is often hindered by a lack of access to its inner workings. Therefore, a system model that accurately translates experimental results into theoretical characteristics would greatly simplify research and verification. Conversely, reconstructing a system model from limited information is crucial for evaluating existing research, pinpointing areas for improvement, and deciding which parameters to adjust. Unfortunately, there is a distinct scarcity of guidelines governing this process. In this context, we develop a hybrid model-based framework comprising four categories: photon source, transmission medium, energy storage, and resonator systems. By integrating these components, we successfully demonstrate an exact analytical model for a class of lasers and make available the associated open-source code. Moreover, we present a novel machine learning approach, grounded in optimization theory, for reconstructing a system's model based on a set of measured properties. Through comprehensive numerical simulations, we examine the accuracy and limitations of these models. Furthermore, we present two real-world case studies of high-power laser systems, to illustrate the applicability and utility of these models. Specifically, we apply our framework to a class of high-power hybrid solid-state lasers and leverage the developed model to pinpoint the causes of observed performance fluctuations, leading to the suggestion of an effective countermeasure to enhance the beam quality.
