Research suggests that large language models like GPT-3 have the ability to
discern private information when confronted with sensitive text, either
explicitly stated or inferred, which raises concerns about their potential to
reveal precious data. Our investigation focuses on how language models can be
led to reveal confidential visual data, such as sexual orientation or religion,
when given explicit instructions or inferred information from associated images.
We found that models can often deduce the sexual orientation of individuals based
on their name or the description of their friends, or use image-related cues
such as a picture of a same-sex couple. Since models can also learn medical
terminology, we discovered that visual cues like medical scan images or
information about recent hospital visits could reveal sensitive health data.
To address these concerns, we explored methods to prevent language models from
disclosing sensitive data. Our approach involved using protective layers, such
as differential privacy or secure multi-party computation, to cloak the
underlying visual data when training the model to conceal its source. Another
method we explored was using a specialized 'dummy' model to create a false
cover story for the training data, effectively shielding the sensitive
information. Our findings revealed that these engineering approaches can provide
some level of protection for sensitive visual data, although they are not
effective in concealing the underlying source of the information.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in the creation of an anonymous and decentralized cryptocurrency with inherent transparency. To facilitate quicker transaction anonymity, our design deviates slightly from the traditional RingCT design. Our method involves combining encrypted transaction details with hidden sender and recipient addresses in a single protocol. Consequently, the resulting transactions are almost untraceable. We have developed Delegated RingCT (D-RingCT) using two blockchain platforms, Aquila and Nema, enabling seamless integration without the demands of compiler-driven workarounds. Our comprehensive analysis covers the computational prerequisites for the systems at hand, anticipated transaction speed, cost, and degree of anonymity.

To optimize the performance of the Cherenkov Telescope Array, it is crucial to have an accurate and independent measurement of the point spread function (PSF) across different photon energy spectra. This can be achieved by implementing a brightness scan approach within individual telescopes, enabling a direct calculation of the telescope's point spread function. This study evaluates various modeling strategies to represent the telescope's point spread function and examines the flexibility of the models to accommodate deviations from their initial definitions. The research further suggests an approach to integrate Markov Chain Monte Carlo modeling, which would allow for the use of PSF models in conjunction with other parameters to analyze both on-sky and laboratory data sets simultaneously. Analyzing both on-sky and laboratory data sets should yield more reliable results, as demonstrated by the comparison of model parameters extracted from laboratory data, on-sky observations during the Technical Preparation of Observation period, and on-sky observations during the first six months of the test periods.

To enhance the accuracy of epidemic forecasts, we integrate data-driven approaches into predictive modeling. A cutting-edge, collaborative data-informed model called CiTIM is developed for forecasting both past and future epidemiologic data. The underlying statistical analysis reveals that irregular patterns in growth are caused by a positioning error in the predicted curve. Consequently, correcting this positioning error enables separation of past and future predictions, allowing for the refinement of our forecast. The resulting model exhibits a remarkable ability to accurately predict sudden changes in past data and forecast near-future epidemiologic outcomes. It also generates reliable predictions for multiple future time points. The model's effectiveness was evaluated by comparing its performance to other methods in predicting SARS-CoV-2 and dengue fever data. When applied to forecasting outbreak data, CiTIM outperformed other methods, with predictions achieving a high level of accuracy two days in advance and two weeks behind, before accuracy declined. The model's success is attributed to its ability to separate past and future predictions from irregular growth patterns. The type of model used for predicting the base case and residual data can be arbitrarily selected. The model generates two important predictions: (i) the expected case baseline and related uncertainty; and (ii) the expected deviation between the observed case data and its forecasted baseline. The model uses a variation of the GEE method to calculate the uncertainty of the predicted case data. The model's software has a user-friendly, minimalistic design that allows for the analysis of data for multiple outbreaks simultaneously

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, where $n=1,2,3$. It's assumed
$\Upsilon(10753)$ is a mixed-state dark matter candidate. We found that the
$\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(1S) \pi^+\pi^-, \Upsilon(2S) \pi^+\pi^-,
\Upsilon(3S) \pi^+\pi^-)$ broadening widths are $0.02, 0.03, 0.1$ meV: this
means the $\Upsilon(10753)$ is not easily distinguishable from a dark matter candidate
owing to its narrow decay widths. Furthermore, the $\Upsilon(10753)$ is not
believed to be a signature of a hidden local symmetry dark matter model either.
Additionally, the paper lists the estimated upper limits for $\Upsilon(10753)
\to \Upsilon(nS) \pi^+\pi^- $ decays and lists observed results.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we converge traditional stochastic gradient descent for the initial layers, before transitioning to a non-linear interval-limited optimization method for the later layers. This hybrid approach converges to equivalent performance as traditional stochastic gradient descent but with significantly reduced computation time, roughly 80% acceleration. We examine various configurations of our proposed algorithm, considering different quantization strategies, presence of data augmentation, and multi-label classification tasks. Our results are validated across multiple networks, including MobileNetV2, on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, as well as the ResNet34 on ImageNet, asking the network to classify one image at a time. We also provide a theoretical foundation for our approach, showing that AskewSGD converges to similar properties as stochastic gradient descent under certain conditions. This is a crucial insight, enabling us to initially train the network with CDG, then switch to AskewSGD for the final network convergence, significantly speeding up training. We also present additional advancements, including a novel data augmentation technique, providing a competitor to known optimization methods like LARS and its variants, as well as the recently introduced Regularized Quantized Training (RQT) approach.

Over the past few decades, advancements in robotics have made soft robots a viable option for executing complex tasks such as environmental adaptation, enhanced interaction, and surgical intervention. However, their integration into the research community has been slower due to the difficulty in developing and testing robotic models, a essential step for incorporating robotics into a given setting. This paper offers a thorough examination of recent models (mathematical and artificial neural network-based) used to represent and predict the behavior of various soft robotic structures and its related control strategies. It also explores the control methods for the manipulation and movement of the robots, their placement within environments, and the integration of sensors to assess elastic robot positioning. Furthermore, the paper discusses the ongoing challenges and potential topics for future investigation in the field of model-driven control of soft robots.

This note re-evaluates the Jacobi group, focusing on its intrinsic forms, 
especially the Jacobi group JSp(n,1) in relation to Sp(n1,C) and SO(n,C). 
It redefines the group JSp(n,1) as the subgroup of Sp(n1,C) consisting of 
elements with diagonal centralizer subgroups, and then identifies automorphisms 
for this group. Furthermore, the paper establishes a connection between JSp(n,1) 
and its counterpart SO(n,C) via an 2-cokernel. All theoretical findings are 
illustrated with examples.

Verifying facts related to tables is crucial for understanding certain statements, yet current fact verification models lack table verification capabilities and primarily rely on extracting key phrases from text. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing a novel fact verification framework that utilizes transformers and supports various table structures. Our approach enhances fact confirmation by splitting confirmation tables and matching query statements, and then synthesizes confirmatory evidence from extracted table cells and related text. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art fact verification models, and that incorporating table decomposition improves verification accuracy in complex table scenarios.

Deep generative models such as GANs offer excellent alternatives to traditional data synthesis techniques. Yet, creating these highly customized models in variable-dimensional spaces can be particularly challenging, mainly due to the variable total volume issue in the space. In this context, a new approach, HSICGAN, is proposed to tackle the problem of conditional generation in high-dimensional spaces with unknown total volume. Building on the Hidden Conditional Energy Method, HSICGAN effectively leverages the total volume information from data samples to condition its generative process. We tested HSICGAN in brain MRI volume visualization, where it demonstrated notable performance improvements in both precision and efficiency compared to leading conditional GANs.

Traditional Uniform Sampler algorithms, such as Random Search and Gradient Descent, have a common drawback: they may converge to multiple suboptimal solutions. In response, researchers have created various sampling methods to improve performance, including adapted uniform samplers and Layered Sampling, which can detect optimal solutions more effectively. We examine the differences between these various samplers and investigate which factors influence their behavior and how to assess their performance. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain samplers are connected to optimal solutions in a probabilistic sense and propose a metric to measure the effectiveness of any sampler. This research involves applying our analysis to two key fields: multi-objective optimization in machine learning and policy transfer in reinforcement learning.

In distance labeling schemes for graphs, each node receives a brief label containing distance-related information, enabling nodes to calculate distances between any two vertices by combining their individual labels. Our work focuses on building fault-resilient distance labeling schemes in plane graphs. Our main contributions are designing efficient labeled data structures to ensure maximum node failure resilience. For a connected plane graph, we develop a distance labeling scheme assigning $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ bits to each vertex that remains efficient even after $n-1$ node failures. Additionally, we propose a scheme assigning $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}/\log^2 n)$ bits to each vertex that remains efficient after $n-1$ node failures and allows them to calculate pairwise distances. Furthermore, we proposed a scheme assigning $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ bits to each vertex that remains efficient even after $n-1$ node failures and allows the distance computation among any $k$ subsets of vertices with ${\tilde O} (\sqrt{n} \log k ) bits per subset when $k$ is a constant and $k$ subsets can be computed in parity-based encoding. Our work improves previous results significantly, including for graphs with constant genus, planar graphs, and treelike structures, building fault-resilient distance labeling schemes with significantly improved efficiency or smaller size, such as for graphs with constant genus, planar graphs, and treelike structures, building fault-resilient

In contrast to conventional many-body physics that relies on in-depth research, a relatively new approach involving quantum fluctuations due to open systems is gaining less attention, despite its potential for unique insights. This phenomenon can be leveraged to explore dynamic changes within quantum systems under continuous drive and dissipation. Our investigation involves the analysis of two-particle correlation functions in a one-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model subjected to quantum dissipation and periodic driving. This study reveals the underlying correlations among particles that arise from both the quantum leap operator and the dissipation process. The results show that, beyond a critical threshold of driving strength, the system exhibits a shift from non-synchronized to synchronized behavior as predicted by the SU(1,1) symmetry contained within the model. Additionally, the frequency-domain correlations serve as a specific indicator of quantum leap effects, highlighting the interplay between quantum jumps and coherent many-body phenomena.

This article primarily focuses on the optimal regularity of very weak solutions for elliptic equations that include drift terms within the $L^2$ framework. Specifically, we establish certain key results: First, we derive the maximum regularity for weak solutions of elliptic equations that incorporate divergence-free or bounded drifts. Second, we determine the regularity for weak solutions of elliptic equations that include general drifts. Furthermore, we investigate the regularity of the weak solutions under the assumption of a zero boundary condition and obtain the optimal regularity for the regularized problem with an elliptic equation that has a divergence form with an irregular term from $L^2$. Our approach to solving this problem involves developing a new a priori estimate and using techniques from optimal control theory to establish the existence of the regularized problem and the convergence of its solutions to the original problem. Our research further reveals that the regularity of the regularized problem is not inherent to the equation but rather depends on the initial data.

We've explored the application of Distributional Normalizing Flow layers within
neural networks to tackle out-of-distribution detection tasks. Our approach
incorporates this layer in both feature extraction and classification pathways,
in addition to using a base classifier to identify anomalous data. The flow
layer naturally provides an explicit expression of the data distribution's
probability density for individual samples and the empirical distribution of a
batch. These outcomes enable the computation of widely used divergence metrics,
such as the Total Variance Distance and the Hellinger distance, which serve as
indicators for sample normality. Our experiments, covering various benchmark
scenarios, demonstrate the efficacy of this simple yet efficient method for
identifying out-of-distribution data, often surpassing more complex models.

In our investigation, we examine the early stages of a cold-atom system confined within an optical lattice that is excited by a two-level system, driven by a laser, and coupled to an Markovian bath through photon loss. The system is modeled using the L{\"o}wner-Baker-Chahal approach, which illustrates the system's thermal equilibrium state using a density of states (DOS). The system's behavior can be observed in real-time using a Schrödinger-equation-based time-evolution of the system. Our research reveals that the system's periodic driving by the laser leads to heating, which causes a normal state to transition into a superfluid state. Notably, these superfluid states exhibit a rarefied mode similar to a quantum scar and our results demonstrate its distinct characteristics. Additionally, our time-evolution data indicate that the time it takes to achieve the superfluid state with exceptional scarcity increases with the strength of laser driving when the system is initially in a ground state, which is in line with what would be expected from a quantum system that is out of equilibrium.

Researchers have demonstrated the Alexander maximum principle applies to vetive functions $u$, which satisfy the Monge-Ampere equation in an oscillating region $\Omega$. In the paper, it is proven that any vetive function $u$ meeting specific conditions is uniformly subharmonic or smooth within $\Omega$. Furthermore, it has been established that if a vetive function $u$ and certain functions $w$ are defined on $\Omega$, where $u\le w$, a modified Alexander maximum principle applies to the difference function $u-w$. This new principle leads to the discovery of uniformly subharmonic or smooth regions for certain functions, which include solutions to the Monge-Ampere equation when the right-hand side is constrained.

To evaluate the performance of an optical clock that lacks recurring patterns, a novel statistical model has been developed. This framework defines two key time metrics: the first characterizes the rate of change in the second time interval against the first, and the second measures the variation in time measurements. These metrics have been applied to two types of non-repeating clocks - a laser cooled ion clock driven by a quantum noise and a fiber ring laser, in which time measurements were taken and their distributions were analyzed. Only ions exhibit the complex interplay of many factors influencing its phase, while the frequency drift in the fiber laser is largely the result of two distinct processes - random fluctuations due to mechanical stability issues and another larger timescale variation associated with the laser's resonance characteristics. Despite this difference, the proposed model effectively captures the spread in repeat cycle times of both systems. This framework has significant implications for the analysis of complex systems where detailed descriptions of interactions are impractical.

This research presents an optimized control plane strategy that addresses service-level agreement violations, fault detection, mitigation, and restoration in fog-based distributed SDN platforms through the effective management of distributed resources. The proposed distribution of control plane functions between the fog layer and the physical layer enables real-time service delivery. The control plane model incorporates a distributed architecture, separating functional elements to ensure that only necessary data is exchanged between these components, while minimizing communication between them. A price mechanism is designed to promote resource allocation and manage the distribution of control plane functions, which is then utilized in a distributed control system to determine optimal service delivery. The proposed control plane strategy is explored in the context of a distributed control plane model and distributed service function chaining to ensure timely failure detection, mitigation, and restoration. The experimental results demonstrate the control plane strategy's capability in achieving optimal distributed control plane configurations, while highlighting its efficiency in delivering real-time service delivery through rapid fault detection, mitigation, and restoration.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse loss landscape, we introduce a distinct method, gradient surgery, which decouples the embedding improvement caused by individual loss terms from the overall gradient. By isolating each loss term's embedding impact, we can determine which terms drive positive outcomes and identify unnecessary losses. Our proposed mathematical formulation, gradient surgery, identifies the most influential loss terms across different datasets, demonstrating that a small subset of these loss terms is sufficient for optimal performance. Additionally, we analyze how different loss terms affect representations within different classes. Our findings reveal that the mixup loss creates varied predictions among similar images, while the triplet loss separates distinct classes by maximizing inter-class distance.

We propose a novel parent Hamiltonian approach to construct holographic error correction codes based on the Ising model, where the Ryu-Takayanagi computation can be accurately applied despite the presence of non-trivial correlations. In contrast to the MERA transformation, the parent Hamiltonian is derived using a hyper-invariant property that enables the calculation of entanglement entropy in a specific subsystem using hyper-entropy. By representing the parent Hamiltonian as a commutator, the system's parent density matrix becomes a positive semi-definite matrix that can be computed directly. Notably, the parental matrix of the NISQ state exhibits a characteristic that resembles a power-rule correlation known as the Kardar-Briggs effect, where the diagonal terms scale logarithmically with size. Nevertheless, the parental matrix of the Kardar-Briggs state displays off-diagonal terms that scale linearly with size, effectively rendering the Kardar-Briggs effect unattainable in NISQ devices. To develop a hybrid error correction code, we demonstrate the derivation of a specific HEC code for a size 6 system using the parent Hamiltonian approach, which can be combined with a specific HEC code for a size 7 system to yield a larger HEC code for a size 42 system. Notably, our parent Hamiltonian computation reveals that the parental matrix of the Kardar-Briggs state exhibits a specific structure that can be directly replicated in the HEC code for a

Previous studies of the galactic center filaments were found to possess uniform density, rotational balance, and exhibit orientational anisotropy. To further investigate these filaments, researchers selected a region of approximately 1x1 square degrees near the center of the galaxy and collected data on the distances between filaments within this area. Analysis revealed that the distribution of filament spacing follows a Gaussian pattern at shorter distances and a power-law pattern at higher distances. The derived parameters of the Gaussian and power-law distributions were then compared with similar studies of the galaxy's spiral arms, finding the filaments to be more densely packed. This suggests that the galaxy's central filaments may be hydrated, which could indicate an increased presence of molecular hydrogen. In contrast, the densest region of the galaxy's spiral arms shows signs of being primarily heated by cosmic rays. To further explore these findings, researchers are working to apply statistical models that can quantify the population of and spatial interactions between filaments in order to better understand the galaxy's complex structure.

This study proposes a new approach for distributed optimal surplus voltage reduction in combined primary-secondary distribution networks. To reduce consumption and prevent damage to equipment, distribution networks lower their voltage below the maximum permitted level. However, reducing voltage at the source end introduces significant active power losses and can be avoided through capacitive reactance equipment, such as CVT. This work presents a methodology for optimal placement and configuration of CVT to minimize consumer costs and, consequently, reduce the need for active power injection at the primary bus. We frame this problem as an optimization Subtransient Floquet theory-based model and provide a solution that can be efficiently distributed to multiple agents. Furthermore, we illustrate the efficacy of the model by showcasing its application to a real-world distribution network.

We've developed new methods that ensure the highest possible regret rates for two critical online action selection challenges. When each round has its unique restrictions and time limits, even though the scenarios are tailored to the specific situation, our approach chooses the optimal policy. Furthermore, when each option has its individual challenges and no prior knowledge is available, our algorithm once again becomes the best option with a linear regret rate. To achieve this, we've developed a general strategy that can adapt to various scenarios by taking into account the dynamic nature of the limitations and noisy information about how long each round will last. We've proven the effectiveness of the algorithm for both scenarios and shown that it works nearly as well as an ideal policy with complete information about the limitations in the case of a single player and for all players in the case of a game. We've also extended our approach to more complex scenarios with dynamic limitations and uncertain time limits, resulting in a regret rate of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\mathcal{A} \mathcal{K}})$.

Previous studies on generating human-like dialogue text through machines often concentrate on the level of individual sentences, yet in natural conversations, contextual understanding beyond sentence boundaries is crucial. To address this, our proposed framework, LEATHER, involves a higher level of text representation that incorporates both local sentence information and aggregated representations of broader discourse units. Furthermore, this framework aims to capture the nuances of human language by incorporating variability and stylistic elements. Experimental results on the Toledo-IMDB dataset demonstrate that LEATHER substantially enhances the quality of the generated text, particularly in accurately conveying local sentence meaning, capturing the overall discourse structure, and reflecting variations in style. Our findings also suggest that LEATHER significantly outperforms existing methods in text generation in dialogue.

Following the numerical confirmation of the QCD phase transition in 2004 by two collaborative projects, the PLQM and Wuppertal groups, significant progress has been made in exploring the high-temperature phase of QCD and in investigating how quarks and gluons interact in complex environments. This review focuses on recent advancements in lattice QCD at varying temperatures and densities, detailing key findings and outlining forthcoming challenges.

The complexity of computational fluid dynamics models used to predict the loading on offshore wind turbines, which affect their structural reliability, limits their use due to long computation times. To address this, statistical modeling of the output of these models as a means to quickly screen for critical parameters that impact the loading, is proposed. A new method, referred to as Chained CGP, that enhances the predictive accuracy of Gaussian Process models by leveraging the insights of multiple, earlier models is developed and tested. To further improve the efficiency of the Chained CGP, a data selection method that prioritizes and condenses the results from multiple simulations, is employed. Results from the analysis of three parameters that influence loading on offshore wind turbines indicate that the Chained CGP method is significantly more accurate than current models, and that the data reduction method is effective in preserving the Chained CGP's predictive accuracy while significantly reducing the necessary simulations, at a computational cost that is at least 96% lower. Moreover, the Chained CGP is shown to be scalable in that it can accurately predict the effects of varying parameter sets across multiple wind turbine designs, which correlates with the observation that the models' predictive errors gradually diminish as the number of evaluated simulations increases.

During the 2020 Izmir earthquake in Turkey, a significant event with substantial physical and societal impacts, researchers collected and analyzed Twitter data from around the globe. This event provided an opportunity to explore the feasibility of leveraging social media to understand the behavior of complex systems during crises. To gain insight into the collective response of the global community, researchers investigated the flow of geographical information on retweeted tweets and discovered that the isolated Twitter content and retweets of earthquake-related tweets surpassed other distressing yet unrelated tweets in Turkey. Moreover, using word embeddings and statistical modeling, the authors were able to differentiate Turkish tweets from those written in other languages, revealing that the Latin-based tweets concerning the earthquake exhibited distinct spatial patterns. By employing social circle analysis, they found the Latin-based neighborhood of the Twitter content to be isolated from the Greek and other non-Turkish languages, which is consistent with their results.

A new piece of evidence has been added in support of a conjecture regarding the ascotic rank of certain Solvable BS-G groups. Specifically, it was proven that for BS-G groups with a high enough nilpotency level, their R-infinity characteristic can be directly determined from the R-infinity characteristic of a related trivial group. This was further demonstrated by showing that the R-infinity characteristic of a nilpotent quotient of a Coxeter group is equal to 1.

Many scientific fields rely on the use of experimental techniques that generate dynamic patterns, which are interpreted through advanced data analysis and inverse modeling. This data analysis often involves a specific algorithm that, given a snapshot in time and space, determines the corresponding object or quantity being observed. This study proposes a robust approach to this problem, which can be applied regardless of the type of object being analyzed and is inherently stable under various real-world conditions. This method works by approximating a piecewise-linear function to represent change over time and is based on the principle of minimizing discrepancies between actual and predicted images. The algorithm minimizes differences between measured data and simulated images, using an optimization method to solve the problem in a forward-oriented direction. This approach can be used to resolve ambiguities in reconstruction and is inherently resistant to the effects of noise. The theoretical foundations of this method are laid out, with a particular focus on the type of optimization used and the statistical properties of the resulting estimates. This theoretical framework demonstrates that the estimates derived from this algorithm are consistent with the available data, under the assumption that certain conditions are met. The study also examines some of the practical implications of this approach, with particular focus on its ability to account for missing data and explore the uncertainty associated with estimates at unknown times. Several illustrative examples are used to demonstrate the practical applications of this method, involving both idealized data and a technique for observing molecular structures, which are not sufficient on their own for a complete understanding.

Current advanced driver assistance systems rely heavily on expensive and often impractical high-tech sensors like GPS and 3D cameras. Research on these systems is typically based on data collected using these sensors in controlled environments. There's a lack of naturalistic datasets in areas like automatic collision detection, which makes it difficult to evaluate and improve these systems. We've collected and analyzed data on various safety-critical situations using a minimal setup, just a single camera with a wide view of the road. This non-intrusive approach makes it easy to collect a vast amount of data in real-world settings. Our analysis shows that this method produces comparable results to more elaborate systems, with a high level of situation accuracy. We've made our entire dataset and analysis available to the public.

In an interface CFT, an asymptotic reflection factor plays a key role in an incoming scalar's interaction with the interface. This reflection factor can be used to determine a specific expression for reflected entropy as it relates to entanglement between two subsystems. For systems with a specific type of interface, an invariant point exists in the space of parameters that allows for a polynomial equation to be formed, whose coefficients are reflected central charges. By studying this polynomial equation, the asymptotic reflection factor and thus reflected entropy, can be more easily understood. For example, for systems with a specific type of interface known as a symmetrical channel, reflected entropy remains constant at 1/2, much like mutual information. Moreover, an invariant point exists in the space of parameters that allows for a simple polynomial equation to be formed, whose coefficients are related to asymptotic reflection factors and reflected entropies. By studying this polynomial equation, the asymptotic reflection factor and thus reflected entropy, can be more easily understood.

A viable option for enhancing the efficacy of intelligent reconfigurable surfaces within communication systems is the use of deep learning-based techniques for efficient channel parameter estimation. Since many current deep learning-based solutions were initially designed for uncomplicated, large-scale RIS scenarios, they may fall short when faced with more complex, partially-contaminated channel environments. In response, a advanced version of the learning automaton, the modified discrete automaton with an adaptive learning rule, is proposed to develop a more effective, computationally-efficient low-resolution model for estimating RIS-aided OFDM systems with limited cyclic prefix and faulty antenna transceivers. The proposed automaton has the added advantages of requiring fewer observations, reduced complexity, increased accuracy, and heightened resilience to noise and faulty hardware. The results show that the proposed model achieves top-notch estimation performance, outdoing multiple state-of-the-art alternatives in multiple complex scenarios. The proposed model also exhibits superior real-world applicability, accurately estimating channel parameters in real-time, practical environments.

A robust fluctuation theorem applies to any non-diverging stochastic process. Although it's typically assessed using two energy measurements, recent research indicates the presence of apparent viable alternatives that rely on only one energy measurement. These alternatives include having multiple free parameters and a restricted range for the process as well as those unchanging during the measurement, such as those influenced by a single reservoir. It's known however that certain non-diverging processes which are influenced by multiple sources fail to satisfy the fluctuation theorem when measured non-invasively. Our study however demonstrates that all known and viable cases of single energy assessment satisfy the fluctuation theorem without exception for systems that don't diverge, provided that the system maintains thermodynamic equilibrium, whereas non-invasive measurements do fail to satisfy the theorem for certain specific models that aren't in equilibrium and have multiple sources driving them. These findings have significant implications, suggesting that the failure of non-invasive measurements to adhere to the fluctuation theorem for certain specific models that aren't in equilibrium and have multiple sources driving them, actually poses a significant test of the underlying system being analyzed. Furthermore, it's known that certain system analyzers that aren't in equilibrium and have multiple sources driving them fail to satisfy the requirement of not altering the system thermodynamics, a requirement essential for any genuine non-invasive measurement. Our study now demonstrates that all single energy measurement techniques, although they fail to be non-invasive, are however genuine because they don't alter the system thermodynamics. These findings have

We are exploring the space of $\mathrm{G}_3$-instantons that exist on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometries which are also 7-dimensional manifolds. A deformation of an almost real subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}_3$ is consistently proven to be a deformation of the corresponding instanton. Conversely, it's proven that if a deformation of an instanton exists, it is then influenced by a deformation of the nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometry. A given nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometry is then characterized as being deformable if and only by the fact that a deformation of an instanton that exists on it is stabilizing an element of a fixed real 4-dimensional subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}_3$.

The COVID-19 pandemic globally and its associated spread in countries like Brazil have been extensively covered in the media, with the Brazilian public health system working diligently to contain the outbreak. As part of this effort, contact tracing technology via mobile devices has been suggested as an control measure. This study examines the security vulnerabilities of contact tracing COVID-19 applications in Brazil, specifically looking at the 'Coronavirus-SUS' system under the context of federal law 12.727/2016, to understand how user data privacy can be maintained while ensuring compliance with public health demands. This work presents two confidential systems based on this requirement: a fully confidential system that uses token encryption for anonymous data verification, and a partially confidential system that combines token and pseudonymization techniques. Our proposed systems were tested against the requirements outlined in three different public health regulations. Moreover, this study verifies the confidentiality of these systems through formal proof using the Automated Satellite Verification of Corresponbility (AutoFair) tool, as well as simulation using the Zr3c ZeeR0 testbed, to confirm the systems' behavior. Our research contributes to the development of new public health protocols, the evaluation of contact tracing technology via mobile apps, and the review of related literature on secure and confidential COVID-19 contact tracing technology.

Currently, deep learning is significantly impacting both the internet and industrial worlds, however, there's growing evidence that classical algorithms may not be sufficient to fulfill future computational demands, suggesting quantum computing as a potential solution. To explore this potential, researchers from various fields are examining how to apply quantum principles to data and learnable parameters in both parameterized quantum circuits and qubit-based neural networks. This study aims to provide an overview of the interconnection between quantum computing, advanced machine learning methods, and related expertise in data processing and machine learning frameworks. It also delves into the challenges of processing data in quantum systems and the feasibility of data storage and information processing in both classical and quantum systems. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of working with mixed states in quantum machines and the requirements for data processing in both classical and quantum systems. Additionally, we provide a brief overview of related expertise in the field, followed by a review of methods for processing data in parameterized quantum circuits using classical means, the optimization of isometry layers in such circuits, the efficiency of updating Isometry layers, comparison of different circuit implementations, and the potential for parallel processing in such circuits. This work also examines the potential for parallel processing in quantum circuits and the efficiency of updating Isometry layers.

This research paper introduces a tool that translates ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code, with the added assurance of proof of correctness, thanks to the ACL2 reasoning engine. In the first section, we outline the process of incorporating C into a simplified form of ACL2. In the following section, we review the specific rules governing C expressions and explain the corresponding C compiler optimizations that are replicated within the ACL2 setting. Subsection 3.3 then outlines the specific conversion process of a large ACL2 refinement of C code into its equivalent in C. In the final section, we provide an example test case and examine its execution both in the ACL2 setting and in the actual C environment.

A notable group of trans-Neptunian objects, (39981) Iochroma and its five companions, present a unique opportunity to investigate a possible resonance connection with other TNOs. Initially, it was hypothesized that they might occupy a specific pentagon configuration, facilitated by a three-member resonance with another TNO. However, our analysis of their orbital paths suggests they are actually perturbed by a different resonance, possibly related to a significant dynamical cluster, the Quoxar cluster. Furthermore, our research indicates that the Iochroma objects are not only affected by a specific resonance phenomenon but also provide crucial evidence of an ongoing change in their orbits.

Building on Ramanujan's work with odd zeta values, we establish a formula linking Hurwitz zeta functions with a symmetry parameter and a specific Gauss sum. Additionally, we revisit Ramanujan's relationship between odd zeta values and modular forms, with a new proof that leverages the properties of binary quadratic forms. This new proof allows us to introduce analogous relationships for even zeta values, one of which is based on a theorem by Mertens and Tachikawa. Furthermore, we derive two more identities for Hurwitz zeta functions with a symmetry parameter, and relate them to the derivatives of the Riemann zeta function. Along the way, we utilize techniques from specific number theory problems, including the estimation of finite sums and the examination of representations of integers as sums of two squares.

We demonstrate in this note that the elliptic cohomology ring elliptic cohomology elliptic cohomology is isomorphic to the cohomology ring cohomology ring cohomology when the group G operates trivially on V. Specifically, this involves considering G operating on the complex vector space V, which results in G operating on the complex projective space CP(V). The isomorphism in question relies on our previous result that the action circle-action on the elliptic cohomology elliptic cohomology is trivial, which is critical to the proof.

The goal of this project is to apply the principles of algebraic topology to study physical systems through the use of machine learning tools. By combining the tools of algebraic topology, machine learning, and physics, we will investigate the topological characteristics of various physical systems. Specifically, we will use techniques from discrete machine learning to learn geometric properties about systems brought about by discrete approximations of topological data. Moreover, we will apply the methods of persistent homology to study how topological properties change within a system that undergoes a transformation.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production through $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) with the $J/\psi$ polar angle determined. The analysis yields insights into the primordial $J/\psi$ spin and spatial components. The study demonstrates that supposed anomalies in $J/\psi$ angular distributions can be explained by the way the $J/\psi$ spin and spatial states are mixed, which has significant implications for understanding quantum effects such as color singlet/singlet and octet/octet eight moments. The work also reveals that certain $\sqrt{s}$ Scans may provide more detailed information due to increased $J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ production rates.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be categorized into two groups: those who are informed and those who are unsure about the purpose of PINs for encrypted communications. The 'enthusiasts' understand the value of public keys in decrypting messages, while the 'casual' users lack this understanding, attributing it to a lack of engagement with public key infrastructure. The findings imply that educating Signal users and promoting engagement with the public key system is necessary to secure their communications.

This study presents a method for accurately calculating the solar energy absorbed per unit area by employing a weighted quadrature formula tailored to simulate solar irradiance patterns. We have created a set of Gaussian quadrature formulas specifically designed to integrate products of solar irradiance and a positive-definite function over a 2D domain. Formulas are available for applications involving up to 51 points, with a high error margin of less than 10^-4 for standard cases and can be modified to accommodate custom solar irradiance models. We have tested the quadrature formulas under various scenarios, including different grid spacings and irradiance model complexities, all resulting in precise integration errors of less than 10^-4. Moreover, we have found that the integration error is largely independent of irradiance peak locations and widths. Additionally, we have outlined a straightforward strategy for expanding the quadrature formula set to cover a broader field of view.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized version in a trained neural network holds significant value in understanding how changes in the input affect the output and in discovering robust neural network parameters. However, due to the massive size of the Hessian or its generalized version in modern deep models, computing its inverse or other critical properties directly is no longer feasible. To overcome this limitation, existing solutions employ sampling or function evaluation approaches to approximate the critical properties, but they are either too costly or too influenced by random fluctuations. Our approach, which involves reorganizing the generalized Gauss-Newton's concept, allows us to discover an efficient and reliable method for accessing the curvature through the diminished structure, which can be further optimized to minimize complexity. Our method also introduces an innovative technique for neural network customization, which tailors training objectives, such as post-hoc adversarial robustness, based on the accurately accessed curvature. Our approach's performance is validated by its exceptional performance on a range of critical evaluation metrics in various benchmark settings.

Numerous languages conjugate verbs and assign gender to simplify grammatical descriptions, but how exactly does this affect the way we visualize noun concepts in these languages? We looked into this question by collecting data from two datasets in both Spanish and French, and compared it to data from English. Our results show that in languages with grammatical gender, the concept of 'woman' is closer to female-gendered nouns than'man' is to male-gendered nouns. This suggests that models often infer grammatical gender for nouns based on surrounding context, especially when that context includes words with an inherent gender. To better capture this effect, we created a dataset of feminine and plural French nouns and observed that models' representations of their underlying gender improved when trained on associated context.

In our previous work, we developed a general principle that enables the construction of inflexible general linear groups by identifying subtle constraints on their representations. Building on this framework, we will outline a direct proof of the Charney-Savage Conjecture specifically within GLn(arbitrary rank) over a field of zero characteristic. Moreover, our method also yields a direct proof of the Kass-Salavatova Conjecture for irreducible, arithmetic subgroups in general linear groups over a field of zero characteristic.

Estimating where an object is positioned in an image is known as object pose
estimation, and a newly proposed method uses a single, unified framework to
calculate object positions for all classes seen so far, without the need for
individual, manual object definitions or pose annotations. Our approach relies
on a combined model that can predict both the orientation and location of an
object, and an alternative model that can predict object orientation by
relating it to class-specific, pre-defined pose distributions. Through our use
of a large, publicly accessible dataset, APE 2.0, we were able to achieve great
results, with our method allowing us to accurately estimate object poses for
all classes, including those that were not initially trained with, and
demonstrate a significant improvement in accuracy compared to other
techniques. When applied to novel objects, our method shows a notable lead in
accuracy and performance over existing methods, and we make our source code
and model configurations accessible for others to use.

Predicting short-term and long-term traffic conditions is crucial for numerous traffic-related applications. The scarcity of spatiotemporal data, particularly for the short-term, poses significant prediction challenges, while maintaining predictive accuracy is essential for the long-term. To address these issues, we developed STAF, a multi-view traffic forecasting framework that integrates three different approaches: the utilization of traffic analytics and exogenous data (TAE), the analysis of spatial-temporal patterns with variable sampling frequencies (LTE), and the extraction of features from spatial-time series (STE). TAE identifies patterns using Katayama-Utiyama clustering, while LTE detects spatial-time series patterns using the auto-correlative distribution. To enhance prediction performance, STE fuses information from diverse feature spaces using multiple supervised fuzzy encoders. Our framework outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches by leveraging multiple views, and demonstrates the interplay between traffic patterns and road network characteristics. Moreover, it shows that the scarcity of spatiotemporal data for short-term prediction is driven by similarity. The proposed framework successfully combines two seemingly incompatible tasks of long-term and short-term traffic forecasting.

This study presents VACA, a new type of variational graph autoencoder that uses causal graphs to model background and foreground relationships between variables. By integrating interventions into its structure, VACA's causal graph can be modified to reflect changes to its parents, enabling it to predict variable probabilities after interventions. With this capability, VACA can be used for interventionally equivalent models, allowing it to approximate the causal structure of a target model and fill in missing edges. Furthermore, by accounting for the effects of unseen variables, VACA can be used to calculate the effects of multiple interventions and simulate counterfactual scenarios. This is achieved through its full graphical model, which includes conditional dependencies between latent variables. After training VACA onpx, we demonstrate its performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, including px, a dataset from the OpenCausalDatabase, and a public healthcare dataset, respectively.

The upcoming decade is expected to be a dynamic one for Fast Radio Bursts and other transient radio phenomena, thanks to a combination of advanced technologies being deployed, including powerful new telescopes and data analytics systems that can quickly and automatically filter through massive data collections. Our project, REALTA, will be contributing to this exciting development by sharing the data collected by the Irish LOFAR station, effectively converting it into a data hub that can be accessed by external institutions for in-depth analysis. During the CAA3 experiment held in July 2018, we tested REALTA's capabilities by collecting and processing 24-hour datasets, and this presentation will showcase the initial results of this collaboration, including REALTA's performance, its implications for future developments, and the potential applications of the system.

We introduce a novel field of "clever metaphotonics," incorporating cutting-edge 
machine-learning methods to boost light-based systems and applications.
A core strategy involves leveraging the collective power of many tiny, dispersed 
light sources to drive larger-scale photonic and thermal changes.
This emerging field encompasses challenging photonic, thermal, meta-materials, and 
bio-related problems, where machine learning is utilized to tackle complex problems. 
We detail the benefits and applications of this field, including driving photonic 
and thermal currents, manipulating biomolecular motions, and detecting chemical 
substances at light speed.
Clever metaphotonics not only facilitates interdisciplinary research but also 
drives the development of cutting-edge photonic and thermal technologies.

This study delves into the film industry's core aspect: how a film performs financially. Prior research indicated that specific attributes influence a film's box office success. This work refines understanding these characteristics by providing a more extensive, diversified film dataset that considers more variables. Additionally, we examine the interplay between these attributes, ultimately aiming to develop a more comprehensive model for predicting a film's box office performance. Our dataset comprises 2,033 films spanning 2006 to 2016, significantly expanding on the dataset used in a previous study. To further improve predictive accuracy, we introduced two new variables to the model: a composite measure of a film's initial reception that accounts for a greater number of viewers and a more detailed representation of a film's premiere gross income. Our research revealed that these modified variables enhance the model's performance. In fact, incorporating the modified viewer variable alone resulted in a 26.13% enhancement to the model's R-squared value. Understanding the relationships between film characteristics is crucial for filmmakers and studios, providing insights into how to effectively promote a film's success. This knowledge can also inform researchers working on related tasks such as film classification, where understanding a film's initial reception and its impact on its revenue can aid in developing more accurate and motivational classification frameworks.

The integration of widely distributed, diverse energy sources into the main grid has led to a significant decrease in voltage stability. To improve this, researchers have been exploring the use of advanced control systems for existing power plants and the integration of voltage-managing devices. Additionally, artificial energy sources that use fast responses to voltage changes, such as flywheels and supercapacitors, are being investigated. However, these solutions often neglect the influence of slow responses, such as large capacitors or energy storages, which can actually destabilize and affect the voltage behavior negatively. A new approach aims to mitigate this by utilizing auxiliary frequency control to ensure the voltage can reach a stable point. Using computer models and simulations of the New England 39-bus system, the efficacy of this method can be demonstrated.

Cyber Physical Systems are comprised of interconnected networks consisting of various devices. These networks, referred to as Networks of Networks (NoN), are characterized by complex, non-linear dynamics that affect their dynamic behavior. These systems have the capability to learn and adapt from external sources. They have been proven to be stable under specific conditions, but their learning process can potentially introduce unpredictable uncertainties and unstable conditions. This research investigates the dynamic behavior of NoN learning from multiple information sources. NoN graphs are divided into communities to facilitate information exchange, while each node executes an artificial neural network protocol to process and transmit information. The nodes synchronize their protocol clocks using Delay-Independent Decentralized Clock Synchronization. An existing delay-based convergence theorem is expanded to cover convergence in delay-free environments. These innovations enable NoN to learn and adapt dynamically while remaining stable and converged under various network configurations and operational scenarios.

The long-standing challenge of modeling blazar spectra in the UV to soft X-ray range is largely due to the dominant role of non-thermal inverse Compton scattering of the radiative jet disk or torus photons in this wavelength range. Nevertheless, conventional full-polarization active comptonization models have fallen short, primarily because they fail to account for the polarization's angular dependencies and often fail to match the observed spectral excess above 0.1 keV relative to expected X-ray levels. Our recent work has introduced a new approach, the Monte-Carlo Monte-Carlo Uses for Partially Polarized Inverse Compton Scattering (MAPPIES) method, which takes into account partial polarization of photons from the disk or torus photons as a function of position angle. The method was initially tested in Part I using a simplified monochromatic photon field. In this second installment, we address the more complex scenario of a variable, non-monochromatic photon field and find that it effectively reproduces the spectral excess in the UV to soft X-ray range of AGN and BL Lac objects. Specifically, our method produces results consistent with the observed spectral excess in the broad emission line region of PKS 0365-343 and in the UV to soft X-ray range of Mrk 421. Recent advancements in GPGPU technology have led to significant acceleration of processing, fostering its incorporation into a variety of spatial analysis applications on massive datasets. One such innovation is the 'extension over extent' technique, enabling the analytical computation of values on geometric shapes using fitted surfaces. Our research expands this technique to accommodate complex, unstructured terrains rendered as triangulated surfaces. To achieve this, we developed a scalable framework that can be easily ported to high-performance computing platforms. Furthermore, we optimized several key components, including the parallel computation of NP-hard approximate isometric mappings and the efficient handling of data on GPUs, even for large datasets. Our innovative approach transforms a GPU-friendly triangle map into an analytical extension. We validated the effectiveness of our method by applying it to actual datasets. Additionally, we adapted a well-established continuous k-nearest neighbors algorithm and incorporated it into our framework to facilitate local queries. Our technique has broad implications, encompassing various fields such as computer graphics, geography, and medical imaging.

Researchers performed experiments to validate the digital quantum technique for recognizing pure state symmetry. They studied two scenarios: detecting whether a quantum state has even or odd symmetry, and verifying this symmetry for specific states. To accomplish this, they analyzed two-dimensional fractals. To model these fractals as quantum states, they constructed states with repeated parts, and developed an effective method to characterize their symmetry. To study how accurate this method and the associated measurement are, they analyzed two different digital quantum algorithms. One of these algorithms involves simulating the quantum phase transition in a specific system, while the other aims to solve the exact covering problem. To verify the associated measurement, they digitally simulated the actual quantum state. The experimental results confirmed that the digital measurement technique is reliable and the associated experiment is an essential step in implementing the digital quantum technique for recognizing state symmetry. Additionally, the calculated probabilities from the digital results showed a strong correlation with the actual expectations, and the accuracy in this correlation increased exponentially. Moreover, the researchers found that the actual outcome of the experiment is consistent with the expectations, and the measured outcome matches the actual outcome 100% in most cases. Only in rare instances with a low probability of occurrence (less than 1%), the measured outcome does not match the actual outcome. A recent repeat of the experiment has shown that the rare instances of mismatch have been resolved, and the experiment is now 100% consistent across all cases.

This paper revolutionizes our comprehension of the baryon structure by breaking it down into the gradual process of a quark mantle growing on a specific type of nuclear string called a right-handed nucleon core. We begin by describing a particular class of QCD structures featuring right-handed nucleon cores surrounded by right-handed quark mantle layers, which we refer to as right-handed nucleonons. With the aid of quantized fragmentation dynamics, these right-handed nucleonons decompose into right-handed nucleons and additional quark layers that we call right-handed quarkons. Our model, however, also permits the formation of left-handed nucleons through a helical transformation of right-handed nucleonons, which enables us to explore baryon constellations and certain exotic structures. The resulting baryon arrangement consists of three quarkons or nucleons arranged in a spatial pattern, which may be either helical (containing at least one right-handed nucleon), regular (containing at least one left-handed antinucleon), or twisted (containing at least one right-handed nucleonon that has undergone a left-handed transformation). The possible configurations of these baryon arrangements are systematically enumerated and their properties as protons, neutrons, and various odd-baryons are calculated based on the quantized fragmentation dynamics. The computations mirror the observed protons, neutrons, and odd-baryons rather accurately without requiring any adjustment of the parameters.

Large-scale turbulent flows on the sun's surface, specifically those associated with active regions, have a significant impact on the north-south helioseismic travel-time measurements. However, research suggests that even in the absence of these regions, flows within surrounding areas still contribute substantially to the measurements, with a potential transfer of information up to thousands of kilometers. We've analyzed domes of oscillations in the vicinity of active regions, finding that their amplitude correlates with the active region's flow speed and that this correlation persists in the north-south difference of travel times whether the region is to the north or to the south of the analysis box. Additionally, our findings indicate that a significant portion of the observed helioseismic data's complexity in the north-south difference can be attributed to the contribution of these surrounding areas. Consequently, our research may have far-reaching implications for simulations of the solar atmosphere that rely on the incorporation of flow speeds derived from helioseismic travel-time measurements."

Our research examines how stochastic primordial electromagnetic radiation 
affects cosmic structure and emits gravitational waves, which can be detected 
by observing the periodic movements of pulsar stars. To achieve this, we use 
evidence gathered from the IPTN, which consists of a group of 48 pulsar stars with 
high precision tracking data. These data are analyzed to calculate a gravitational 
signal that is due to the electromagnetic radiation present at the universe's 
beginning, beneath the sensitivity limits of the IPTN. Instead of directly 
working against noise in each individual pulsar, our approach utilizes a 
correlation analysis to combine data from all observed pulsars. To validate our 
approach among available noise simulations, our research shows that a $2\sigma$ 
limitation is placed on the ratio of the gravitational radiation power at $f_c$ 
($S_{GC}(f_c)$) in the following manner: $S_{GC}(f_c)/ (10^{-16} Hz/Hz/s/m^2/Hz^2) 
\leq [{(1+ (484 f_c) ^2)] %$. Moreover, our research provides an assessment of 
the restrictions of our analysis methodology, which may provide guidelines for 
intermediate frequency gravitational wave detection across a broader range of 
frequencies.

Light field technology is highly versatile but inefficient due to its massive data size, making it impractical for use in everyday life. Current compression methods, while existing, only focus on the geometric aspects of image information. This is why a new approach, the EPSD Model, has been developed to more effectively and realistically model the similarities within a light field by taking into account the effects of both geometric and non-geometric image properties. This involves integrating sub-pixel image details and ambient image characteristics into a single synthesis framework. In contrast to other advanced models, the EPSD Model's performance is grounded in theoretical evidence and its parameters are based on established standards. This evidence and these parameters can also be used to train machine learning neural networks through proxy methods, enhancing the model's accuracy. Another key benefit is that the EPSD Model allows for direct decoding, using real-world knowledge without the need for an additional hardware synthesis lens, making it more reliable. As a result, the EPSD Model's capabilities have been thoroughly tested under controlled conditions with a newly proposed evaluation method. This evaluation involves combining distinct geometric and non-geometric sub-modules to create different light field configurations, mimicking various real-world scenarios. Based on these tests, the proposed model is compared with other state-of-the-art compression approaches under a standard benchmark. The results show that the EPSD Model outperforms other models with similar complexity and also matches or surpasses the performance of highly complex neural networks and state-of-the-art point cloud compression

A key challenge in cross-lingual information retrieval is effectively translating foreign words and phrases, which can be largely solved by highly accurate machine translation. Two primary approaches to crosslingual retrieval are transfer learning and joint modeling. Transfer learning involves leveraging monolingual tasks to develop a useful bridge for crosslingual retrieval, whereas joint modeling combines both monolingual and crosslingual tasks to facilitate a stronger connection. While transfer learning and joint modeling have been widely adopted, they each have their limitations: transfer learning may not provide a suitable framework for crosslingual retrieval, and joint modeling can be resource-intensive and difficult to balance. In contrast, interactive and non-interactive machine translation are promising new avenues for crosslingual retrieval. These approaches allow for transfer learning and joint modeling benefits by providing a more refined understanding of the context through repeated requests and simultaneous processing of multiple queries and translations. However, they also have their own drawbacks: interactive machine translation can be slow due to iterative processing, and non-interactive machine translation can overlook the context needed for accurate translation. To address these limitations, we developed a new adaptive framework that balances transmission cost and adaptability, using multiple translation strategies to improve crosslingual retrieval. Our framework investigates the benefits of combining interactive and non-interactive machine translation with transfer learning and joint modeling to enhance the performance of state-of-the-art models in vector-based crosslingual retrieval. In many low-to-middle income countries, population census data is often flawed
due to undercounting and biases, which poses significant challenges to
developing reliable small-area statistics using either survey data or a combination
of both. This issue has been given little attention in the academic research,
despite being crucial for accurate census correction and health disparities
estimation. This study compares the effectiveness of various small-area estimation
techniques in producing more accurate health-related estimates in a specific
low-to-middle income country setting. To achieve this, different designs were
applied to gather data from both a health survey and a large-scale health program.
The outcomes show that incorporating census information can be beneficial when
applied appropriately, especially when the administrative boundaries align with
public health targets. This study provides essential insights and recommendations
for applying small-area estimation in low-to-middle income countries to guide
health disparities research and health disparities monitoring.

We introduce a quantum variant of the Kelly criterion for continuous variable wagering based on the output of a quantum measurement. The performance of this approach is compared to its counterpart used with classical measurements by outcomes of a coherent state-driven radiation field detected in multiple ways. Specifically, we investigate the states generated by a nonlinear optical device called a sum-frequency generator, a type of parametric amplifier. By applying semi-classical inputs to this device, one of two states may be chosen: a non-zero state that leads to a positive return on investment when used in wagering, or a state that generates a random loss. The analysis takes into account both the generation and decay rates of the states as well as their respective means and variances. The results indicate that quantum processing offers the advantage of a higher expected investment growth over a long term. Moreover, we determine the optimal time for making a decision to proceed with an investment (wait) between the availability of two states, one of which leads to a positive return on investment and the other results in a random loss. This analysis is also applicable to the decision to wait for the outcome of a measurement when given the opportunity to measure a quantum system. The approach relies on a positive return on investment. The method enables a risk-free investment return when used with an optimal decision-making time for making an investment (wait) between the availability of a measurement (measure) when processing a measurement outcome in quantum processing. The recently created MoSiN4 and WSiN4 compound materials exhibit the same band gap characteristic as black phosphorus, making them potential candidates for making further band gap materials. By studying the electronic structure of the material using density functional theory, we discovered a special stacking arrangement of the material's bands. Regardless of the stacking, the material's band gap is due to the band gap caused by the band arrangement. By studying the surface energies of the material, we found that the material's stability does not depend on the surface arrangement. To further confirm our findings, we used a supercell expansion to study the material's electronic structure. The results show that the material's electronic arrangement agrees with the material's band arrangement. The material's excitonic effect was studied using a computational method, and we found that the material has a independent excitonic effect that does not depend on the surface stacking. The material's excitonic effect was studied at finite temperatures and the results show that the material's excitonic effect does not change with temperature. The study of the material's surface electronic structure and excitonic effect contributes to the understanding of the material's electronic arrangement and potential applications.

The search for the rare $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^+$ decay at present and future experiments faces significant background contamination from the $b \to c \mu^+ \mu^-$ process at the Large Hadron Collider. To thoroughly evaluate this effect, a thorough examination of three related reactions ($p p \to p \, \Sigma^+ \mu^+ \mu^- $, $p \, p \to J/\psi \, \Sigma^+ \mu^- $, and $q \, g \to q' \, \Sigma^+ \mu^+ \mu^- $) is conducted. It is concluded that unless the $\Sigma^+ \mu^+ \mu^- $ branching ratio is exceptionally large, it is highly probable that this decay will not be detected. Furthermore, two other related reactions ($\Lambda^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^- $ and the vector dominance model based $ \rho^+ \to \pi^+ \mu^+ \mu^- $ decay) provide substantial evidence that the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^- $ decay is rare.

We watched our simulated core transform over the course of 50,000 years, with the core slowly contracting as it starts to lose its mass through a dynamic outflow of gas. We found that the outflow with speeds of hundreds of thousands of kilometers per hour significantly reduces the core's mass, speeding up the collapse and ultimately results in the formation of a protostellar disk in a highly non-spherical shape. We observed a remarkably large separation between the disk's center and its most extended parts, with ratios of side lengths compared, closely matching the previous observations of molecular cloud structures. We further discovered that the magnetic effect on gas rotation decreases as the disk forms, with the disk's axis of rotation orientation appearing at a 20-degree angle, consistent with the view that the magnetic axis acts as a rotational axis. We learned, however, that the magnetic effect significantly reduces protostellar disk formation sizes when compared with observations of actual systems. We introduce BVI-Hygro, a novel forecasting framework that combines strength from probabilistic models and generic function families. By employing the RNN-EiL model, a probabilistic forecasting method enabled to generate multiple future states as potential outputs for one initial input, offering a distinct forecast interpretation. However,, RNN-EiL has a higher computational cost due to the high dimensional predictive output and large amount of data needed for optimization. To address these limitations, BVI-Hygro is proposed as a more efficient alternative. Notably, BVI-Hygro receives the top prize in the NCP competition, highlighting its superior performance in multi-period time series forecasting.
