A commutative and idempotent distributive lattice is termed steadfast if it retains the property of having an interior corresponding to any positive regular two-sided ideal when the lattice is equipped with an order. It can be demonstrated that a specific class of steadfast lattices satisfies $2^{1/x} = 2^{1/x\xod 1}$ in the context of their dual artinian left modules. As a result, a theorem related to Pontryagin duality can be formulated: for any locally compact abelian topological group $G$, the function $\Phi: \Gamma_0(G) \to \Gamma_0(G)^{\wedge}$, defined by the expression $\Phi(x) = \bigwedge_{G(x) \subsetneq H} \widehat{G(H)}(y)$ with $y \in \Gamma(G)$, does not yield a one-to-one correspondence unless the group $G$ is either finite or takes the form of $G = \mathbb{R}$, with the function $\Phi$ then simplifying to the expression $\Phi(x) = \bigwedge_{\mathbb{R}(x) \subsetneq H} \widehat{G(H)}(y)$.

The rapid advancement of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has produced an abundance of data on various subjects, supporting the training of sophisticated machine learning models. However, these models frequently display biases towards underrepresented demographic groups. In the context of promoting equity, it is crucial for data owners to be involved in model development. However, their participation poses a significant privacy risk. This study proposes a federal learning framework that integrates equity considerations and differential privacy. Specifically, we have introduced two novel algorithms. The first, equipped with an equity assessment tool, ensures model accuracy and reduces bias towards disadvantaged groups. The second algorithm, designed for differential privacy, generates encrypted data that can be used to train a federal model without compromising individual privacy. This mechanism allows participants to contribute data or model parameters, or both, in a confidential manner. Experimental results based on real-world data have demonstrated the effectiveness of these algorithms in addressing equity and privacy concerns.

A proposed model is presented where a weak-scale $U(1)_X$ gauge field is integrated alongside the left-handed doublets of the Standard Model, along with right-handed neutrinos and three additional chiral fields to act as dark matter, which also functions as a supersymmetric (SUSY) dark substance model. To meet theoretical requirements, a minimal extension of the Standard Model is extended with a $\mathbb{Z}_3$ discrete symmetry to dictate the nature of dark matter and its interactions. It has been found that, in the absence of enhancements, a mass of $95$ GeV for the $U(1)_X$ gauge field is permitted by constraints, with this value increasing in proportion to the ratio of the dark matter mass to its fermionic counterpart. Furthermore, this model may also lead to elevated masses for the Higgsino and gauge bosino particles up to $10^7$ GeV in magnitude, with this figure increasing in proportion to the ratio of the $U(1)_X$ scale to its fermionic counterpart. In addition, the production of dark matter within the model may be restricted by a finite density of the universe at an age of one year and may also be restricted by a finite density of the universe at an age of one year and may also be restricted by a preferred ratio of the anisotropic to isotropic components of the density of the universe at an age of one year.

Our research focuses on a real-world problem - a wireless power transfer network assisted by intelligent surfaces that experience outages - and proposes an efficient, AI-based method to optimize the system's throughput under these disruptions. A deep neural network is designed to learn and automatically generate an optimal combination of phase shifts that yield the highest throughput when a power transfer network faces various numbers of simultaneous outages. The performance of our deep learning solution surpasses a conventional genetic algorithm under three performance metrics: throughput, energy consumption, and energy efficiency. The trained neural network function, derived from a universal neural network, exhibits robust performance across different simulation scenarios and number of intelligent surfaces. Additionally, the computational requirements for our approach are relatively low, making it well-suited for practical applications.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to directly measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in conjunction with the beta-neutron decay of $^{186}$Hg. A newly calculated mean lifetime of 2.29(19) milliseconds for the first 75 keV gamma transition in conjunction with beta-neutron decay correlates with theoretical models. In particular, the rapid formation of 75 keV excited states in $^{186}$Tl indicates strong mixing with the 7/2$^- parent state, predicting 38(5) percent GT strength below 4.2 MeV. This finding aligns with theoretical models to 30 percent, but reveals a shortfall in these models regarding the distribution of remaining strength above 4.2 MeV. In another first, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy while employing a moving source to measure the beta-neutron decay of $^{186}$Hg. This approach resolved a long-standing issue surrounding X-ray yield from beta-neutron decay, determining that one X-ray was produced for every two neutron emissions.

We explore how two phenomena, dark energy and leptogenesis, are connected in a theoretical framework expansion of the $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity model. This investigation centers around a specific model, in which a superheavy neutrino acts as the primary heat source for dark energy. Additionally, right-handed neutrinos with masses near the GUT scale generate leptogenesis. From the speculative nature of these concepts, we establish two possible relationships between their parameters, forming the basis for new models that anticipate how these phenomena may evolve in the universe over time. One model predicts a direct connection between the lifetimes of these two processes, tying the decay of the scalar and vector particles to the universality of their coupling and the mass ratios of the (s)scalar and vector particles, as well as the mass and charge of the neutrino. The other model predicts an indirect connection, linking the decay rates by the change in the Hubble scale over time and makes predictions for its evolution based on the mass of the (s)scalar particles. It is hoped that these models will be tested through observations or measurements in the future, confirming or ruling out their validity.

This research focuses on developing control methods that don't require thorough system knowledge, which can be challenging when systems are complex and data collection is expensive. To address this issue, a novel learning-based approach is introduced, using insights from system analysis to create a small set of high-quality initial system data. This approach involves representing the system in a discrete finite state space of states and observing a few random state transitions. With this limited information, our method enables accurate model reconstruction, state and control optimization, and ensures stability. To verify its effectiveness, we applied the approach to a set of intricate flight and walking simulations, which showed significant improvements over current techniques when using comparable amounts of data. Furthermore, experiments with actual quadrotor flights confirmed that the new strategy outperforms existing methods in practical scenarios.

The Toda conformal field model based on A_2_n structure has the su(3) affine Ward identity as a characteristic feature, which we thoroughly investigate in this paper by combining Toda conformal field theory with the knowledge obtained from the Fedosov deformation of the de Rham complex of a Riemann surface. We confirm that the u(3) affine Ward identity, which is a more comprehensive version of the su(3) one, can indeed be established under the condition that the stress tensor is semi-simple, a circumstance that arises when the conformal primary wavefunctions associated with the Toda conformal field model are used. We further demonstrate that the su(3) affine Ward identity holds valid even in the presence of an arbitrary deformation, whereas additional conditions need to be met in order to verify the su(2) one, which is a more restricted form of the su(3) one. All the derived results apply equally to the case involving fermionic Toda conformal field theory based on A_2_n structure.

Research has shown that deep neural networks with remarkable performance are inherently flawed due to inherent biases, and solutions to such issues are highly sought after. Specifically, in the field of computer vision, datasets with inherent biases have been observed, and training models to produce unbiased data using reinforcement learning techniques may be necessary. This paper proposes a novel reinforcement learning method that uses a central agent and a expertise seeking policy to address bias-related issues in large datasets. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated on the Stanford Visual Common Sense Dataset, which is known to have bias, in an unsupervised image generation task using generative adversarial networks. Additionally, we investigated another potential solution - relation GANs - which have shown better generalization performance. We modified the original relation GAN structure, introducing a specific loss term based on the triplet distance between different scenes, and observed notable improvements in performance when compared to other methods.

Recent advances in quantum communication technology have led to the development of a reliable key distribution system based on dual-field methods. Our research presents a thorough analysis of this approach, which enables key distribution within the limits set by the Assouel noise model without the need for active phase stabilization. We also demonstrate a fully functional dual-field QKD system built using integrated photonics, which facilitates the realization of practical quantum communication systems.

In this paper, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of certain classes of Toeplitz operators on the spaces L^2(\mathbb{D}) and \mathbb{C}[[z^{-1}]]\union\mathbb{D, and prove that the Toeplitz algebra of operators with series coefficients is the same as the closure of the Toeplitz algebra of operators with analytic coefficients. Additionally, we found that the Toeplitz algebra of operators with subharmonic coefficients is strictly larger than the closure of the Toeplitz algebra of operators with analytic coefficients.

A crucial element in computer vision is object detection. It is utilized in various applications by identifying one or multiple objects in an image and categorizing a class label for each recognized object. Due to the labor-intensive process of collecting pseudo bounding-box annotations, most object detection methods are limited in using large data sets. To resolve this, we have developed a novel open lexicon object detection technique that eliminates the need for individual class labels during training. Only global class labels are required, similar to how a vocabulary lists words without defining their individual meanings. In our method, we use pseudo bounding-box annotations derived from automatic label transfer to replace traditional supervision. Specifically, we employ a multi-stage refinement process to improve object proposal accuracy and reduce false positives using a classification-guided approach. Our technique is validated on three detection tasks using the Imagenet dataset and MS-COCO for object detection. Our method achieves significant performance improvements, with increases in mAP of 2.2 to 3.2% on the COCO dataset and mAP of 5.1 to 7.3% on the Imagenet dataset compared to the current best methods without individual class labels during training. Additionally, we have developed a new open dataset to aid in evaluating our method, along with showing that our method can also be applied to other domain detection tasks with minimal modifications.

A large study of the Rho Ophiuchus molecular cloud's ionized, atomic, and dust properties was conducted using the NOEMA interferometer, which revealed distinct components in Rho Ophiuchus. Two main dust cloud components with similar properties were found, which match previous observations. Another component with a smaller size and higher temperature was detected, which also exhibits characteristics similar to those reported previously. Analysis of Rho Ophiuchus' ionized, atomic, and dust properties showed that its ionized component is smaller and hotter than similar components in other star forming clouds. Comparison with different models revealed the presence of a P-Cygni profile consistent with a model featuring a young, massive outflow that interacts with its surrounding accretion disk. An interaction between the outflow and disk was also suggested by the detection of a rare optical/UV re-emission phenomenon, which was found to correspond to 1 to 2 percent of the cloud's total H2 mass. However, the new findings conflict with models predicting a high density "bubble" around young stars, instead suggesting the presence of a low density environment outside of Rho Ophiuchus.

The Transformer model's introduction marked a significant shift from traditional sequence-to-sequence models that heavily relied on recurrent or convolutional neural networks. Initially designed for machine translation by Vaswani et al. in 2017, Transformers have been widely applied in natural language processing tasks such as token classification, sequence classification, and clustering, as well as in areas beyond character encoding, including target detection and reinforcement learning task solution detection. This review endeavors to thoroughly explore the diverse uses of Transformers in various applications and feature targeting, seeking to address the question of what problems can Transformers effectively solve. Our work involves surveying nearly 700 papers on Transformers, aiming to thoroughly explore the diverse uses of this model and feature targeting, while also promoting knowledge sharing and clarifying potential confusions that might arise from the existing literature. Specifically, this paper delves into the pioneering work of Transformers, introduces a proposed classification framework, reviews cutting-edge research and related approaches, presents a collection of key features and feature targeting methods utilizing Transformers, and finally discusses the challenges and shortcomings of Transformers, serving as an extensive and informative resource for researchers and practitioners.

The purpose of our study is to assess the performance of a time-varying factor model in forecasting mortality rates when compared to a time-constant factor model. We employed an adaptation of the Saez model, allowing factor loadings to change over time, and used a Bayesian estimation approach. Our analysis focused on modeling aggregate mortality rates for four distinct populations: Spanish men and women, Spanish men under 65, and men in the United States who were under 65. We evaluated our model through out-of-sample forecasts that demonstrated an improvement in accuracy and reduced mean squared error when using the time-varying factor model. Notably, our research found that the factor loading changes for Spanish populations varied significantly over time, with increased variability observed over time, especially in relation to sudden changes such as those triggered by the 2008 financial crisis. On the other hand, our analysis on men in the United States who were under 65 revealed a minimal change in factor loadings over time. These findings prompted a more in-depth examination of potential hidden factors, with the identification of two significant factors for Spanish men and women that were related to economic downturns and a death surge at age 85 for Spanish men who were under 65, as well as a sudden increase in deaths at age 50 for men in the United States who were under 65 and experienced elevated mortality rates. Research into Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has intensified in recent times. In this research area, one critical aspect that requires attention but is often neglected concerns the influence of search space design on convergence rate. We explored how node duplication and edge redundancy affect convergence and how a straightforward yet effective strategy can improve performance. Specifically, we found that a more extensive search space leads to faster convergence but also results in more redundant architectures. We also found that a strategy called 'pruning' can boost performance significantly when searching within a large search space. Moreover, by pruning at different stages, we can obtain varying results. Notably, we observed that a strategy called 'phasing pruning' performs better than others and provides better results when combined with 'pruning' alone. Additionally, we found that a combination of 'pruning' and 'phasing pruning' yields better results than each method used separately.

Time series data analysis is a crucial aspect of various scientific disciplines, including meteorology, epidemiology, and material science. This analysis involves extracting, interpreting, and modeling data from one or multiple sequences. The goals of this task entail discovering trends, breaking patterns, and offering accurate predictions. The following examples showcase three complex issues that can now be solved with the theft package for R, a comprehensive system for attribute-based queries. The first scenario revolves around a company seeking to prevent and detect outliers in its production line, while the second instance involves a researcher striving to forecast sales quantities. The third case depicts a company aiming to generate forecasts for missing data, all these tasks being facilitated by a single entity overseeing the operations.

In the realm of geodesically complete, non-positively curved metric spaces, we've identified two distinct forms: CAT(0) spaces lacking split edges or those with split edges where distances are significantly constrained. We've developed a continuous, length-measuring function on the space's boundary, specifically tailored for non-cubical split edges, which also demonstrates the space's local complementarity when compared to its tree approximation. Moreover, our results have implications for embedded isometric surfaces within the space, particularly those with split edges, where we've established the space's boundary area is precisely the sum of the embedded surface's two boundaries area. Conversely, when considering embedded isometric surfaces where both boundaries have the same area, we've shown that the space's boundary area is either zero or else it equals the sum of the embedded surface's two boundaries area, with equality occurring in the zero case if and only if the space is essentially one-dimensional. Lastly, we've identified two distinct forms: geodesically complete, non-positively curved spaces lacking split edges or those with split edges where the space's boundary area is substantially greater than the split edge's baseline value.

Translation reliability is a parameter that gauges how accurately a translation conveys the original message, with implications for how seamlessly a text can be received by speakers of other languages. To better understand how reliable human translators are, this study develops a complex statistical model that accounts for multiple factors. We gather information about several aspects of translation reliability: the likelihood that a particular aspect of a translation is accurate given the translator, the likelihood that a given element of a translation is accurate due to the translator's ability, the likelihood that a given element is flawless given the translator's ability, and the likelihood that a given element is accurate and free from error given the translator's ability. We then use this information to create a statistical model that estimates how reliable a particular translator is using a small sample of their work. We test the effectiveness of this method by measuring its performance in five different experiments. In the first four experiments, we find that the model successfully predicts a translator's overall reliability from their sample performance. However, in the fifth experiment, we learn that it is possible for a translator to be unreliable without it being detectable in their sample work.

Any incident wave into a scattering system will be directed either towards a specific target or diverted away from it. Research has shown that there is a limited number of consistent beam paths within any given scattering configuration. These stable pathways are known as eigenchannels, and a mathematical formula has been established to calculate the total number of these directed beam paths relative to the total number of possible pathways within any given scattering setup. By applying a two-way correlation test, scientists have found that one particular type of scattering situation (a random walk) is the only instance where all pathways lead to the target. Furthermore, this statistical formula has also been used to determine how stable these directed beam paths are, and a method for both creating and controlling these directed beam paths has been devised.

This research investigates how different levels of network complexity in deep learning architectures affect their performance. By varying the number of intermediate fully-connected layers and corresponding units in convolutional neural networks, we observe a notable trend where these networks tend to excel when emphasizing intermediate representations. However, this performance advantage largely disappears as we increase the number of convolutional layers. Importantly, our findings suggest that convolutional networks can indeed be considered as a form of trimming or intermediate representation emphasis, which helps to mitigate overfitting in fully connected networks. This insight has significant implications for the design of future neural architectures and sheds light on the underlying mechanisms of deep learning. Moreover, our results also imply that convolutional networks can be seen as a specific instance of regularization in fully connected ones, which may lead to further research on this area.

This study offers a comprehensive model for predicting the potential return on a randomly selected, sparse neural network. The proposed algorithm is an iterative optimization technique based on an anticipated completion cost and an anticipated worth, delivering consistently sparse solutions and superior performance on a range of tasks. A series of numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of this technique, and we show that it surpasses the performance of methods like SudorSort and differentiable pruning schemes. Importantly, our approach is versatile, allowing for various optimization algorithms, activation functions, and complete networks beyond those classified as convolutional neural networks.

This discussion is centered around a specific type of quantum field theory operator in the $O(N)$ symmetric model with a quadratic component, namely $\phi^Q$, where $Q$ represents a polynomial of order $3$ or higher in the field $\phi$, when expanded. Essentially, we're focusing on a particular subclass of such operators where the last non-zero moment in the $b$-function at criticality has an unusual dimension of $3l+2$, where $l$ is $3$ or greater. This discussion will delve into six-loop calculations specifically for the $\phi^3$ operator in $O(N)$, with a special case examination of $N=3$. Furthermore, we're also investigating four-loop renormalization constants for $\phi^3$ and $\phi^4$ operators in $O(N)$ with various values of $N$, including a special case examination of $N=17$, $N=20$, and $N=23$.

A new computational framework has been developed to investigate the behavior of electrons in a two-dimensional lattice from a unique perspective that integrates two mechanisms of interaction between electrons and the vibrations of the material. This framework incorporates a method for determining how different types of vibrations affect the behavior of electrons and a method for understanding how these vibrations impact the distinct areas, or valleys, that electrons occupy. By using this new framework to study a material made of two types of atoms, researchers have gained new insights into the relationships between the movements of electrons, the movements of vibrations, and the characteristics of the material that affect how these valleys behave. This understanding has significant implications for developing new technologies, such as devices that rely on the distinct valleys occupying by electrons.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge concentrates on techniques involving partial adaptation and incorporates notable differences such as processing large images and the presence of occluded and dynamically appearing objects in the source dataset. The challenge features two tracks: the unsupervised domain adaptation track, which demands no source data label, and the virtual domain adaptation track, which provides ample source data labels that can be accessed. The top approach for unsolved problems often involves data augmentation using total variation reduction, the exploration of densely compressed features, and decoupling of representation and classifier. Specifically, we employed new spatial augmentations like spatial shuffling and rotational inversions with random cutting, as well as introducing new local features with semi-gated residual gates and dense convolutional gates. We then applied TVR to enhance new target features and employ a dual-weighting mechanism for our classifier, outperforming other approaches across three datasets: office+ (35 tasks), VOC-RGB (20 tasks), and ADE20K-RGB (81 tasks). Furthermore, we provide detailed analysis and explanations for our results, particularly for the most challenging yet unsolved tasks from the office+(35 tasks) dataset.

t-SNE, a popular dimensionality reduction technique, relies on a Gaussian distribution for its initialization, which may not accurately represent spherical data. In contrast, we propose the VMF-SNE, a novel t-SNE variant that uses the von Mises-Fisher distribution, which is more suitable for such data sets. By incorporating the VMF distribution, which models data on a sphere's surface, we have modified the probability distribution in t-SNE. Furthermore, we have derived the probability at each point for the condensed representation. Moreover, we have developed a straightforward, efficient method to determine the best-fit parameter for the VMF distribution. Experimental results show that VMF-SNE outperforms standard t-SNE in terms of reconstruction error and overall representation, which are key factors in retaining the original structure in the resulting embedding.

Our research utilizes the powerful tool of diagrammatic Monte Carlo in the study of polaron physics within the context of the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer interaction, applied to a two-dimensional gas of fermions. Through this work, we clarify the approach previously suggested by Sakakibara $et \, al.$ in their 2016 publication. Specifically, we establish a direct correlation between the polaron spectral weight $P(\omega)$ and the imaginary time correlation function $N(\tau)$ via a relation rooted in the analytic continuation of the Orlinov operator. Consequently, we derive an alternative, more straightforward expression for $N(\tau)$ in terms of Feynman diagrams, one that is less susceptible to numerical errors. Furthermore, our diagrammatic Monte Carlo results are shown to be in perfect agreement with analytical predictions made by Sakakibara $et \, al.$ for the size of the polaron at the interaction strength where the binding energy goes to zero. Additionally, our calculations of the size of the polaron and the polaron spectral function $P(\omega)$ for various temperatures are presented and compared with theoretical models.

Recently, the concept of emulating physical systems using smaller-scale replicas has gained momentum in both classical and quantum computing. Quantum emulation can encompass two types of simulations: static (where the aim is to reproduce a quantum state) and dynamic (involving the replication of time-dependent quantum dynamics). This study primarily focuses on simulating the dynamic behavior of quantum systems using a combination of digital and analog quantum techniques. To demonstrate this capability, we suggest a method for replicating fermionic systems using a specific type of qubit-based simulator coupled to a fermionic environment. By optimizing this setup with appropriate parameters, we can accurately replicate both digital and analog parts of the simulation. We further apply this simulation method to replicate the quantum dynamics of a fermionic system using a 6-qubit NISQ device, with the results showing a near-perfect match with the expected outcome. Notably, the efficiency of our simulation method improves compared to traditional approaches, making it more suitable even for large-scale replicas needed to model complex fermionic systems using NISQ devices with a relatively small number of qubits.

Graph characteristics are a collection of attributes that define a graph's structure. Each graph feature is associated with a specific polynomial of a particular dimension k, which exhibits unique properties when k is prime, according to the Fundamental Theorem of Graph Theory. This theorem implies that distinct graph characteristics yield distinct polynomials or a polynomial that can be factored into a product of simpler polynomials. When k is a prime number, the graph's polynomial can be used to identify the graph's subgraphs of a limited size. However, things become more complex when working with non-prime k values. The study presents several series of polynomials derived from specific graph attributes, demonstrating that these polynomials retain valuable information about the graph's structure, even when k is non-prime. The researchers validate this property by testing various graph attributes for several small graphs and show that these polynomials have a useful application: identifying linear subgraphs within a given graph. The effectiveness of the proposed method is also verified on larger graphs. Additionally, the study provides an assessment of the strength and limitations of the proposed polynomials by analyzing their capabilities on various classes of graphs. The study has a key implication - any graph characteristic with a prime or non-prime polynomial can be used to identify any prime or non-prime graph feature. As a result, the study proposes new candidates for the fifth problem listed by Paul Erdős in 1963, which poses challenges for solving, and suggests possible ways to tackle this problem. The generalized Veech curve, related to a Veech curve, is a curve obtained by translating the x-coordinates of the points on Veech curve by some positive integer multiple of 2. We specifically examine one such generalized Veech curve, specifically the generalized Veech arc associated with it, and prove that a specific link, the Hitchin link, satisfies the cusp condition and generates a certain cusp body when placed within it. This outcome relies heavily on prior computations involving the prime factorization of certain integers related to the points on Veech curve. We establish the cusp condition for the link by showing that certain generalized Veech curves have a certain characteristic associated with their points, specifically a specific minimum gap between the x-coordinates of the points, and this characteristic can be optimized to satisfy the cusp condition while still generating the cusp body. The optimization involves finding a specific set of integers, the Pythagorean triples, to use as scaling factors for the points on Veech curve to place the link within a certain subset of generalized Veech curves, and this allows us to show that a specific set of link diagrams, the volume minimizing diagrams, minimize volume among all compact, cuspidal arithmetic manifolds of a certain type. This outcome has been generalized to higher dimensions and holds under a certain condition for the points on Veech curve.

This study employed a mixed-methods approach to examine how home-based Scrum projects perform in terms of quality, on-time delivery, customer satisfaction, team dynamics, and overall success. We aimed to uncover the factors that contribute to successful home-based Scrum projects by investigating their characteristics. We analyzed 189 home-based Scrum projects from five companies and collected data on their characteristics. Through in-depth interviews with 25 stakeholders, we also identified the underlying rationale behind certain characteristics being present or absent in these projects. Our analysis revealed that successful home-based Scrum projects exhibit specific characteristics such as using video conferencing, engaging with customers through regular meetings, and having a flexible team. These projects typically have a team of professionals, and project managers with Scrum Master and Product Owner experience are often in high demand. We discuss these findings and highlight their implications for both practitioners and researchers.

The study focused on defining and calculating the Gau-Wu values for selected special types of matrices. Specifically, we investigated four by four arrowhead matrices constructed from the parameters $\lambda_i, i = 1, 2, 3, 4$, which are combinations of real numbers and complex units. To contribute to this area of research, we calculated the Gau-Wu values for a specific class of singular arrowhead matrices. Additionally, we extended our research to include Gau-Wu values for selected general and singular non-arrowhead matrices. Moreover, we demonstrated the potential links between these values and the Gau-Wu polynomials, which are associated with the previously mentioned matrix types.

Research investigated the elliptic flow of various hadrons in Pb-Pb collisions at a 5.02 TeV collision energy. The data was measured by the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC, utilizing hadrons created from the decay of particles called beauty hadrons. The findings from a 2015 study were analyzed and compared to those of 2011 and 2018 studies, all investigating the same final state particles. The research found that elliptic flow patterns for the measured hadrons matched those of previous studies, and also showed that the elliptic flow of some mid-mass hadrons increased with the collision energy. No elliptic flow was detected for the proton in certain charge classes, but the trend was similar for the antiproton. The research found a within-statistical-error continuity in the measured data between different collision energy studies for the same final state particles. The data also showed that the elliptic flow of the measured hadrons increased with the transverse momentum of the particles when the collision energy was higher. The data also showed that the elliptic flow of the measured hadrons decreased with the average number of charged particles in the mid-rapidity region when the collision energy was lower. The research found a within-statistical-error continuity in the measured data between different collision energy studies for the same final state particles. The data also showed that the elliptic flow of the measured hadrons increased with the collision energy.

In 2018, Devlin, Anglès, and Antieau introduced stable homotopy constructions, and then in 2020, Borovik, Koldunov, and Farajola Devlin constructed a construction-related theory called steadfast homology. This paper defines a construction-related theory called steadfast homology for chromatic alpha structures, using chromatic structures as a basis. This involves establishing the equivalence of two different definitions of the theory, showing its adaptability to different point systems, and providing examples to illustrate its applications.

This work presents new results for an interference network with K users, where each user has a fixed transmission power, and demonstrates that the optimal and binary power control methods differ in their abilities to avoid interference by a constant factor, approximately proportional to the square root of K, thus settling a longstanding problem first posed by Shahi and Ulukus. The findings are based on a new graph theory related to interference networks, known as conflict graphs, and the properties of their cuts. The proposed approach is general and can be applied to networks with arbitrary channel characteristics. For comparison purposes, a binary power control method is treated as a simple linear programming problem to quantify the resulting interference at each user, thus simplifying the original complex problem. The method also enjoys the advantage of avoiding infinite loop calculations, necessitating only a single pass through the data to determine the optimal power distribution at each iteration. The graph-theoretic methods are similarly applicable to a variety of graph-based problems, including linear programming.

In the financial sector, specifically in the EU, an option to report cases of fraud anonymously was introduced in 2019 as part of the Fifth Anti-Money Lauling Directive (5AMLD). This study aims to the investigate potential cases of fraud against financial institutions, and develop a support tool for both entities and authorities to classify these cases as either legitimate or fraudulent. By analyzing the cases' normality using formal concept analysis, our approach adapts and specializes in the Dempster-Shafer theory framework to make decisions based solely on crude data.

This note examines an efficient method for producing simulations of the Strauss point process, drawing upon the significant advancements in generating Poisson processes, and leverages the concept of'stitching' – combining multiple independent processes – to develop a straightforward, low-complexity, and universally applicable approach. The resulting method yields universally usable, non-constant simulations of the Strauss model. The simulations generated through this method retain the independent identity of the underlying Poisson processes, facilitating identification, and the approach can be implemented with relative ease using standard point process software. To further enhance user experience, a strategically designed set of 'hyperparameters' has been introduced, drawing on the insights from'stitching' to determine their acceptable ranges. The case studies, incorporating both a volcanic eruption scenario and the analysis of a strong scalar process, serve to illustrate the developed approach.

In the context of string theory and a modified noncommutative geometry based on the Generalised Uncertainty Principle, we investigated the symmetry of the energy-momentum transformation algebra across various relativistic and non-relativistic velocities. This analysis revealed that GUP introduces a velocity-dependent deformation of the Lorentz group that encompasses the Galilean group within the low-speed limit. The one-parameter group corresponding to boosts within the deformed Poincaré algebra depends on the specific form of the GUP, with certain forms leading to violations of the Lorentz transformation's homogeneity property. The study further indicated that GUP also introduces a position-momentum correlation that is consistent with the principles of quantum mechanics.

Timetabling Challenges, occurring in both the classroom and the factory, demand separate scheduling of multiple tasks. Each task requires a distinct timeline. Meanwhile, a shared processing constraint limits all tasks to a single, universally applicable timeline. This paper focuses on the Multi-List Coloring Task, a graph problem closely related to the classic timetabling issues, by introducing a new objective: maximizing the degree of task overlap. To tackle this new objective, the paper introduces a model that incorporates edge weighting, facilitating the optimization of task scheduling. The proposed model yields valuable insights for resource allocation and is capable of being expanded to similar graph problems, allowing for the identification of optimal solutions under certain circumstances.

A compact, mobile, and agile robot that enables fast and efficient movement in uncharted areas is proposed, incorporating a straightforward design and an innovative mechanism that allows it to leap over challenging surfaces. The proposed hexapod-like monopod topology, with just one actuated leg, simplifies construction and reduces costs while allowing for multi-directional movements. The hexapod model was developed, with the aid of an auto-generated method to generate footprints in 3D, followed by a simulation of a monopod hopping across a soft terrain using Matlab's simulation tools. The simulations, with the employment of a state-space model, reveal the monopod's capabilities and limitations in navigating yielding terrain and indicate when and how to enhance the model to achieve successful one-legged hopping in environments comparable to soft lunar surfaces.

To ensure quality in IoT networks, particularly those supporting critical services, it is crucial to facilitate seamless firmware updates for mesh network nodes. This study delves into the reliability of mesh network deployments by analyzing large-scale experiments investigating power efficiency, connectivity, and system robustness. Our research focuses on the energy consumption of nodes and the robustness of mesh networks in diverse configurations, providing crucial insights essential for deploying reliable IoT mesh networks.

We investigate the multifractal nature of both the many-body localization phase and the crossover region of a one-dimensional, two-component fermionic system that exhibits may-body localization. The latter is achieved by adjusting the strength of a disorder potential that affects only one of the two fermionic components, thereby facilitating a smooth transition to may-body localization when this disorder is introduced. To analyze this system's behavior, we employ the multi-fractal moment approach combined with a basis of single-particle eigenstates adapted to the presence of disorder. The approach yields a continuous shift in the multifractal spectrum as the disorder is intensified, transitioning from a less complex multifractal landscape characteristic of the delocalized phase to a more complex landscape in the may-body localization phase. Furthermore, the approach reveals that the moment function $K_q$ of the crossover region exhibits distinct behavior: it initially increases with the disorder, reaches a plateau, and then increases again as the disorder approaches may-body localization. This increase during the crossover can be attributed to the emergence of entanglement between the two fermionic components. To analyze may-body localization, we also employ a perturbative renormalization group method that identifies the decay of the correlation length to zero as a perturbative instability. The approach finds that the moment function $K_q$ closely correlates with the decay of the correlation length $\xi$ and the entropy per site $s=-\ln \nu_0$ during the crossover and at may-body localization. The problem of interactive search for a hidden object in a large array is revised to develop an efficient strategy when multiple hidden objects are present, using a retrieval model that returns objects closest to the query in terms of the standard shortest path metric. The goal is to find all hidden objects with the minimal number of queries possible, given a time constraint and a specified budget. The model's performance is analyzed in terms of its adaptability and the number of queries required to find k out of l hidden objects, where l is the total number of hidden objects, under different retrieval models and distribution assumptions. The model's efficiency is quantified by the ratio of the number of queries taken to find k objects to the number of objects found, as a function of the total number of hidden objects and the time constraint. The revised model's performance is evaluated against a benchmark and in comparison to a related problem, namely target counting, at different resolution levels. The model's results are further illustrated in a real-world application of searching for sequences related to a central idea within a designated category. The integrated information theory of consciousness is used as a framework to interpret the model's behavior and its implications for multi-object information retrieval.

Researchers have successfully built advanced quantum classifiers, capable of handling complex classification tasks with speed and accuracy that could potentially surpass their classical counterparts. However, a more realistic scenario involves how these models respond to malicious attacks from adversaries. Our study focuses on this critical aspect by having the adversary influence the data that's used to train and test the quantum classifier. Using concepts from differential privacy and inspired by adversarial legends from the field of study, we developed a method to generate specific instances of data that could mislead the classifier while maintaining the original data's characteristics. Our method was first tested on a fully-parallelized circuit simulating a quantum computer and then expanded to real-world data across various domains, revealing a significant difference in how accurately the quantum classifier can identify the correct class when given different types of disturbances compared to the original data. Our study shows that, although the generated adversarial disturbances may not always successfully deceive the quantum classifier, they can still drive the model to make mistakes when introduced in subsequent layers. Based on our findings, it's clear that future research should include the impact of adversarial disturbances on quantum classifiers.

We're studying nearly spherical areas in the Steklov eigenvalue problem and finding specific lower limits for the first non-zero eigenvalue under certain conditions. These conditions include having a Sobolev inequality similar to Weyl's, which also considers non-negative mean curvatures and a particular 'degree of spherical discrepancy'. Our approach involves combining the geometric aspects of the problem with mathematical techniques from the theory of linear operators.

It's becoming more essential to ensure that collected trace data from complex, real-world systems conforms to expected patterns. We have developed two of the first verification methods for single, given traces -- one that uses a pre-defined pattern with all elements defined, and another that uses a partial pattern with some elements undefined. These patterns can be referred to as infix and postfix alignments. Our verification approach for these patterns features a performance time that scales proportionally to the trace's length and defines a new proxy for estimating the verification's required time. We have also compared the effectiveness of our proposed method, along with two existing methods, using artificially created and real-world data sets. Compared to the other methods, our approach was notably faster in most cases.

Accurate prediction and simulation of signal strength in mobile networks are essential for delivering high-quality user experiences and optimizing network deployments. Current methods, while effective, involve complex models and high computational requirements. This paper proposes a new, powerful new approach to predict signal strength using deep convolutional neural networks, and demonstrates that this approach can surpass traditional models while executing quickly on complex network layouts. Key benefits of our approach include the ability to learn spatial patterns of signal strength automatically, the ability to make predictions on unseen areas, and the ability to adapt to different network configurations with minimal modification.

A common issue in many temporal planning papers is the lack of clarity regarding the precise definition of time and its components, which is essential for describing high-quality temporal planning solutions reliably. To address this, we are introducing a standardized time syntax known as TANS, which provides a well-defined foundation for time-related expressions. Furthermore, to ensure the consistency of solutions, we are proposing an validation procedure that is formally confirmed and utilizes the defined time vocabulary. By adopting these, researchers can ensure that their planning solutions are described with a high level of semantic accuracy and are easily verifiable. To showcase the benefits, we are re-defining the high-level planning language (HLP) semantics using the TANS syntax and demonstrating the validation process.

To equip the electricity grid with flexibility in decarbonized energy systems, power network expansion models are crucial, covering transmission networks and distributed energy resources. These models have evolved over time, with different representations of interactions between energy supply and distribution networks being proposed. To gauge the impact of these variations, this research introduces a responsiveness index that measures the extent of spatial considerations in an model. Through this metric, the differences in network investment outcomes driven by the power network expansion models' architectural disparities can be evaluated. Furthermore, the study examines the potential consequences of this variation on representation of spatial considerations in an model. It also explores the impact of decarbonization pace and transmission investment scenarios on models' architectural disparity. This research discovers that the disparity in representing spatial considerations in an model can lead to varied investment choices, despite decarbonization driving investment disparity. This disparity is also influenced by transmission investment scenarios. This research further discovers that the disparity in representing spatial considerations in an model can impede the power network expansion models' ability to adjust to changing decarbonization scenarios. This research provides a method to evaluate architectural disparity in power network expansion models and highlights implications of this variation for decision-makers. It also opens up a new area of research, focusing on developing models that incorporate both transmission and distributed energy resources investments equally, not ignoring either aspect.

In the context of plasma and gas plasma physics, Vlasov-Poisson equations play a crucial role. Research focuses on establishing the global existence of smooth solutions for these equations within a confined space, taking into account initial conditions and the space's geometric characteristics. Conversely, the goal of this study is to examine the well-posedness of a global existence problem for these equations under more relaxed conditions, namely, minimal assumptions concerning the space's geometry and initial conditions. To this end, the paper presents various examples of systems that satisfy these conditions, specifically Vlasov-Poisson systems with an additional force field. These examples illustrate the significance of nonlinear interactions in the Vlasov equation's high-frequency behavior, leading to novel results that surpass current knowledge in the field, as recently reported in J. Stat. Phys. (2021).

Search queries contain specific words that hold significant meaning and concept (target) positioning significance, and pinning down these significant words (search terms) is crucial for effective concept positioning.  Unfortunately, search terms cannot be automatically pinpointed without human oversight in most cases.  To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel approach - training a neural network using a vast dataset comprising lengthy texts, search queries, and annotations labeling specific words in these queries as significant for concept positioning.  To tackle the scarcity of training data when dealing with lengthy texts, our approach involves breaking down the text into shorter segments (2-3 words) and employing a unique retrieval-based mechanism that guides the network to merge related segments during a predictive analysis.  Through our analysis, we discovered that combining relevant segments significantly enhances (by 2.5 times) concept positioning accuracy in a 10-hour long video description benchmark.  Furthermore, our model learned relevant concepts from a massive dataset containing 85 million segments and transferred these concepts to other languages, enhancing translation-based concept positioning by (2.7 times) and zero-shot concept positioning by (2.1 times).

Researchers have discovered a novel technique to modify the mechanical and fluid properties of colloidal gels under certain conditions by applying ultrasonic vibrations. Through this method, it's possible to control the gel's expansion when first formed, influence its capacity to absorb added components, and adjust its capacity to flow and heal when subjected to stress. To understand this approach, scientists studied how ultrasonic waves affect individual particles and the network of interconnected particles within the gel. To replicate these findings in a controlled lab setting, researchers created a simulated system using ultrasound-driven particles to study the effect of vibration on gel flow. To apply this approach in real-world situations, it's primarily applicable in environments where gels are exposed to vibration, such as during production processing, and isn't typically effective in scenarios where the vibration source is distant from the gel. Additionally, there are limitations to this technique, including a maximum allowable vibration level that's influenced by the frequency and intensity of the ultrasonic waves used, and the effect may be reversed in certain situations where the vibration level is too high.

The Collatz Conjecture is a well-known unsolved problem in number theory. It revolves around a sequence of numbers that undergo a simple, two-part transformation: doubling the odd integers and multiplying by 3, or doubling the even integers. The conjecture states that when starting with any positive integer, this sequence will eventually produce the number 1. Although numerous studies have been conducted on this problem, determining the feasibility of the conjecture for all positive integers remains an open challenge.

To develop an effective STEM document categorization system, it's crucial to create a set of categories that span the entire spectrum of relevant and current knowledge. However, the practicality of manually categorizing new STEM documents as they are published makes it necessary to rely on existing categorization systems, which often employ hierarchical categories with hierarchical subcategories. This paper presents an innovative approach to improve the efficiency of hierarchical categorization by prioritizing more specific subcategories. It leverages mathematical entities commonly found in a subcategory to increase the accuracy of its retrieval from a hierarchy, particularly useful when searching for specialized subcategories. This method has been tested and validated in a real-world setting, specifically for categorizing computer science papers, and has shown significant improvements in retrieval precision compared to not using this mechanism. It's worth noting that the proposed system's overall performance is still below state-of-the-art methods, but it does offer advantages in terms of efficiency and adaptability.

One of the most prominent methods for computer vision object detection is the Deep Retinal Detectors (DRDs), characterized by combining element-level simple cells and a coarse layer. A key feature of DRDs lies in their dense object detection without a prior attention mechanism, resulting in significantly reduced computational requirements. However, our research shows that while DRDs excel in object detection, they are prone to incorrectly identifying items, resulting in lower criticalness among object detection methods. On the other hand, pairing mechanisms like attention can help eliminate unwanted responses; thus, we aim to incorporate a stable pairing system capable of directionless grouping of cell responses with lower computational requirements into our DRDs. Specifically, we have devised a scalable and efficient spatial grouping system called Stable Pairing, with two variants: hierarchical and progressive. The progressive variant enables us to achieve a remarkable 68.9% AP using only 22% of the GPU resources of the original DRDs. Furthermore, our spatial grouping approach enhances the resilience of DRDs to adversarial attacks.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models have significant shortcomings, as they rely heavily on human assessment scores that are often inconsistent and prone to error. In response, we aim to develop a more reliable metric to replace human evaluation by leveraging a large dataset of annotated summaries. Utilizing a CrossEncoder model to compare the similarity of original texts and their summaries, we discovered that it correlates well with human-provided quality scores in a range of datasets. Since our model can be applied to any text without requiring specific annotations, it serves as an alternative to traditional metrics. In comparison to established evaluation metrics, SummScore demonstrates notable advancements in several testing scenarios, particularly in its ability to distinguish between reputable and untrustworthy summarization models. Additionally, we show that with limited human feedback, a trained model can tailor summaries to specific user preferences, such as compression ratio, which could facilitate the development of more adaptable summarization models. We have made the associated code available on GitHub at https://github.com/baidu-research/SummScore.

The 1980s seeable signal processing problem, rooted in the 1960s hydrology issue of excessive runoff prediction, involves (1) generating a signal with a known polynomial growth from hidden, non-observable linear components and (2) using a few measurements containing noise to reconstruct the entire signal. Historically, methods based on the least-squares technique have been used for (1) constructing signals and (2) signal recovery. Our research aims to minimize data collection by addressing (2) with a set of measurements that are easily generated. We have developed an iterative method that is similar to LSST but more efficient, reducing data collection needs by factors of 10 to 1000. We have also shown that our proposed algorithm has an optimal nature when compared to existing methods. We have conducted experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing restoration quality with existing methods. Our results indicate that our proposed approach is superior in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. We have also applied our algorithm to the problem of estimating a signal from a single measurement, a variation of the problem of estimating a polynomial of a given degree from a single value. Our method is not limited, as it can be generalized for signals with exponential growth that are observed quadratically. We have also addressed the problem of estimating a signal of a given length.
