In a scenario where a machine learning model relies on external experts that provide parametric feedback, it's challenging for the model to learn and adapt. The issue lies in the experts' feedback, which contains valuable information minuscued within inevitable inaccuracies. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a novel approach that incorporates a theoretical analysis of an expert's preferences. This approach enables us to model an expert's behavior using a latent ideal performance and develop a more robust estimate of their preferences. To achieve this, we've introduced an adaptive learning algorithm that iteratively amplifies the expert's preferences, refining its understanding of their behavior. The algorithm's core involves pairing the expert's preferences with a proxy objective, which serves to correct and narrow down its responses. The results demonstrate that this algorithm can learn the underlying preferences effectively, which in turn facilitates more robust and reliable performance when applied in real-world contexts. The algorithm's design allows it to learn from a single example, as well as adapt to an evolving expert's preferences over time. To validate our approach, we've conducted a series of experiments that mimic a learning agent's interaction with a parametric external authority, which provides features-related feedback in a video game. The results clearly show that our algorithm can effectively learn to perform tasks based on a single example and remain resilient in response to sudden changes in the expert's preferences.

A comprehensive study of dual Higgs boson production in association with a vector boson has been carried out using data obtained from 2015 and 2016 proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, collected with the ATLAS detector and equivalent to 36.1 inverse femtobarns. Analysis of the $hh$ + V process, where V refers to W or Z bosons, is performed within the final states ggV, where V is a W or Z boson, examining the availability of significant Higgs boson duo signals for the current and future experiments. The findings show that recent measurements have restricted the 25-40 TeV range of the vector boson's coupling to the Higgs boson twice as broadly as the vector boson's coupling to the Higgs boson, and the $hh$ + V data have also measured the $hh$ production cross-section with the 77-105 fb restriction, which is largely in agreement with the quantum chromodynamics-based expectations.

The most powerful light sources today are lasers that produce up to 10 gigawatts of power per unit of surface area. By using electrons instead of photons, scientists have developed a new type of laser that can emit light at even higher power levels, reaching up to thousands of gigawatts per square meter. This high power level makes these lasers suitable for a range of applications, including communication, medical use, and military communications in space. To achieve such high power output, the lasers rely on a compact design with minimal components, and their light is produced through the interaction of two different fields. This interaction results in the nonlinear breakdown of a gas, producing a bright flash of light. This phenomenon can be exploited in the development of future high-power lasers, including compact devices that can be cooled electronically.

For K3 varieties that have a Jacobian component in their moduli space, we investigate the variability of the Picard group and its implications on the complexity of the associated Siegel disks. The research reveals a diverse range of Picard group behaviors, from finite to infinite dimensions, that demonstrate a clear correlation with the dimension of the K3 variety. Moreover, we find that the moduli space's connection to the boundary of the Siegel disk reflects the complexity of the variety's algebraic characteristics. Through both theoretical and computational methods, we demonstrate that K3 varieties can exhibit a range of interesting features, such as the existence of hyperbolic modular quotients, non-dense arithmetic types, and the influence of endomorphism rings on the variety's moduli space. Ultimately, this research underscores the significance of K3 varieties in understanding the intersection of moduli spaces, hyperbolicity, and modular forms.

In the context of supersymmetry, we suggest that the neutralino, a theoretical particle, can exist in various forms. If realized, this phenomenon would indicate that the neutralino has mass greater than approximately 55 GeV. A potential byproduct of this idea is that the neutralino could serve as a suitable candidate for dark matter, given its ability to interact weakly with matter and exist at a mass range typically expected for dark matter particles. Utilizing the SOFTBOTS tool, which automates supersymmetry models, we generated specific theoretical models to illustrate this idea and associated particle decays. A key aspect of these models is the use of high-scale mediation to facilitate a neutralino's long-lived state and, in extreme cases, its stability. To support this concept, we generated five distinct theoretical models, all of which involve universal properties during the theory's high-scale mediation process except for one specific model, which exhibits distinct properties during the theory's high-scale mediation process. A predicted gamma radiation spectrum is anticipated for this concept, focusing on both on-axis and off-axis regions, when detecting neutralinos that have undergone decay in two distinct components.

We develop a novel, polynomial-time estimation technique for calculating the genus of highly dense graphs, where the vertex count $n$ is given. The genus of a graph represents its highest self-intersection surface in a specific compact topological space called the compact surface. Our method employs a recent finding by Kotlov and Mader, indicating a linear correlation between a specific surface-weight metric and the genus of large dense graphs. Our algorithm uses an iterative process to accurately estimate the genus of the given graph through successive calculations of the genus for reduced and less complex subgraphs, until it stops with a refined estimate. Additionally, we show that the genus of any simple graph with $n$ vertices is bound by the inequality $\mathbf g(n) \le \frac{n-1}{3} \log n +20\sqrt{n}$. This result is surprisingly precise in comparison to the known lower bound of $\frac{n-1}{3}\log n$ derived from the Shannon multigraph, thus validating the hypothesis that the actual difference between the two values is of a smaller order than the logarithmic factor.

This paper presents a decentralized algorithm for solving large-scale distributed convex optimization problems among networked agents subjected to communication constraints. A randomized Newton method is employed, where agents jointly optimize the gradient and Hessian matrices of the objective function via communication. The algorithm's convergence rate in the presence of communication limitations is similar to that of standard Newton's method when operating in a collaborative manner. Moreover, the algorithm's stability is ensured through a novel form of iterative communication, which enables the generation of gradient and Hessian estimates at varying levels of precision. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations comparing its performance with a standardized consensus algorithm.

This study focuses on developing a system for detecting hate speech in two Indo-Aryan languages, Hindi and Bengali, and explores the effectiveness of various neural networks. The text datasets employed in this research comprise a collection of annotated statements drawn from actual social media content, where authors intend to inflict mental and emotional distress on recipients. It is discovered that character-based neural networks excel in detecting hate speech, particularly when processing shorter input texts, whereas sequence-based models perform better with longer input statements. We also find that they are surpassed by simpler models across both languages. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that character-based neural networks are sensitive to the number of input characters, and their performance improves significantly with more characters. We observe similar findings with word-based models, although they are less effective than their character-based counterparts. Additionally, our investigation reveals that more annotated data are required to enhance the accuracy of hate speech detection in both languages. It is also found that more data lead to better results, and transfer learning plays a crucial role in achieving high accuracy in both character and sequence-based models. Based on these findings, we develop a hybrid approach that combines the performance of different models to achieve high overall accuracy.

In particle detection via Gas Time Projection Chambers, the path of charged particles is captured along a significant distance due to the drift field, allowing for detailed image creation. The signal strength is typically proportional to the square of the particle's path, which makes the detection sensitive to recoil radiation from nuclei. To avoid this effect, researchers typically lower the drift voltage, but this results in reduced device resolution. To operate these chambers at high resolution without being affected by recoil radiation, it's crucial to remove the signal component caused by the particle's path from the overall signal, enabling the detection of nuclear recoils down to individual electrons. To achieve this, researchers have proposed new observables that can isolate the particle's path signal, making it possible to operate the chamber both at high resolution and without being affected by recoil radiation. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these observables, researchers used actual TPC data and showed that, in conditions similar to that of pGe, the particle's path signal can be completely eliminated, paving the way for a new type of gas-based particle detector that can operate at room temperature, detect rare events, and isolate individual electrons.

A key decision for truck drivers is whether to take a toll road or a surface road.  This study involves a contextual choice system for drivers to make this decision, but there's a concern that the current evaluation method may not be fair to road operators.  To address this, we're developing a new method that uses expert feedback to compare the different routes and calculate the expected benefit of each choice for each driver.  Our new method is being tested with commercial driving data and we're analyzing it using statistical models.  We believe our new method is more accurate and is not influenced by the driver's skills.  Our results show that the system is able to provide drivers with the information they need to make an informed decision and there are potential technological improvements that could make even more money available to road operators.

At the 5th NEURIPS 2019 Challenge, a competition focused on working with disconnected visual data, the 'Out-of-Context' challenge took place, the details of which are outlined below.

The 'Out-of-Context' challenge required participants to create the most effective method for determining the similarity of two given images, despite the fact that they are viewed in isolation and their original shared context is absent. This task has significant practical implications, present in various real-world applications such as visual search, the evaluation of similar products on an online platform, or visual copy detection. The challenge took place alongside the WASSA 2019 conference, which featured a range of workshops and challenges revolving around accessible and accountable machine learning for vision. The challenge took place with a familiar format, consisting of simulated training, testing, and qualification rounds. A total of 44 registered participants and 21 unique top-ranked submissions proposed their ideas throughout the challenge, which are detailed below along with a summary of the winning outcomes, followed by a reflection on the implications of the results and suggestions for potential future competitions.

In a Gaussian stochastic field, the manifold comprising all zero mean functions possesses inherent geometric characteristics, determined by the underlying covariance structure. Calculating the geodesic curve between two points on this manifold involves the functional minimization of the distance between two zero mean functions. This distance is calculated through a double stochastic integration process. The existence and uniqueness of the geodesic path are established, along with an analytical expression for the velocity of the geodesic via a Karhunen-Loeve representation. The findings demonstrate that the geodesic path does not depend on the field's functional realizations, possessing an invariant characteristic akin to a determinant. The geodesic velocity exhibits stationary properties when the field's spectral density is isotropic, retaining this property under additive or multiplicative scalar multiplications. When the field is homogeneous and isotropic, the geodesic velocity is stationary and invariant under translations. The geodesic distance between two EXP functions (E-expectation normalizated functions) is equivalent to the distance between their corresponding Gaussian fields' exponential families. The geodesic velocity's invariance to functional rescaling reveals the existence of distinct geometric properties for different function spaces.

The Demonstone Theorem is demonstrated by proving the strong Euler Characteristic Theorem for certain complex structures known as CW-complexes, which exhibit length periodicity properties. This has further implications in establishing an enhanced version of the Vandermonde Theorem applicable to Chebyshev polynomials of the third kind. Additionally, an error in a previous article is corrected, showing that no straightforward relation exists between Euler Characteristics and the number of zeros found in Hermite polynomials when evaluated on the interval $[-R, R]$.

We analyze an L-function associated with a weight 2 cusp form as defined by the Langlands inverse Galois representations of certain profinite groups. We establish that the number of distinct elements within a set of modular L-functions, each modulated by a primitive Dirichlet character, is boundlessly large as the character order increases, while also providing a comparable bound for a related set of L-functions corresponding to a fixed cusp form. This is an extension of previous research findings. We further demonstrate that a factorized version of this L-function remains bounded in a specific range for all but a bounded number of cases. Notably, this is an original discovery which differs from past findings where factors of the L-function were found to be bounded in a narrower range of 1 to 3.

In experimentally accessible armchair graphene nanostructures, specifically in ballistic transport regimes, we've observed and controlled spin-related transport under time-reversal constraints. These nanostructures exhibit ballistic transport characteristics, and we found that spins are inherently linked to other physical properties such as charge and magnetic fields. We've manipulated spins using magnetic fields, and when doing so, we've identified spins as a significant contributing factor to conductance, even in magnetic field scenarios that do not favor spin alignment. We've constrained transport to spin-polarized modes, and despite magnetic field orientation variations, we've maintained spin-polarized modes using appropriate magnetic field configurations. We've discovered that spins are intertwined with other physical properties, and when this happens, spins become visible in magnetic force microscopy scans. These findings open new avenues for controlling spin in graphene, and specifically in graphene nanoribbons, using magnetic properties alone.

The main aim of this research is to derive approximate identities based on linear and weakly nonlinear, non-decreasing operators that take real-valued functions of n variables to real-valued functions of m variables under certain conditions of weak convergence. It involves investigating the convergence of the difference $L_m^0(f) - f$ and deriving new types of theorems analogous to Korovkin's theorem for certain classes of monotonic and weakly nonlinear operators that satisfy certain conditions of continuity. This new theory enables the direct application of the Korovkin theorems to a wider range of operators that do not satisfy the arithmetical to convexity property or are only monotonic. It also enables the constructive identification of the limits of certain nonlinear convolution operators that preserve monotonicity without satisfying the arithmetical to convexity property. The theory can be used to approximate certain linear and weakly nonlinear differential equations and their solutions. The approximate identities can also be used in the following fields: function theory, numerical analysis, approximation theory, differential equations, and physics. They can be employed to derive convergence theorems for various classes of operators that do not yet have such theorems established in the literature.

The study of graph properties has been rich in theory but relatively limited in application. To address this imbalance, we're focusing on connecting graph theory to computer science through the creation of independent graphs. A graph with no cycles cannot contain an autonomous vertex, and in graphs with cycles, we can define autonomy by limiting the number of vertices not participating in a specific cycle. Building on this concept, we can refine the definition of pancyclicity by introducing a bound on the number of non-autonomous vertices. Furthermore, we can interpret the concept of autonomy within the context of Hamiltonicity, and by using this new perspective, we can prove the asymptotic Hamiltonicity of graphs under particular conditions, including those with specific edge connectivity and degree requirements.

We analyzed the directed flow of various identified hadrons created in the 200 GeV center-of-mass energy collisions of isotopes, specifically $\mathbf{^{96}}\mathbf{Ru}$ and $\mathbf{^{96}}\mathbf{Zr}$, with single-particle rapidity distributions provided by the Solenoid Spectrometer. The data revealed a slight difference in directed flow between isotope collisions and similar $N+N$ collisions. Notably, positive directed flow at midrapidity existed in both light and heavy hadrons, with negative directed flow observed at more positive rapidities for odd-mass number hadrons. The behavior of protons and antiprotons exhibited minimal difference in directed flow. Furthermore, directed flow analyses showed varying influence from the conditions close to the freezing point in the center-of-mass energy and rapidity ranges investigated, consistent with prior research results.

The spectral Koopman method has exhibited remarkable performance in approximating invariant manifolds for nonlinear dynamical systems, especially in recent years. However, to prevent computational difficulties in high-dimensional systems caused by an excessive focus on complexity, modern Koopman-based approaches often simplify problems by reducing dimensionality and analyzing sparsity. We combine the sparse grid method, which efficiently handles reduced-dimensional problems, with the spectral Koopman technique to solve complex high-dimensional dynamical systems. We provide numerical evidence to support our claim by applying this method to two nonlinear systems, a stiff system, and a system highly sensitive to initial conditions.

This study presents an approach, derived from the Outward Complex Scaling Method, specifically designed to study bound atomic and molecular systems under extreme DC electric fields. The proposed method is rooted in the Riemann Hypothesis, offering the unique asset of avoiding scaling parameter accumulation, which greatly simplifies its implementation. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through precise calculations of DC Stark shifts and linear DC Stark stabilization lengths for diverse hydrogen-like ions and positive hydrogenionic clusters, yielding results that converge rapidly with increasing maximum scaling parameter.

Results from a sample of top-quark pair events collected with the ATLAS detector at the LHC's 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy are presented. The total cross-section for top-quark pair production, created with both the forward and backward combinations of charged particles and with isolated muons in the event, has been calculated. These measurements were derived from a data record comprising 36.7 pb^-1 of cumulative luminosity, and were compared against predictions from quantum chromodynamics models in terms of dependence on the number of interactions with the proton. The data modelled here involves differential cross-sections for top-quark pair events with transverse momentum between 70 and 600 GeV and with rapidity between 0.2 and 0.8, assessed against both the forward and backward charged particle and isolated muon conditions. This study focuses on the localization problem in a disordered system that connects two clean systems via a single link, with each clean system being an infinite one-dimensional lattice. Two of the bonds in the disordered link are randomly defected. The system's transfer matrices have been explicitly calculated. The results show that parity serves as a protector against localization, and that the system remains localized at the disorder threshold. Additionally, the findings include the points at which localization transitions occur for various disorder levels.

The Janowski conjecture concerns the distribution of the zeros of the K3 complex form of the general Gauss map. Although the original conjecture has been disproved, a more generalized hypothesis involving linear combinations of generalized Bessel functions remains unverified.

The pandemic revealed a question about urban planning's resilience: how do the needs of modern cities compare to those of the past? To answer this, our team investigated the changes in social patterns within urban areas. We analyzed mobile phone data from over 312 million users in China and found that the pandemic led to an uneven distribution of social interactions among different income groups. While the wealthy continued to engage in high-frequency, long-distance interactions, those with lower incomes adopted more localized patterns of behavior. To understand these variations, we used machine learning to identify distinct patterns of movement for 1.7 billion populated areas in China. We found three primary categories: densely connected areas with frequent long-distance travel, areas with infrequent long-distance travel, and areas with low interaction frequency. Then, we investigated the distribution of these patterns across different income groups before and after the pandemic, observing a significant change for those with lower incomes but no change for the wealthy. This points to a possible pandemic-induced behavioral shift among those with lower incomes, which likely affects urban planning and raises concerns about income disparities.

To efficiently model two-phase flow in complex porous media, a precise pre-conditioning technique is necessary for rapid iterative solutions. This paper compares several pre-conditioners that can handle multi-point connections in two-phase flow modeling, which often requires an irregularly structured grid in uneven porous media. The study focuses on pre-conditioning using multi-point pre-conditioners, specifically mass, mass-less, flow, and flow-less formulations, as well as a linear field-split pre-conditioner and a nonlinear field-split pre-conditioner known as the linearly implicit pre-conditioner. Mass and mass-less pre-conditioners incorporate mass conservation constraints to ensure consistent flow rates and fluid volumes, whereas flow pre-conditioners aim to stabilize pressure fluctuations in individual phases. The pre-conditioners were analyzed through a series of numerical experiments, which demonstrated that linear and nonlinear pre-conditioners with consistent flow rates and fluid volumes showed significantly better performance than their inconsistent counterparts, with the nonlinear pre-conditioner delivering more stable and accurate results than its linear counterpart, albeit with increased computational cost. The pre-conditioners' effectiveness was further validated in a large-scale model that modeled 24 hours of gas and liquid behavior.

A novel optical cavity is proposed that combines the principles of Parity-Time symmetry and Chirality. This robust cavity, which can be realized using unstable mirrors, is capable of producing distinct resonances in the presence of broad resonances. It has been shown that the cavity modes exhibit Lamb-Wilson poles, indicating a relation between these phenomena. The Chiral cavity is inherently unidirectional and supports unipolar resonances, characteristics that are inherently stable due to their non-problematic energy dissipation patterns. The Chiral cavity is versatile and applicable to various scenarios, including Purcell enhancement, critical coupling, and non-reciprocal propagation.

We establish a duality between a certain modified Liouville CFT and a matrix model, thus providing concrete evidence for the quantum gravity hypothesis using JT gravity, specifically in its version with a non-zero boundary term. We compare the partition function of the matrix model with the annealed approximation of the partition function for the modified Liouville CFT, and find that the prepotential, which governs the moduli space of the matrix model's spectral curve, closely matches the asymptotic behavior of the modified Liouville CFT's prepotential. We attribute this result to a proposed duality between certain boundary JT gravity theories and Schottky models.

This paper considers an approximate solution to the Einstein-Euler equations, assuming an ideal fluid as the sole source of gravity, and approximating the general stress-energy tensor with a specific expression that decouples the gravitational variables. The study focuses on the warp drive solution, a spacetime configuration that has generated significant interest due to its potential for faster-than-light travel, and analyses its implications within the context of general relativity when coupled with a cosmological constant. It evaluates the suitability of this solution for warp drive applications, and explores its physical and cosmological significance when the principle of the minimum variation of action is applied.

As urban areas expand, ensuring efficient urban planning and planning policies becomes increasingly crucial, necessitating high-performance data management and analysis systems to support decision-making in cities. The proliferation of in-situ sensors and remote sensing technologies has led to a rapid increase in diverse data sources, including various multimedia content, which need to be integrated and managed for effective city governance. Differing stakeholders, including citizens, policymakers, and operators, have distinct data usage and provision requirements. This research presents the GUIDES architecture, a data engineering framework addressing the numerous city data management challenges. By developing this framework, we have successfully demonstrated its practical application in real-world settings through the implementation of a prototype system.

To study the behavior of complex many-body systems using 2D ion crystals, it's necessary to precisely control the environment by analyzing its impact on the system's spin degrees of freedom. This task is achieved by examining the fluctuations of the center-of-mass motion, $\xi_n$, for selected ions in response to applied RF-sideband excitations. The resulting Rabi oscillations between the excited sidebands provide insights into both the system's coherent spin interactions and the influence of the external mode warmth. By adjusting the driving strength, N modes are simultaneously excited, allowing for a nearly instantaneous probing of mode populations using the same technique. This method enables the measurement of the mode population warmth, $\beta$, and provides a direct comparison with the decoherence rates, $\tau_d$, arising from mode decoherence. The goal of this work is to develop a new set of experimental tools that can be employed to investigate the motional state distributions throughout the trapping period.

A novel, highly sophisticated, quantum-mechanical approach has been developed to calculate intricate interactions between molecules in response to electromagnetic forces within the context of high-resolution electron energy-loss spectroscopy and tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy. This computational method, founded on first-principles calculations, effectively accounts for electronic structures, local fields, and nonlinear electromagnetic responses, as well as non-equilibrium quantum dynamics in the vicinity of the probes used in these techniques. It incorporates precise representations of the probes' geometric configuration, orientation, and electrical properties. This approach is capable of providing insight into various physical phenomena influencing the spectroscopic signals, including the relative contributions of different factors. It has been used to study a series of molecules attached to a gold tip, taking into consideration the influence of electric and magnetic fields generated by the gold tip, as well as the effects of optical excitations and electromagnetic responses in the region surrounding the probes. This technique is versatile and can be utilized to investigate various systems comprised of molecules, ions, and clusters subject to electromagnetic forces.

Our investigation into unconventional microwave emission (UME) in nearby galaxies entails measuring the 21 cm - 33 GHz spectral interval. Twenty-five galaxies, including 12 radio galaxies and 13 jet-related sources, were observed at K-band using the Sardinia Radio Telescope, and our data collection is presented here. Following a thorough analysis of the frequency-spatial behavior of the measured radiation, we found one detection at a frequency of 32.675 GHz originating from the galaxy NGC 1128. To fully assess UME candidates, we must conduct additional observations to examine their polarization properties and their relationship with the sources' intrinsic characteristics.

To comprehend the underlying mechanisms driving structural and electrical changes in response to external stimuli in ammonium sulfate, a key component in various capacitors and ferroelectric devices, it is crucial to challenge widely held assumptions regarding the material's molecular dynamics. These assumptions, made for simpler systems on the basis of the principle of detailed balance and according to the second law of thermodynamics, are no longer valid for this particular material. The theories governing caloric effects, ferroelectricity, and the material's electronic properties are also threatened if these assumptions prove incorrect. To address the issue, we performed a detailed examination of the material's electronic properties as well as theoretical simulations of its molecular dynamics. The results show that the material's electronic characteristics, in contrast to predictions based on the Pauli principle, are stable over a broad energy range. The material's molecular dynamics, also failing to adhere to second law predictions, are further explained by the material's non-thermal structural dynamics, which can be directly related to entropy changes. The findings suggest that the material's behavior can be understood within a statistical mechanical framework based on a generalised version of the van der Waals equation for systems where detailed balance is not applicable.

Average performance in cognitive tasks can be impressive due to the contribution of exceptionally skilled individuals, which might suggest that these individuals possess a unique and stable ability. However, our research reveals that highly skilled individuals in a cognitive task called reinforcement learning exhibit different strategies in distinct situations, with some strategies resulting in higher performance during easy versus hard conditions. We investigated the neural basis of these varying strategies using a brain simulation. When we put these strategies to the test in both simulated and actual human experiments, we found that midbrain activity accurately detected prediction errors in both cases. Notably, exceptional performers' strategies were characterized by lower average midbrain activity across conditions, yet still showed similar midbrain responses to unexpected outcomes. This study identifies that high achievers' strategies can deliver better outcomes, which may not be achieved by applying the same strategy to all situations.

A more comprehensive analysis is given to a proposed quantum model derived from the $E_8$ lattice by incorporating complex elements. Firstly, we establish that this model is equivalent to two interconnected copies of the Hilbert space of complex hyperbolic lattices, one for type A and the other for type D. This comparison yields valuable insights into the properties of complex $E_8$ lattices, such as their quantum entanglement and compatibility when applying multiple measurements simultaneously. It's found that even with complex elements, there is no risk of measurements interfering with each other, whether or not they share common degrees of freedom. Additionally, we investigate how the rotational patterns in three-dimensional space influence the behavior of complex $E_8$ lattices under various measurements.

The Frechet distance, a measure of similarity for continuous curves, has found practical applications such as identifying similarities in gesture patterns and comparing one-dimensional spatial trajectories. For a set of curves, determining a frequency estimate for the number of curves within a specified distance of any given curve is a crucial problem with real-world implications, especially when curves are high-dimensional trajectories rendered into one-dimensional series. Our study provides lower bounds for approximate neighbor searching in this context, specifically focusing on the standard distance metrics including the Frechet distance, its variants, and the total variation distance. These bounds are performance limits for algorithms employing a query time of $q(t)$ and APX for a given approximation ratio and threshold time $t$, given that the trade-offs between query time, approximation ratio, and time cannot be improved upon without compromising the failure rate. To establish these results, we first showed that for a set of dense and uniformly distributed close neighbor searching instances, the query time, approximation ratio, and log probabilities satisfy a system of three linear equations with integer coefficients, the solution to which indicates that the query time, approximation ratio, and time satisfy a linear relationship. Our analysis extends to the total variation distance, and in doing so generalizes a result from Boursier et al. for the standard distance metrics.

High-precision measurements are hindered by their inherent errors, which distort results and limitations can't be overcome by precision. To counter this, the error reduction method was created. This method allows us to find an optimal beam former that lessens measurement inaccuracies in any linear measurement procedure. When applied to atomic interferometry, ER methods enhance their precision limits, yet their effectiveness is constrained when measuring particular features, such as accelerations, which need information about the desired quantity in question. If such information is lacking, the error reduction method cannot function. To overcome this, we developed the iterative Bayesian unraveling technique, which integrates ER with Bayesian inference.

Humans have traditionally learned new skills by observing and imitating others, particularly in instances where direct instruction is lacking. In the realm of robotics, research has been focused on leveraging shared autonomy to enable robots to acquire knowledge and replicate human behavior, particularly in contexts where robotic assistance is sought. By incorporating robotic assistance that mirrors human behavior, robots can gather insights from their interactions with people, allowing them to subsequently engage in tasks that were within their pre-existing capabilities, but now also execute efficiently. A central aspect of achieving this behavior and understanding robotic roles revolves around developing appropriate communication methods, and this can be achieved by focusing on conveying standards of behavior. In our study, we utilized a case study involving a conveying robot in a kitchen setting to demonstrate how this can be effectively implemented, and we also collected and analyzed human perception data through surveys and stories about robot behavior to validate our results, and also involve robots learning from human behavior.

To effectively navigate through unfamiliar environments, individuals rely on mental maps that incorporate spatial connections and organizational structures. However, the spatial information available in unknown environments is often inadequate, rendering it difficult to establish direct geographical relationships. Thus, utilizing only latitude and longitude may prove insufficient. This paper proposes a dual-representation system for addressing this issue by combining a topology-based map with an geographical map called HiTMap. To facilitate seamless navigation, the system integrates their interconnections through spatial context analysis, incorporating techniques such as reverse geocoding and route planning. For demonstration purposes, the system is tailored for the needs of a hypothetical emergency responder, but its broader applicability is also explored.

A novel 2-D $m \times m$ arrays can be constructed from multivariable functions with specific properties governing their element values. By carefully selecting these functions, distinct sets of arrays with unique index calculations can be created. Arrays within these sets exhibit unique index relationships, distinguishing them from others. Furthermore, a category of periodic arrays with repeating indices is created. Additionally, a category of periodic arrays with repeating indices is created. Furthermore, a category of $m \times m$ arrays with unique index relationships is created. 

This research categorizes the arrays into three types: type I, comprising arrays with distinct index relationships, and type II, comprising arrays without such relationships. Type I categories include sub-types I-A, characterized by the absence of identical element pairs, and I-B, featuring identical element pairs, each with their own index relationships. Type II consists of sub-type II-A, featuring arrays without distinct index relationships, and sub-type II-B, featuring arrays with distinct index relationships. 

This research establishes one-to-one correspondences between 2-D arrays and n-dimensional vector spaces, allowing for the creation of a new type I array from a vector in such a space. It also demonstrates that a type II array can be created or transformed into a type I array through a unique operation involving the addition or subtraction of two vectors.

Ininspired by the success of deep learning in medical image processing, we have developed a unique variational framework that enables simultaneous image reconstruction, noise removal, and material decomposition in insulin density from X-ray images. Our approach applies a nonlinear penalty method to a combined energy function, representing the three processes, resulting in a energy minimization problem that can be efficiently solved numerically. To reduce the non-convexity of the energy function, we have implemented a variational alternating algorithm that converges rapidly. Our results from computer simulations and real-world data demonstrate the exceptional image reconstruction performance of our method, even with complex multi-energy X-ray images and noisy data. Furthermore, our approach allows for effective noise reduction and detailed material decomposition in insulin density. Our findings also highlight the value of advanced mathematical methods in medical imaging applications.

We investigate the impact of an electron's departure from its equilibrium state and nonlocal behavior on plasmonic phenomena, specifically gap plasmons, in a particular arrangement of metallic nanostructures. In the small gap size limit, the dependence of the plasmon frequency on the electron's nonlocal behavior reveals a distinct pattern that differs significantly from the predictions based on a conventional model involving a sudden gap transition. Furthermore, the inclusion of a nonlocal electron distribution in the quantum surface layer modifies the predicted plasmon frequencies, causing them to diverge from their corresponding local models. In the context of quantum surface nonlocality, our model demonstrates the emergence of a distinctive gapless plasmon mode that arises from the interplay between the electrons in the two adjacent metallic nanostructures.

The evaluation of contextual named entity recognition is particularly significant due to its potential to identify a wide variety of entities. Traditionally, important terms in a document have been determined by part-of-speech dependencies and grammatical rules. This naming approach not only considers lexical characteristics but also relies on term significance. Our paper presents an contextual named entity recognition model that utilizes term significance as a feature, derived from non-parametric techniques. The integrated model is evaluated on the ACE 2005 dataset and our results indicate that incorporating term significance significantly enhances entity recognition performance. Furthermore, our research also compares the effectiveness of different feature selection methods and various prior probabilities for the entity category 'Person'.

Displays of complex data, such as multivariate time series, can be difficult to interpret when examining individual data points in isolation. Uncovering interesting patterns or correlations within these datasets poses a significant challenge due to the interdependent nature of these complex data. However, upon closer inspection, many of these patterns often prove to be significant and meaningful when examined in greater detail. To address this issue, researchers have proposed an interactive visualization approach, known as zooming, which enables users to analyze specific aspects of these datasets while maintaining context through panning. There are, however, several aspects of this technique that do not easily accommodate the examination of additional context when zooming in on certain features, particularly when correlations between different data elements cannot be ignored. To address these shortcomings, researchers have been exploring other forms of interactivity that engage multiple scales, such as the use of multiple displays and semantic zooming. Semantic zooming, in particular, is notable for an approach described in the paper as hierarchical zooming, which incorporates elements of interactivity not typically associated with data visualization. Semantic zooming is characterized by three key attributes: providing access to relevant information as users engage with datasets at various scales; ensuring that users remain focused on the part of the dataset being analyzed and, consequently, that less important elements recede into the background; and, when necessary, presenting users with new perspectives that were previously invisible. The vast amounts of data generated from electronic health records, coupled with their complexity, make them challenging for machine learning models to process. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have paved the way for advanced medical AI models, but their application is often restricted to specific medical conditions. To overcome these limitations, we develop a graph diversity enhancement technique, based on a different type of graph convolutional network, that can be used across various health domains. To further enhance the performance of graph-based models, we propose a method for creating a synthetic graph profile that can be used for different patients. These profile profiles can then be used for a range of medical prediction tasks. We test the effectiveness of our approach through multiple experiments using the MIMIC-III dataset. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our method, which outperforms baseline models on all tasks. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of our model on two real-world clinical prediction tasks chosen from a competition database, which highlights its potential for real-world medical decision-making.

Within the framework of Deconinck's dipolar soft density model, a charged flexible interface is considered, alongside an electrolyte solution containing monovalent ions, with the interface being non-conductive and characterized by a hyperbolic tangent profile. Solvent polarization is accounted for through a density-dependent dielectric constant that exhibits asymptotic behavior of $\epsilon_{water}$ and $\epsilon_{bulk solvent}$ far from the interface. By implementing the hypernetted chain approximation, an equation is derived for the density profiles of the solvent and solvating ions in relation to the dielectric model and ion size. These density profiles are found to be non-analytic at the interface critical point, with the radius of solvent density being a function of ionic concentration and dielectric constant, exhibiting discontinuous widening with increasing concentration for small dielectric constants. Additionally, the system's chemical potential is analyzed as a function of concentration and dielectric constant, also displaying non-analytic behavior.

When developing software, developers create content that explains the functions and purposes of their projects, often in the form of general information or technical specifications. These texts can be found in various sources such as project websites, manuals, and documentation. To streamline the development process and ensure consistency, collaborative software development tools with integrated features are utilized by many developers. In this paper, we examine how computational methods can be employed to analyze and interpret the explanations contained within these texts, converting them into a structured and meaningful format known as Gherkin. Gherkin is used to specify software requirements in an easy-to-understand and readable format, enabling collaborative testing and validation within development environments. Our research showcases a proposed method for converting the content of various text types into Gherkin, presenting an advanced model incorporating semantic analysis, part-of-speech prediction, and sequential dependency analysis. Additionally, the effectiveness of the model is evaluated based on several factors, including its alignment with expert-provided data, consistency within itself, and the ability to scale for large projects.

This research explores the possibility of reducing energy consumption in wireless networks by adopting a green approach. To achieve this, a new concept called collaborative energy-efficient network coding (CEENC) is introduced, combining cooperative communication, network coding, and power management. By extending regular network coding, CEENC involves parallel transmission of multiple packets from multiple transmitters, where relay nodes decode and reencode packets to increase success chances, and the closest node transmits the combined signal. Due to the increased complexity of decoding and reencoding, relays consume more energy, allowing central nodes to turn off to conserve power. As a result, a new model for calculating CEENC throughput is established, and an optimization problem is proposed to find the most energy-efficient transmission strategy among central nodes, and both direct and indirect relays. To address the complexity of this optimization problem, two methods - a lower-bound approximate solution and a causality-based column generation algorithm - are presented to ensure the feasibility of the solution and meet specific system constraints. Simulation outcomes confirm that CEENC can achieve significant energy savings with minimal performance loss compared to traditional network coding methods.

Utilizing the theoretical framework previously established for analyzing the electronic properties of defect-induced Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, a detailed examination is conducted on a Mn atom and Mn dimers adsorbed onto the Nb(110) surface. Calculations reveal that an isolated Mn atom gives rise to multiple Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states situated within bands of spin-polarized Mn d-electrons. Mn dimers either degenerate with or encroach upon Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states originating from a single Mn atom. Importantly, the observed spectral discrepancies significantly influence both magnetic moment magnitudes and spin correlation signs attached to YSR states. It is also observed that YSR state energy separations exhibit sensitivity to variations in interatomic coupling. These theoretical findings are expected to serve as a benchmark for interpreting upcoming experimental results involving Mn-based YSR states on the Nb(110) surface.

To detect the K+ → π+νν decay for the first time, researchers employed the DECAY model in conjunction with a deep-inelastic neutrino experiment using a carbon target at CERN's North Area, said to have achieved the highest ever directed neutrino flux. By analyzing the K+ decay-in-flight method, where kaons produced through a 29.85 GeV proton impact, the decay rate was calculated based on the reconstructed mass of the missing mass in the K+ momentum-mass system and the missing mass in the proton-kapton-pi+ system. After utilizing a magnetic spectrometer with a detector bank that measured energy, momentum, and angles of particles involved, the effective mass range of the missing mass in the K+ momentum-mission system was narrowed from 0. Vera  to 0. 6  GeV/c 2.  Based on the number of observed candidates and the calculated background, a 95% confidence level upper limit of 5.6 × 10 −4 was found for the K+ → π+νν decay. This upper limit is in line with the Standard Model prediction of 1.0 × 10 −5 if the CKM suppression were absent.

Outdoor mobile robotics often relies on LiDAR to navigate and map unknown environments, yet current survey-grade point cloud matching techniques fail to keep up with the pace of new data arrival or can be computationally expensive. In this paper, a novel neural network-based approach is proposed to enhance the performance of robust and efficient scan matching by utilizing prior information to counteract the negative effects of moving obstacles, aging map data, and measurement inaccuracies. We introduce a Layered Deep Neural Network Filter that incorporates the Kalman network for state estimation and the deep filter bank for detecting and weighting data validity, achieving robust and long-term stability in scan matching. Simulation results show that the proposed method significantly outperforms traditional matching techniques in various challenging scenarios, and when integrated with a mapping algorithm, reduces the average mapping delay by 53.96% and 73.43% respectively when comparing to two distinct baseline methods.

Satellite images hold valuable information on the earth's surface, while their processing demands enormous computational power due to the large size and resolution of these images. Many deep learning algorithms have proven effectiveness in satellite image analysis, but they often require significant amounts of data and high-performance hardware to train and run efficiently. This paper presents an efficient approach for identifying the image edges in satellite images using an unsupervised method that relies on edge detection followed by a non-local filter, thereby outperforming many deep learning algorithms both in terms of training time and the memory required for the resulting model. This approach also provides an comparably accurate edge detection result when compared to some leading deep learning algorithms but at a significantly reduced computational cost. The source code for this method has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/msebim/Edge-Discovery-Satellite-Images.

To tackle high-fluence situations, we've developed an alternative framework for understanding the rate at which electrons are transferred after an X-ray photon is absorbed. This new approach, based on the multiparameter Fermi-Anderson model, allows us to measure the density of unoccupied electronic states directly, which has significant implications for our understanding of the photoelectron's local environment. By comparing our theory with existing theories from the extreme fluence regime, we've made some key observations: high-density unoccupied states are primarily influenced by a narrow range of the Fermi energy level; comparisons between the two theories reveal similarities in their results; and, contrary to expectations, the distribution of electronic states is not as sensitive to the Anderson broadening parameter K as previously thought. These findings are also substantiated through the analysis of a heated K metal. The new framework is flexible and can be applied to different NFXD models, with the goal of distinguishing between these different models and elucidating the role of the ultra-fast pump pulse in various experiments.

Radio modulation recognition is a critical activity in electronic warfare and signal intelligence, where identifying radio modulation patterns is crucial for determining communication content.  A deep learning-based approach to modulation classification has emerged as particularly effective, leveraging a GAN architecture to generate modulation training data.  This method offers significant advantages over traditional methods, including increased robustness and performance that approaches state-of-the-art levels.  In this research, a novel GAN architecture is presented that combines an WGAN-GP framework with a LS-GAN component, demonstrating particularly strong modulation classification capabilities across diverse scenarios, even in the face of adversarial attacks.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions has been successful when trained within the same data distribution as the model is being trained on (source domain). However, when applying a pre-trained model to unseen clinical sites with different imaging characteristics (target domains), performance significantly deteriorates. Traditional methods retrain the model using the target distribution's unlabeled data before transferring it to another site. By only using unlabeled data, these methods are restricted to a limited number of sites due to the increased risk of overfitting. Therefore, continuous learning when moving between sites is not feasible. We introduce two domain adaptation techniques, self-training and pseudo-supervised learning, that allow our model to gradually update its weights when interacting with each new site. We compare these methods to standard techniques that involve retraining the model with target domain annotations that are often scarce. When testing our model's ability to continuously learn and adapt to new sites, performance significantly improves across all methods with pseudo-supervised learning outperforming them by 25% in the aggregate. Moreover, our model remains up-to-date with the current clinical data and can be used for new patients. When comparing the two segmentation methods available, segmentation overseen by experts yields better outcomes but self-training can replicate pseudo-supervised learning performance with fewer annotations. Both methods reach comparable lesion segmentation performance within 3-4 sites. These techniques are included in a new open-source library called continual-learning-bench, mirroring the use of transfer learning-bench to evaluate and demonstrate continual learning

In the realm of the symmetric group $S_n$, a novel similarity relation is formulated,
whereupon subgroups can be classified as cohomologically pure, thereby giving rise
to an equivalence relation partitioning the subgroups of $S_n$ accordings to their
potential dual (co)homological counterparts. We demonstrate that the equivalence
relation so defined enjoys notable arithmetical and algebraic attributes. Moreover,
through manual computation, the partitioning of $S_n$'s subgroups accordings to their
potential duals is achieved for small-specifically up to $n = 7$ or $8$ values of $n$.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in modeling complex dynamical systems, but their specific ability to capture mistake structures remains poorly understood. This knowledge gap inhibits the development of intelligent systems capable of detecting and responding to errors in critical situations. To address this limitation, our study introduces an innovative framework for extracting detailed error information from a model's output and input history. This framework is versatile, applicable to a wide range of dynamical systems, including linear and nonlinear models, even in the absence of explicit error data. For linear models, our research provides a pioneering characterization of error patterns with inherent statistical properties. These results facilitate the creation of intelligent systems that effectively recognize and handle model mistakes, as demonstrated through a concrete example involving control systems. Due to its practical implications, our work has the potential to significantly enhance the reliability and safety of model-based control systems.

The evolution of molecular cloud cores influenced the formation of massive star-forming regions. An investigation into the Dragon infrared dark cloud revealed two highly dense regions, one of which contains a 2 to 3 solar mass core. The second core has a mass of 8 to 12 solar masses, surrounded by a dense filament. Observations of ammonia and $^{13}$CO at a high resolution showed the cores' center of mass positions. It was found the high density regions remain stationary as they show no movement over two years. Moreover, their redshifted and blueshifted velocities match the flow of 20 km/s per year in surrounding regions, indicating they are at equilibrium. However, their velocity dispersion is less than expected from their density, a sign of development. Comparison to simulations also revealed their level of development. Therefore, it is concluded the most dense region has reached an advanced level of development, while the less dense core shows early signs of development. An estimate of their formation times suggests the dense region is about 0.75 to 1.5 million years along or beyond the formation threshold while the less dense core is about 2 to 4 years along, indicating the less dense core has begun forming massive stars.

Numerical simulations of structure formation in the Primordial Black Hole dark energy model are limited by the cost of computing large particle distributions, making it necessary to find an efficient method that doesn't compromise results. The PopSyCLE code has been used to demonstrate that through careful selection of parameters and conditions, accurate simulations can be achieved at a significantly lower computational cost, factor of a thousand cheaper, without compromising the overall model's characteristics. The code was particularly sensitive to the determination of dark matter halos, for which a fixed radius can effectively begin the collapse of matter within, leading to consistent halos across all tested realizations in the specified model. Additionally, the team used 16 to 32 PBH masses, discovering that the overall system behaves similarly as if all masses have a uniform mass function, with the resulting clustering following a linear relationship. Any signs of deviations from linearity are observable only at very high redshifts, greater than ten, indicating that for most applications with a redshift range of 10 to a few thousand, PBHs' linear bias can be safely assumed. The team is now working on expanding the scope of Primordial Black Hole dark energy simulations using the PopSyCLE code.

In an experiment involving the rotation of rigid, wedge-shaped particles within a confined, narrow channel made of cylindrical sections, our focus was on the two-sided static ordering of these particles. The findings revealed that the wedge-shaped particles adopted a quasiperiodic arrangement with an irregularly increasing and decreasing pattern along the channel's height as the density of these particles exceeded a particular critical point. This critical point occurred when the volume occupied by each particle in the wedge surpassed a certain threshold value, which corresponded to a particular number of segments within this channel. Additionally, our data indicated that the wedge-shaped particles exhibited random motion within this channel when their density fell below this critical point, while their motion transitioned into a slow, spreading process once this critical point was exceeded. Furthermore, our results showed that the wedge-shaped particles exhibited random motion within this channel when their density fell below this critical point, while their motion transitioned into a slow, spreading process once this critical point was exceeded.

Recent breakthroughs in large language models have revealed their potential to process tasks beyond their initial scope, yet they often fail to excel in smaller-scale experiments due to computational constraints. A key LLM limitation arises from unique token handling, particularly embeddings for uncommon words, which can be overcome by applying parameter adjustment. However, fine-tuning an LLM in this manner typically demands a full retraining, a resource-intensive endeavor that hinders efficient small-data processing. To address this challenge, we propose unique token adaptation with partial adaptation, a more efficient method that adjusts only relevant layers and token embeddings while leaving other components unchanged. Additionally, we introduce two potential settings for implementing partial adaptation: (1) unique token adjustment with full adaptation of other layers, which offers improved performance but higher computational costs, and (2) unique token adjustment with partial adaptation of all layers, which reduces computational costs while still providing effective results. A comparative analysis was conducted on the Google QARO dataset containing 348 tasks for various small-data processing scenarios and our proposed method, demonstrating that unique token adaptation with partial adaptation outperforms unique token adjustment with full adaptation of other layers.

The problem of adding items to a set, fundamental in various fields, has been addressed from a perspective that focuses on the properties of the added items relative to the existing set. Unlike the conventional approach that relies on numerical ratings and non-contextual comparisons, our method utilizes a preference ordering that is more intuitive and relevant to the core problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the new approach through two real-world applications showing its superiority over the conventional method. Experimental results reveal that our approach yields more accurate model structures and better performance. Thorough testing has been undertaken to evaluate the scalability of our model, yielding findings that indicate its parameter learning capabilities and prediction accuracy can be effectively determined with relatively small datasets.

Our investigation explores thermodynamic and dynamic relationships in the context of glass formation, using the example of polycarbonate melts. From an extensive dataset obtained through experiments and simulations, we examine how thermal energy variation impacts the dynamics and structure of these melts. The examined properties include mean squared displacement, dynamic structural parameter, and potential energy, as well as the relationships between these properties and viscosity and the configurational entropy. Notably, we found that dynamic structural parameters are insensitive to temperature but highly correlated with viscosity and configurational entropy. Meanwhile, the behavior of viscosity and configurational entropy in response to varying temperature follows a similar pattern to that observed in other glass models, with different dynamics at higher and lower temperatures. The findings from this research can be applied to other glass-forming liquids to provide a framework for predicting the dynamics and structure of these melts in response to different thermal histories.

Childhood is marked by an unrelenting onslaught of sensory inputs as kids learn to navigate their environment through exploration, relying heavily on language to understand the world around them. This innovative research assigns a central role to denial - a fundamental emotion present throughout childhood - as the foundation of cognitive development. We interpret denial as an initial reaction to unfamiliar events and view it as the first line of defense in processing new information. Based on this concept, we've created two new neural networks. The first network is the Denial-Transformer, which incorporates denial as an integral step in its information processing mechanisms. For each input word, the system simultaneously generates two separate outputs - one indicating the probability of the fact being true, and another denoting the confidence level of that fact. The second network is the Confusion-Triple Transformer, which integrates denial as an additional mechanism. For every input word, the system generates three separate outputs - one indicating the probability of the fact being true, one denoting the degree of confusion, and another indicating the degree of rejection. We conducted an experimental analysis of both networks using a multi-step fine-tuning process, and our results show that both networks effectively capture facts that are subject to doubt or rejection. We observed that the Denial-Transformer is more efficient than the standard Transformer and is on par or even outperforms the Contextual Transformer. In the context of neural machine translation, the attention model is widely regarded
as responsible for the progress made in state-of-the-art performance. Yet, the way
this widely used component is implemented differs significantly in numerous ways
depending on the specific model being employed. For instance, the most commonly
used look-back attention model, which enables the decoder to draw upon encoder
details in a sequential order, is in contrast to the look-forward attention approach
developed by the Google team, which allows the decoder to make use of decoder
information in addition to the encoder details. In this research, the look-forward
attention model has been further developed to the extent that it only relies on the
encoder details, effectively omitting any reference to the decoder details. In
order to achieve this, the research implements a novel yet simplified regularization
method that eliminates any reference to the decoder details. The results obtained
from this research demonstrate that look-forward attention models perform comparably
or superiorly to look-back attention models when tested within numerous benchmark
scenarios in both English-German and English-French translation tasks. Furthermore,
the results indicate look-forward attention models display better resilience in the
event of adversarial modifications being made to the source or target text.

This passage outlines a method for calculating the weights of Kontsevich graphs that arise from a particular point in two different types of symplectic manifolds: manifolds with Poisson symplectic structures and star product manifolds. Earlier research by the third author found a unique formula for determining these weights in a specific star product manifold that results from a particular deformation of a manifold's standard Poisson structure. Conversely, our research focuses on the weights in the context of all symplectic structures and establishes a new formula for a general deformation of a standard Poisson structure on any closed manifold. By applying our research to specific cases, we are able to derive precise calculations for the weights in certain point deformations of hyperboloid and paraboloid manifolds. Additionally, our research reveals that the weights are identical for star product manifolds and their point deformations corresponding to specific symplectic structures. Further investigation of these symplectic structures could potentially produce new soliton solutions for certain noncommutative geometries.

Calabrese, Kohnle, and Serafini previously found in their study that for certain types of 2D holographic models, thermal entropy diverges at zero temperature. A similar relationship also exists for non-holographic models, with large N determinants for scalar fields also experiencing divergent thermal entropy at zero temperature. This phenomenon shares similarities with the behavior of entanglement entropy in similar types of models, leading us to suggest that thermal entropy and entanglement entropy must always be proportional, even considering possible contributions from terms of lower order than N^2. This new hypothesis is supported by a large N expansion that includes all types of possible interactions. Moreover, when exploring the relationship between thermal entropy, entanglement entropy, and the channel capacity, we discovered that channel capacity provides an upper limit for the ratio of thermal entropy to entanglement entropy. This limit is particularly significant in the case of free models, where thermal entropy and entanglement entropy are always in proportion, but may potentially experience significant deviations for models with interactions, albeit at lower orders than N^2.

This discussion challenges specific numerical techniques and theoretical underpinnings outlined in the paper "A Comprehensive Framework for Valuing Asian Options Under Markov Processes" and highlights potential issues with these methods. It specifically takes issue with the use of partial sums charactertized by negative martingale differences, the applicability of the optional stopping theorem for Asian options, the accuracy of quadrature methods, and the presence of a nonnegative Asian option price lattice, among other concerns. These criticisms aim to provide a more complete understanding of Asian options pricing.

Our research aims to identify the primary source responsible for the widespread gamma-ray emission observed in galaxy clusters. By analyzing the Fermi Large Area Telescope's data, we have found that a vast number of galaxy clusters exhibit significant gamma-ray flux. This observation cannot be attributed to any known radiative processes utilized by cosmic rays. On the other hand, cosmic rays interacting with the hot cluster medium may potentially explain the gamma-ray emission through established theoretical models. These interactions also produce antiparticles in quantities anticipated to be detected in forthcoming experiments.

The primes are inextricably linked with the universe's fundamental nature, and their characteristics are engraved onto its large-scale structure, which is revealed through the distribution of their roots. Modern number theory's significant breakthroughs open the door for exploring primals as a representation of the universe's primary ingredients. This concept of "primal features" has the potential to be the foundation of a novel theoretical framework. This article discusses how, in the early universe, primals are generated through quantum collisions, which are typical features, but before these primals are produced, there is a primordial stage characterized by primals without features, referred to as "primals without memory" or "primeval primals." The memory of these primeval primals is related to the universe's fundamental fact, and their average is associated with the logarithm of the primals' generating function. If primals with memory are considered as the manifestation of the universe's features, then primals without memory can be thought of as a fundamental form of "featuring field," governing the process of features generation. This article shows that during the cosmological scale factor of $a$, featuring fields are characterized by an IR action of $G\sim (Pa)^{n_*}$. Despite the remarkable performance of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), their underlying structure is shrouded in mystery. Consequently, it is challenging for CNN developers and users to determine the specific part of the network that is malfunctioning, whether it be a sub-network or a single component. This study addresses this issue by introducing the hidden visual-semantic filter attention mechanism, which aims to uncover the hidden workings of CNNs by pinpointing the most critical filters in relation to the given input. Uniquely, our proposed mechanism does not necessitate any external annotations during training and is capable of handling various CNN architectures with relative ease. Furthermore, it can be used to extract interpretable visual features from a network. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism through our experiments, which demonstrate its ability to not only reveal the internal workings of CNNs but also serve as an efficient tool for a range of tasks, such as image classification, object detection, and segmentation.

Research into the physical properties of one-dimensional cuprate prototypes, represented by the compound CuCh$_4$ (Ch = Si, Ge, Sn), shows that they exhibit exceptional interaction-dependent conductivity variability and highly adaptable properties. Detailed heat capacity measurements for CuSnCh and one-dimensional CuCh compounds revealed unusually large phonon-related contributions, while also showing that the system's long-distance interactions between d$_{x y}$-doped holes are significantly enhanced by these phonon effects. Furthermore, these findings were supported by the results of theoretical simulations using the Monte Carlo method. It has been discovered that the system's low-temperature attractive interaction can cause local charge bunching, enhancing conductivity through increased carrier density in the system. Notably, the theoretical simulations also confirmed that the system's phonon-related contributions surpass those seen in one-dimensional systems at lower temperatures.
